This place went out and bought its law, deliberately, every decade since it was chartered, meaning to have the lot. The compilations from before the standardization. The directive itself, with its drafting papers. Forty years of consolidations. Every commentary anybody ever wrote about any of it." She took a breath. "I've spent six months on four lines of one clause. Those two floors hold bay after bay. Four of them hold the very decades my clause comes from."

"How long to read them?"

"Properly?" She made it sound like a banquet. "Years. Years and years."

"You sound pleased."

"Cael." She looked at him with complete seriousness. "Every place I've ever been let in, I've read to the back wall. Do you understand? Every library I've ever been let into, I came to the end of. Dellenmoor. Greyvane. Prynn's, very nearly, and Prynn's was the best." She laid her palm on the document. "Today somebody gave me a place I can't come to the end of. Not in the time I've got. I don't think anybody's ever given me anything better."

Lira had come in at the door partway through and stood leaning on the frame with her arms folded, listening. She did not come further in.

"You argued them down," she said.

"I read them their own charter." Karis looked round at her. "It isn't the same thing. Arguing makes people dig in. Reading them their own clause makes them look for the door."

"I'll remember that." Lira said it lightly, but Cael saw her look at the document on the table for a moment longer than she needed to, at the three terms in Bracken's small upright hand, written down, initialled, unamendable by a bad week. Then she pushed off the doorframe. "Practice register's out. I'm eight and nil."

"Eight?" said Brom, sitting up.

"A Mire third-year. He tried to make the floor sticky." She was already going. "It didn't stick."

Karis watched her go, and then turned back to Cael, and her face had gone careful again.

"Three terms," she said. "One for me. Two for the work. And one for you, really, though it's got my name on it." She folded the document along its crease. "You'd better start keeping a list of everything I write on you, so if Bracken's cabinet ever burns down we'll know what was in it."

"You're joking."

"Half," said Karis. "Write the list anyway."

Chapter 11 — Silence on the Skin

[Observant, controlled narration; keep status, leverage, and friendship legible beneath the travel]

The key was still on its nail.

He had walked past it most days for a month, on the path behind the assessment wing that ran down to the low hall, and every time he had looked at it and every time he had left it alone. It hung beside the door on a square iron nail at the height of his shoulder, a plain black key on a loop of leather gone shiny with handling, and the door it belonged to was locked from the outside. He had written both facts down on his first morning on the bluff, and underlined them, and had not been able to think of a single reason for either.

He had not touched it, either. That had been a rule of his own, made on the first morning without quite deciding to make it. A key left out on a nail was an invitation of some kind, and he did not take invitations he could not read. At Greyvane he had learned what it cost to walk through a door because it happened to be open, and he had learned it in front of a panel. So the key had hung there for five weeks, and he had walked past it, and looked at it, and the question had grown a little heavier every time.

On the thirty-third morning he asked the porter, who was sitting on an upturned pail outside the wash-house cleaning the Copper Crown's case-key with a rag and some ash.

"Hers," the porter told the case-key in his hands. "The low hall's hers."

"Whose?"

"Lattice." The porter breathed on the key and rubbed. "There's one instructor teaches it on this hill, and nine students learn it, and that's her hall and nobody else's. Thirty-one years she's had it. She had the lock put on the outside her first year." He held the key up to the light and squinted at it. "You want to go in, you take the key down off the nail. You knock. You wait. If she wants you, she opens it from the inside with her own key, and you hang hers back up. If she doesn't want you, she doesn't open it, and you hang hers back up anyway and go away."

"Why the key outside, then? If she opens it from in?"

The porter looked up at him for perhaps the first time since Cael had come to the bluff, briefly, with a kind of patient pity.

"So you have to stop," he said. "So you've got a key in your hand and a door in front of you and you can't just walk through. Lattice builds things in the air, lad. Lines. You can't see them, mostly, unless the light's right. You walk into a hall where somebody's halfway through building one, you find out where it was with your face." He went back to his rag. "Took a first-year's front tooth, the year before the lock. She's never forgiven herself. Nor him, for running."

"Is she in my eight?" said Cael, before he could stop himself.

"Your what?"

"Nothing." It had come out without his leave. The porter was the third line on the standing list, and had no idea he was on it, and would have found it very odd to be told. "Thank you."

The porter grunted and went back to his rag without asking what an eight might be. He had the incurious patience of a man who had carried every trunk on the bluff and had stopped wondering, years ago, what was in any of them.

It stayed with Cael all morning.

He had watched the Lattice pupils four times, always from too far off: twice in the north hall, where two of them sometimes worked at the far end under a high window, and twice from the Crown yard's tiers, during practice afternoons, when a Lattice third-year had fought on the Copper rings. Every time he had come away with a page he did not trust; at forty yards, Lattice looked like nobody doing anything. The practitioners moved very little. Their opponents moved a great deal, and then stopped moving, and stood looking puzzled, or stepped carefully to one side round nothing Cael could see. He had a page headed Lattice in the observation notebook with a column of lines under it, and every one of them was a guess, and he had marked them all as guesses.

He did not want another guess; he wanted to stand next to one.

So at the change of bell after noon, when the halls emptied and filled again, he went down the path behind the assessment wing, took the key off the nail, and knocked.

Nothing happened for long enough for him to begin turning the key over in his fingers, wondering whether this was a refusal. He did not hang it back. The porter had not said how long to wait, and a rule that did not say how long usually meant longer than you thought.

Then the lock turned from the inside, and the door opened a hand's width, and an old woman looked out at him.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

She was small and very upright, past sixty, in a grey wool dress with the sleeves pinned back above the elbow, and she had the stillest hands he had ever seen on anybody. They hung at her sides as if they had been set down there and told to wait. She looked at him, and at the key in his fingers, and at him again.

"Hang it up," she said.

He hung it on its nail, and the door swung wide.

The low hall was one room, low-ceilinged as its name, with its windows set very high along one wall, so the light came down in long slanting bars and lay across the floor in stripes. The floor was plain stone, swept bare. Two pupils were standing in the middle of it, a fifth-year girl with her hair in a tight knot and a younger boy, and both of them had stopped where they were when the knock came, and had not moved since. Along the back wall a row of pegs held nine grey practice smocks, one for each student of the Path on the bluff, with a name stitched over each peg in blue thread. Below them the stone had been scored with fine straight lines, dozens of them, crossing and recrossing, like the marks a joiner leaves on a bench where he has measured the same cut a thousand times.

The boy looked at Cael with open curiosity and then, catching the instructor's eye, looked hastily at the floor.

"You're the provision," said the Lattice instructor.

"Yes, Magistra."

"I don't take the title." She did not explain. "What do you want?"

He had thought about how to answer that on the path down. He had thought about several answers that were true and short and did not say very much, and he had decided against all of them, because he did not think this woman would let him in on any of them.

"I read pressure," he said. "On the skin. A pace and a half out, I can feel where a weight is and which way it's going, a fraction before it gets there. It works on everything I've ever stood near." He kept his eyes on hers. "I've never stood near Lattice. I'd like to, while somebody builds, if you'll allow it. I want to know what I feel."

Her face gave him nothing whatever.

"Why?"

"Because if it doesn't work on Lattice, I'd rather learn that here," said Cael, "than on a floor where it matters."

Her mouth moved, very slightly.

"Stand there," she said, and pointed with one still finger at a place on the stone a pace and a half from the fifth-year. "Do not move from it. Do not put out a hand. If you feel anything you want to tell me about, tell me afterward, not during." She turned to the girl. "Three points. Quarter speed. Count it so he can follow."

The girl glanced at Cael once, without curiosity, and lifted her hands.

She built slowly, as she had been told, and she counted under her breath while she did it, a low murmur like somebody reciting a lesson. "One, and set." Her right hand closed in the air a little above the height of her shoulder, as if she had taken hold of a thread hanging there. "Two, and set." Her left hand closed lower and farther out, almost level with Cael's forearm. "Draw." Between the two hands, for an instant, as she moved her head, he saw it: a line in the air, finer than a hair, catching one of the slanting bars of window light the way the strand of a web catches light in a hedge in the early morning, and then gone again when the light moved off it.

"Three, and set."

Her right foot slid forward a hand's width on the stone, and her right hand came down and closed at the height of her hip, and he knew without seeing it that the third line had joined the other two, because the air in the place in front of him had become, somehow, a place. He had no account of how he knew it. There was nothing to see. But the space between her three closed hands, eighteen inches from his own forearm, was no longer only air, and he would have staked a great deal on its being something he could not walk through.

The read gave him nothing.

It did not give him a little; it was not thin, the way it went thin at the edge of its pace and a half, or uncertain, the way it went uncertain when two weights arrived at once and he had to choose between them. It gave him exactly what it gave him standing alone in an empty corridor at night. Quiet. The ordinary quiet of his own forearms with nothing near them.

A thing had been built eighteen inches from his skin that could have shut off two of his ways out, and the instrument he had trusted for two years above his own eyes had not stirred.

He stood very still on his place on the stone, as he had been told, and found his mouth had gone dry. It was not fear of the frame. The frame was a lesson, built at quarter speed by a girl who did not care whether he lived or died, and it would go when she let it go. It was something colder and slower than fear, rising from underneath, the feeling of a man who has walked the same path in the dark every night for two years and has just been shown, by daylight, a well at the side of it that he never knew was there.

[Observant, controlled narration; keep status, leverage, and friendship legible beneath the travel]

"Again," he said, when it was over. "Please. With my eyes shut."

The instructor considered him.

"Why shut?"

"Because I saw the line. Once, in the light." He kept his voice level. "I want to know whether the read is quiet on its own, or whether I'm only noticing it's quiet because my eyes are louder."

She nodded to the girl, and the girl let her frame go. It went without any sound or sign at all; he only knew it had gone because the place in front of him stopped being a place. Then she built it again, counting, and he stood with his eyes shut and his whole attention on the skin of his forearms and the back of his neck and the line of his jaw, where the read always came, and it did not come. One, and set. Two, and set. Draw. Three, and set. Nothing. He opened his eyes on a finished frame he still could not see and felt the hair stand up along his arms, not from anything the read had given him, but from the plain fact of its having given him nothing.

"May I touch it?"

"One finger," said the instructor. "Slowly. Where she tells you."

The girl pointed with her chin at a place between her two upper hands. Cael put out his right forefinger, very slowly, toward empty air.

It stopped.

There had been no warning, and that was the thing. His finger was moving, and then it was not, and nothing had arrived on his skin before it stopped: no pressure building, no weight in the air, none of the early signs the read had always laid on him a fraction ahead of a strike. It was not like pushing against a wall, which pushed back. It was more like a sentence arriving at its full stop. His finger had simply been forbidden to go further, and was not going further, and that was all.

"You're listening for a push," said the Lattice instructor.

He looked round at her.

"Every other Path on this bluff is a push of some kind. Force is a push. Blade is a push sharpened. Stone is a push that refuses to move." Her hands still hung quite motionless at her sides. "A frame doesn't push. It forbids. There is nothing moving in it for you to feel. You may as well listen for the weight of a law."

He took his finger back; it tingled faintly.

He stood a while longer looking at the place where he knew the frame was, and then, because the read was still quiet and would go on being quiet, he did the only other thing he could think of. He let the frame go and read the girl.

"Again," he said. "Once more. Please."

She built it again, and this time he felt it. Not the frame. Her. As she said one, and set, her weight went forward over her right foot by the width of a finger, and the read laid that on his forearm, small and clear. On two, it went a little back and left. On three, as her foot slid forward on the stone, it went forward again and down. Each time she set a point, her body paid for it with a small shift of balance, and her body was a weight like any other weight, and the read could feel a weight.

"Nothing from the frame," he said slowly. "But I can feel her setting it. Each point, she moves. Not much."

The girl's face went faintly pink, which was the first thing it had done since he came in.

"Yes," said the Lattice instructor. She sounded, if anything, mildly pleased with him, or perhaps with the girl. "Most of my pupils spend their first two years learning to set a point without moving anything else. Most of them never quite manage it." She glanced at the fifth-year. "She very nearly has."

"She'll have it out of me by the year's end," said the girl, unexpectedly, in a dry low voice, to nobody in particular.

"By the year's end," the instructor agreed. She turned back to Cael. "So you will be able to read her until then, a little. You will be able to read the other eight a little longer than that. You will never read me." She said it without boasting, as a plain fact about the weather. "Hang the key on your way out."

He thanked her. She inclined her head about the width of a finger, which he gathered was a great deal, and turned back to her pupils before he had reached the door.

Outside, the noon light was very bright after the striped dimness of the low hall. He hung the key on its nail and stood with his hand still on the leather loop, looking at it. A month he had walked past it, and a month it had been hanging there, at the height of his shoulder, offering him the plainest piece of information on the whole bluff, and he had left it alone because he could not read the invitation. The invitation had been perfectly simple. Stop. Knock. Wait. Caution had hidden it from him.

Behind the door he heard the girl begin to count again, low and steady. One, and set. He went back up the path before he could hear the second.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

At the desk by the window that night he put the frightening part first, so he could not soften it by getting there slowly.

Low hall, thirty-third day. The read and Lattice: nothing. I don't mean faint. I mean the quiet I get alone on a stair at night, while a girl built, twice, a thing eighteen inches from my arm that could have pinned me where I stood.

Guess, unproven: the read only knows weight on the move. A frame is three held points and the shape between them. No weight travels in it. So there's nothing there for the read to find, and it finds nothing.

And it said nothing about finding nothing. That's what I want in big letters.

He pressed harder than he needed to on the next part.

When a tool breaks with a noise, you learn where its edges are and keep your hands off them. When it breaks without one, it isn't broken. It's lying, and it lies in the same calm voice it uses for the truth. I've leaned on this one in the dark, in crowds, with my back to doors, for two years. Today it went blind to an entire Path and stayed perfectly calm about it.

Nine people on this bluff build frames. And half the Paths this hill teaches I've never been close to. Some of them it can't see. I won't know which until I'm beside them, and perhaps not even then, unless somebody tells me something's there.

From today: the surface read's silence is not information. Every quiet is an unknown. Every floor, every time.

That last line held him a long while after he had sat back.

Then he did something he had done perhaps four times since Denvash, each time for a thing he could not afford to be without. He took out the observation notebook, opened it to the Halcenvane section, and wrote the rule out again, word for word, on its own page. Whichever book he had in his hand from now on, the rule would be in it.

Correction, to try again: read the builder, not the build. The frame gives nothing, but the person setting it is a weight. Each point costs them a small shift of balance. A pupil still pays it. A master doesn't. So this works against the young and the unfinished, and against nobody else, and it gets worse every year they train.

Price of the correction: reading her body tells me where she set each point, roughly, and when. What the points add up to, it can't say. Three points could be a wall, or a corner, or a door with one side open, and from her weight alone I can't tell which. So even against a pupil I'm reading the hands of a man who's writing, not the letter. Better than nothing. Much less than I'm used to.

Two hidden things this month. The floor that was in my prices. The silence that was in my read. Both of them were in there all along, and I never looked, because I had no reason to think they were there.

Go on looking for the third.

Sleep was a long time coming.

He lay in the dark and went back, as he had not been able to stop himself going back, through every time in two years the read had been quiet and he had taken the quiet as clear. The back stair at the boarding house in Ardenmere, which he had climbed a hundred nights without a lamp because his forearms told him it was empty. The corridor outside the archive at Greyvane, the evening the Compact's officer had walked its length with his cases. The yard behind the residence wing, in the dark before the first bell, where he had turned and turned on frozen stone with his back to the gate. He had trusted all three silences, and every one of them, as it happened, had been empty. But he had not known it. He had only felt nothing, and called the nothing knowledge, and gone on.

He thought, too, of the eleven supervisors and their careful silences. That quiet, too, he had come close to filing as an answer. It was not one. A silence that had been arranged was not the same thing as a room with nobody in it, and he had been very close to forgetting the difference.

Rule, second half: the same goes for people.

He got up in the end, lit the lamp again, and wrote one more line under the rest, smaller, because he wanted it there in the morning when the fright had worn off and he would be tempted to think he had made too much of it.

It was empty every time. That's luck, not knowledge. Don't confuse the two again.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

On the thirty-fifth evening, five weeks from the gate to the day, the wall behind the second quadrangle held all four of them at dusk, each at some private work, and Cael had the binder open on the coping.

At the far end, where an old hitching post stood up out of the turf, Brom was turning nothing at all, as slowly as he knew how. Rooke had given him the post two days before, and the instruction with it, and the instruction was simple and cruel. Brom was to turn nothing until he was certain it was real. He was to stand at the post, and Karis or Lira or Cael would come at him with feeds, honest ones and empty ones mixed, and he was to let every empty one go by without so much as a twitch, and turn only the honest ones. Everything he had built, it ran backward. Tonight it was Lira feeding, from in front of the post, her hands flat, and every third feed she sold was empty, and Brom turned on two of every three of them anyway, and groaned at himself, and went back to the post.

"Worse," he said cheerfully, after one of them. "I'm definitely worse. Write that down."

"I'm writing it down," said Cael.

Cael had taken his turn at the feeds before supper and had found it harder than he expected. To sell Brom an empty strike he had to mean it nearly all the way, with his weight and his breath and his eyes, and then take it back; and Brom, who had known him two years, believed every one, because Cael had never once in two years lied to him on a floor. It had felt very strange to do it on purpose. Brom had not minded at all; again, he had said, every time, beaming. That one got me properly.

Along the flat top of the wall Karis had laid out four documents from carrel eleven to catch the evening light, with a smooth stone on each corner against the river wind. She was reading the third, very slowly, with her finger on the line. Now and then a single word left her, addressed to nobody, and went into the margin.

Lira gave Brom one more empty feed, watched him fail to let it go, and then came and leaned beside Cael on the coping with her eyes on the water. Down at the ferry landing the two grey coats were standing under their lamp, and she watched them.

"Ten past," she said. "They're late changing."

"Are they?"

"Ten minutes." Lira's eyes stayed on them. "First time in a month. Write that down too."

He did. Then, because it had been sitting on him all day, he told Brom about the low hall.

Brom came away from the post and listened with his wraps hanging loose from his hands. When Cael got to the part about the frame and the quiet, he frowned, and turned his right forearm over and looked at the inside of it, the way he looked at it after a fall.

"Mine's the same, then," he said slowly. "If yours came from me. Mine'd be blind to her as well."

"I don't know. I've never seen yours near a Lattice."

"Nor have I." Brom considered his forearm with deep suspicion. "Two years I've been telling you it's the best thing I own." He wound the wrap back up. "I'll ask Rooke. He'll know. He knows everything and tells you a quarter of it."

"Ask him what he does about it," said Cael.

"I'll ask him that too." Brom went back to the post. "He'll say, watch. He says that about everything."

There was no complaint in it. It sounded like a man quoting a cook whose bread had begun, against all his expectations, to rise.

Cael bent over the binder.

Five weeks. Four of us, on four roads.

Brom: a man warned him he'd be made worse, and is making him worse, as promised, and I've never seen Brom so glad of anything.

Lira: nine bouts, nine wins, in a register half the bluff reads with a pencil in hand, and still nothing in it can climb as high as her certificate.

Karis: a key, a seam of law with no back wall, and three terms on paper that keep her work in a cabinet and off the shelves.

Me: a named category, the finest boards I've stood on, half the bluff's Paths still out of reach, a read caught lying this week, and no line anywhere.

It had taken five weeks to be able to put the next part down. He put it down.

Four of us, four doors, all real. A year ago none of us could have walked through any of them. Worth writing down on the days it doesn't feel like enough.

He closed the binder. Behind him, at the post, Brom turned on another empty feed, groaned, and laughed at himself, and Lira went back to give him the next.

Chapter 12 — Doctrine

[Observant, controlled narration; keep status, leverage, and friendship legible beneath the travel]

Karis read the clause to him in carrel eleven with her finger under each word, the way Vell had once taught him to read a ledger, and on the fourth line she stopped.

"There," she said. "That's the part nobody tells you."

He leaned over her shoulder. It was Halcenvane's own copy of the founding clause, with the charter article that carried it set out beneath, and below that the assessment office's standing rule for applying it, in a dry modern hand. He had read all three before, on the first night, and again in Bracken's room, and again on the night the notice came. He had not read them the way Karis read things, which was as if each word had been put there by somebody who might be lying.

The demonstration so made shall stand as the measure of record for the enrollee, and every subsequent demonstration shall be laid against it.

"Laid against," said Karis. "Like a rule against a plank. A plank isn't measured by its length. You measure it by how far it is from the mark." She took her finger off the line. "The office doesn't ask whether you're good. Not once, anywhere in this. It asks whether you're the same as you were, and then whether you're more. That's all a semester evaluation is. The old line, and the new line, and the distance between them."

"So the first line is everything."

"The first line is the only one you get to draw yourself." She sat back in her chair. "Every one after that is drawn by the first."

He walked back to the second quadrangle in the dusk with that sentence turning in his head, and for three nights afterward he slept badly.

It was not the room he feared; he had stood before two hundred people with the Compact's warden at the other table and read a schedule back to them page by page, and no room of instruments could be worse than that. It was the arithmetic: every practitioner on every board had been set down by an Arbiter at fourteen and handed a number. He was being handed a pen, and whatever he drew with it on the day would go into a folder in Gault's cabinet and stay there. One day an inspector would take it out, with a grudge or only with a schedule, and read it on a table, or aloud in a hearing room. Choose with that in mind, Bracken had said, holding out the tag on its cord. Cael had nodded at the time. He was only now beginning to.

By the third night he could see the two ways to cheat it, one low and one high, and he could see neither was right, and he could not yet see what was.

He put it to the others on the fourth evening, in the common room, because three nights alone with it had taught him he was carrying it badly.

Brom was cheerful on the floor with fresh ice on his shoulder, because Ephram had found a new hole in him that afternoon. Lira had her knees drawn up on the window seat. Karis was quarrelling in pencil with a fair copy of the clause.

He gave them the low line first, since it was the one he was ashamed of wanting, and he wanted it out on the table where they could all see it. Show less than he had, carefully, just enough to satisfy the provision; then let the rest out a little each semester and have it written down as growth. Years of easy evaluations, and room to hide in.

"It's comfortable," he said. "That's the trouble with it. Comfortable for years, and then one day not, and all at once." He held up a finger. "Three costs. One: the line's a document. It goes into the file in Gault's hand, and one day an inspector opens the file. Bracken's warned me twice, and Withrow wrote sooner on her sheet with her own pen. Find a feeble line in there and you've found proof the provision lets feeble people in. Somebody uses that against the provision, and I've lost the only floor I stand on."

"Two," said Karis, still in her pencil.

"Two, it runs out." Another finger. "What I've held back is a fixed sum. Spend it as growth, a bit each semester, and one day I'll need to grow for real and find the purse empty. The requirement never stops. Every semester, no exceptions; that's the record I signed."

"Three," said Brom, from the floor.

Cael looked at him.

"You'd have to stand there while he wrote it down," said Brom. He was mild about it, easing the ice along his shoulder. "In his own room. Him being straight with you, and you knowing what you'd left out, and him thanking you for it." He looked up. "I couldn't do that. Not to somebody being straight with me. I'd go red, like you did over the registrar."

There was a short silence.

"And it's a lie," said Cael quietly. "Written down. In the one file I went into a hearing room to get made honest."

The high line took less time, because everybody in the room already knew why it could not be done. He could not show everything. Showing everything meant Pressure, which nobody had ever seen him use, and Compression, which nobody had ever seen at all, and the Ember on a floor in front of a faculty panel, and every one of them was a question with a door behind it that he could not open, and the door behind all the doors was the thing only the four of them knew.

"Low is a lie, then," he said, "and honest can't be done. That's the choice."

"It isn't the choice," said Lira.

They all looked round. She had not moved from the window seat.

"Low or honest, you keep saying. Those aren't the two." She said it calmly. "Three years you've kept things in your pocket on every floor we've stood on. Choosing what goes out and what stays in. I was there for all of it. I never once thought of it as lying, and neither did you."

"That was leaving things unsaid. This is writing a figure against my own name and putting my signature under it."

"It's picking from what's already been said about you." She swung her feet down off the seat. "Out loud, on paper, in public, by people who weren't you. The stationer in Ostrand will sell anybody a copy for six silver. Tell me what's in it."

He could have recited it. Fourteen of Greyvane's monthly sittings had been read into the hearing as exhibits, one after another, and every one of them, under three assessors' names, had said the same two things about him: that he could get out of the way with the Wind, and that he could feel a weight coming before it came. A court had looked at those two and filed them where anybody could find them. Nothing else about how he was made had ever been put where the world could read it, except the Ember, and that only in a single late exhibit, half a page, so thin that showing it on Gault's floor would not confirm anything. It would announce something. Of Pressure and Compression it said nothing.

"Two," he said.

"Then show them those two." Lira leaned forward with her elbows on her knees. "All of them. Not most. Not the safe amount. Every bit you've got, in those two and nowhere else." She held his eyes. "A low line's a lie about you. This is the plain truth about the boy in that transcript. And when you're better in a semester's time, which you will be, because you're fifteen and it'll happen whether you want it or not, you'll be better in exactly the places they're already watching."

Cael was silent a good while.

"That's it," he said.

"I know."

"You've known for days."

"Four days." Lira stood up and stretched until her shoulders cracked. "If I'd said it then you'd have spent the four days finding what was wrong with it, and then argued it out with yourself in front of Gault, halfway through a trial." She paused at the door. "And don't go writing this down as me managing you. That's how you work. I've had three years to learn it."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

That night it went into the binder under method. Lira, he thought, would accept that.

Baseline doctrine. Two capabilities are on the public record. Those two I show at full stretch, with nothing kept back inside either. Everything the record doesn't hold stays held.

Not the low line. Not the whole of me either. It's as much of the public boy as there is. Sworn, and asked if it was fair to the record: yes, at once, with no pause for a clerk to time.

Cost: it hems me in. From now on every semester has to grow those two and only those two, or explain itself. The way through gets tighter each time.

In return: a path I could defend in a hearing room, and I've been inside those rooms. Narrow and defensible beats wide.

He slept, after that, for the first time in four nights, and woke at the fifth bell with his mind quite clear and one thing still sitting in it.

Every bit you've got, in those two. He lay looking at the words in his head, and found he did not know how much that was. He knew his ceiling: four free bursts on timber now, and the fifth to pay. He knew the read's distance and its limits, and one new limit he had found in the low hall. But he had spent three years learning to show three-quarters of everything, on every floor, as a habit, the way a man who has been poor a long time goes on eating half his bread and saving the rest even after he has money. No panel had ever seen the whole of anything from him, and he was no longer sure he knew how to show it.

He told Karis about the Ember the next morning, in carrel eleven, because it was hers before it was his and he did not want her to hear it from the table.

"I'm leaving it out," he said. "The exhibit's thin. If I show it, it's news, not confirmation."

Karis went on copying for a moment. Then she put her pen down and laid both hands flat on the desk, the way she did when she had decided something.

"Good," she said.

"You don't mind?"

"I mind a great deal, in a way that has nothing to do with whether you're right." She looked at him then, and her face was quite steady. "Of everything anybody's ever taken from me, that's the one I was glad to give. I'd like it to stay in our book a while longer before it goes into anybody else's. Gault's included." She picked up the pen again. "That's sentiment, not law. Ignore it if it ever matters. It doesn't matter yet."

He had two supervised sessions left before the day, if the day came when he thought it would. He used them both.

In the first, under a Shield instructor who crossed over at the twelfth minute, he ran the framework at its full pace against nobody, alone on the east hall's timber, and made himself go all the way through every burst instead of easing off at the end, and found he had been easing off at the end for so long it felt like falling. In the second, under a Mire Path instructor who had never supervised him and plainly resented the hour, he stood at the edge of the floor with his eyes shut while two second-years threw practice weights at the boards in front of him, and called the weight and the line of each before it landed. He was right about all of them. It was harder than it had any right to be, because he was trying, for the first time in years, to let the read be as good as it was.

The Mire instructor watched the whole of the second session with her arms folded and her mouth turned down, and crossed over, like everybody, at about the fourteenth minute. But she did one thing none of the others had done. At the end, signing his sheet, she asked the second-years which weights they had thrown, and checked his calls against their answers, one by one, with her pen. They all matched, and she let that pass unremarked. She only signed, and gave him the sheet, and went out. He wrote her into the margin of the supervisors' list with a small mark beside her name: checks.

The notice came on the forty-sixth morning, in his pigeonhole, two days before the day, as the first one had said it would.

The assessment office will receive the entry demonstration of the assay-provision enrollee on the forty-eighth day, at the third bell, in the demonstration room of the assessment wing. Magister Gault presiding. The enrollee will present himself at the near door.

He read it standing in the cloister, and found he was not afraid of it any longer. What he was instead had no name yet. It was a little like the moment on the mark before Edran, when he had found a question was steadier to stand on than an answer.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The night before, Lira took him out to the cracked yard behind the second quadrangle, where nobody went after dark, and made him walk the framework through once at a stroll, with no bursts in it at all.

"Not to practise," she said. "You've practised. Just so your feet know where they're going in the morning."

They walked it through together, slowly, in the starlight. The stone was uneven, like the yard at Greyvane, and she had chosen it for that. When they were done she did not go in. She sat down on the step of the wash-house with her arms round her knees, and after a moment he sat beside her.

"Fenmark," she said, out of nowhere. "When I was fourteen."

He waited. She had told him about Fenmark once, on a road, in the dark, and never again.

"The Arbiter took about a minute and a half." Her eyes were on the wall's dark bulk, not on him. "It came, and I saw it, and it looked at me, and then the station clerk wrote Copper on a sheet and Rank One, and that was me. A minute and a half. Two years now I've been trying to get somebody to look longer than that." She was quiet a moment. "That man tomorrow has a room built for nothing but looking. A dozen instruments. He's got a clerk to time your blinks."

"I know."

"Do you know what I'd give to stand in a room like that?" There was no self-pity in it; she might have been telling him the hour. "Not to win anything. Just to be on a floor before a man whose whole work is getting it right, and have him get me right, and write it down where it can't be lost."

"You'll get one."

"An Arbiter station. One day. When the queue moves." She shrugged. "That's not the same. Same minute and a half, nicer manners."

"So make him look." She turned her head at last. "Not at three-quarters. At you. Make him look the whole time, and at the end, make him write down what he actually saw." Her voice did not change, but something underneath it did. "Somebody in this family ought to get looked at properly by a room like that. It might as well be you first."

There was nothing he could have said to that which would not have been too small. He nodded.

"And sleep," said Lira, getting up. "That's an order, not advice. If you turn up in that room having lain awake all night, I'll know, and Gault will know, and the clerk will write it down."

He sat on the step a while after she had gone, in the dark, with the yard's broken stone pale under the stars, and found the thing she had said was sitting in his chest like a stone of its own, warm from the sun. Somebody in this family. She had never used the word before. Not on any road, not in any town. He did not think she had noticed using it now.

The wash-house door creaked behind him, and Karis came out with his coat over her arm, which he had left in the common room, and dropped it round his shoulders without asking whether he was cold.

"I can't come in tomorrow," she said, sitting down on the step where Lira had been. "Closed panel. I asked Bracken. He said I could read the note afterward, when it's filed, like everybody else, and then he looked at me as if I'd asked to borrow his spectacles."

"I know."

"I'll be in carrel eleven with the door open." She pulled her own coat tighter. "It goes on the list, whatever he writes. The one I told you to keep, of everything anybody writes on you." She glanced sideways at him. "Did you start it?"

"Last week."

"How long is it?"

"Four pages."

Karis nodded slowly.

"It'll be four and a line tomorrow," she said. "That's all it'll be. One line. Everybody's lived through worse lines than one." She got up. "Go to bed. Lira will have told you that already. I'm only saying it so it's from two of us."

He slept, more or less.

In the morning Brom was waiting at the bottom of the quadrangle stair with two pieces of bread wrapped in a cloth, one for each of them.

He walked Cael across the bluff in the early light without saying anything at all, which was what Cael wanted. They went by the long way, round the rim of the Crown yard, where the porter was already out with his pail chalking the practice rings, and past the north hall, where somebody was running a drill alone on the big stone floor, the same somebody perhaps who had been running one there on Cael's first morning. Brom ate his bread. Cael carried his and did not eat it, and Brom noticed and said nothing about that either. The assessment wing's low wall came up ahead of them, pale and new, with its single gate standing open and nobody in it.

At the gate Brom stopped, and put one heavy hand on his shoulder, briefly, and took it away.

"Count the half-second." He turned and went back the way they had come.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

The demonstration room was the most expensive place on the bluff, and he stopped just inside the near door for a moment longer than he had meant to, looking at it.

Weeks ago, from the far side of the low wall, he had guessed at what the place had cost from its own gate and its own wall and the begging letters Karis had pinned up in carrel eleven. The guess had been much too small.

Fifty feet by thirty, the room was floored in oak laid on bearers like the east hall's, and the boards answered his first step. Brass ran through the boards in a grid, finger-wide strips set flush a third of a pace apart, wall to wall in both directions. Nobody at the long table would need to stand to see where a foot had come down. He had grown up at Hesk's bench, watching an instrument-maker scribe a line on brass and check it three times before he cut, and he knew what it cost to set a true line over fifty feet, in any material at all. Whoever had laid this had done it by survey and not by eye. At the far end, where a careless setter's work always wandered, these ran true. The crossings were as sharp at the back wall as at his feet.

Along the north wall stood the apparatus, and it was making its small noises.

Two weeks of asking had got him the names of nine pieces out of the twelve. First a drop-frame: a trigger, a rail, a weight to run down it, and four more weights racked underneath; someone at the far end tested the pawl, and it gave one soft click. A pendulum escapement in a glass case, ticking a steady interval that he found himself breathing in time with before he noticed and stopped. Nine shutters in a board, opened in an order a drum behind them decided; the drum's ratchet made the noise of a thumbnail going slowly down the teeth of a comb. Three spring plates on braces, each with a date of calibration painted on its housing. For footprints, a shallow tray of chalk dust. And at the very end, a thing like a tall brass funnel over a cup, which dripped into the cup with a small bright sound every few seconds, and which he could not name at all.

Facing all of it across the grid, against the south wall, stood a long table with three chairs, and at its end, a little way off, a stool and a sloped desk for the clerk.

Magister Gault was already in the middle chair. He was a heavy man in his fifties, Silver-tier, with a stillness about him that Cael read at once as trained and not natural, the stillness of somebody who had decided long ago that moving was a thing to be done on purpose. He did not stand. On his right sat the Ash Path instructor from the lecture range, the fourth name on Cael's standing list, with her book against her chest. On his left sat the Mire instructor who had resented his last session, and who had plainly not grown to like the hour since. The clerk, a young man with a ledger and three pens laid in a row, had already written something.

"Enrollee." Gault did not offer a hand. "Sit. I will tell you how the morning goes, once. You will have it every half-year from now on, and I would rather not repeat myself."

Cael sat in the single chair that faced the table.

"There is no opponent here." Gault put his broad palm down on the forms. "You will not be scored against anybody. You will do six things for me, and each of them is built to look at one part of you and nothing else. In the gaps I'll put questions to you, and they go in the book with the rest. All of it goes down in my clerk's hand: my question, your answer, and the length of the silence between."

He paused, and Cael understood that the next part was the part Gault cared about.

"Three rules of this room. The first. When you reach something you cannot do, tell me. The book will record that you could not. Nothing more, and nothing held against you; a plain fact, written down. If I have to work out for myself that you've refused, it tells me less than if you had said so." His finger moved a little on the forms. "The second. I want sameness, not your best. Six runs that agree at three-quarters tell me more than a marvel followed by five that contradict it. The third." For the first time his eyes came straight to Cael's. "This morning is your line. You will be laid against it every half-year you are here. So don't do it for me. Do it for the boy who'll stand on this oak five months from now and have to beat whatever you leave here this morning."

Of all the things Cael had readied himself for, he had not thought of this one: that the man holding the measure would name, in his first minute and as a matter of routine, the very thing about the measure that had kept Cael awake for three nights.

"Understood, Magister."

"Then we begin."

Chapter 13 — Baseline

[Observant, controlled narration; keep status, leverage, and friendship legible beneath the travel]

"Fourth brass from the near wall," said Gault. "Stand on the crossing. When the board opens, be somewhere else."

Cael waited for more, and there was none.

He walked out onto the oak and found the crossing, two strips of brass meeting under his boots in a small bright cross, and while he settled his feet on it he tried to find the flaw in what he had just been told, and could not. It gave no distance and no direction. It did not say Wind or framework or evade; it did not say what kind of practitioner was expected to answer it, or how. A square, a signal he had no say in, and the plain request that he not be on the square afterward. Whatever he did to get off it would be his and nobody else's, offered freely, and the room would only note down where he finished and how long it took him. He thought he had never been asked a cleaner question on any floor in his life.

Ten paces off, the shutter-board stood with its nine louvres closed. Somewhere behind them its drum went round with that dry fingernail sound, picking. He could not see which way it would pick. Nobody could, and that was the use of it.

He let his shoulders drop and his breath settle, and kept his eyes on all nine louvres at once.

The fourth one clacked open.

He did not decide anything; he had stopped deciding the first part years ago. His knees softened and his hips sank and the oak under him gave its small breath, and then came the toll at the front, the half-breath held and paid, during which he was all air and no lungs. Then the crossing was empty. He was a long stride to the left of it, and the floor was coming up under his heels.

He had braced for stone without meaning to. What met him was give: the boards taking him a finger's width down and handing him gently back, so that the old blow up the leading side arrived as a long low push instead. Then the fixed beat at the back, the moment when he was only something that had landed, unable yet to turn or reach or do anything but finish arriving. Three years of trying had not taken a hair off it.

The clerk kept his eyes on the pendulum. "Three brass left of the crossing. One forward. Interval—" and a number off the pendulum.

Gault wrote. "Again. The same."

Back to the crossing, and the drum went round.

He did it six times, and the clerk read six crossings and six intervals, and Gault's pen moved six times. Of the first three he felt no price at all. After the fourth there was something warm and low on the leading side, like a coal under ash. After the fifth the warmth had drawn itself into the thread he knew from the east hall, thin and bright, running from the crest of his hip down the inside of his leg to the knee: the bill being written out.

The sixth burst came out a little wide of where he had sent it. The beat at the back of it lasted longer than it ought to have, perhaps by a tenth, and he felt the extra tenth from the inside, plainly, while the pendulum was still swinging toward it. He stood where he had landed and made himself wait for the clerk.

"Three and a half left. One forward." The clerk's frown went to the case and stayed there. "Interval long."

Gault's pen stayed still a moment. He sat with the six lines of figures in front of him and his heavy hands quite still on either side of them.

"Five of these sit inside one brass of each other," he said at last. "The sixth wanders by half a brass and runs slow." He raised his eyes. "You have a figure for that, I think."

Tell me when you can't. The words came back to Cael whole.

"Four, Magister, on a floor that gives like this one. Four I can do without paying for. The fifth I pay for in the morning. I've never done six in one session except in a bout." He kept his feet where they were. "So the sixth came out the way a sixth comes out."

"You had that figure before you stepped onto the brass."

"Yes."

"You kept it to yourself."

"The rule was to speak up if a thing was beyond me." Cael looked at him steadily. "It wasn't. It only cost."

Something went across Gault's face and was gone, like a lamp carried past a window in a dark house.

Gault turned his head an inch toward the clerk, whose pen was already lifted. "Put this down. Enrollee gives a working ceiling of four on sprung timber without being asked, and says what is wrong with the sixth before the instrument does." He turned back to Cael. "Since the brass went into this oak, nobody standing on it has said a more useful sentence. A man's best afternoon tells me very little. His honest ceiling tells me where to stand. Go on."

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

The drop-frame was the Mire instructor's. She cranked the rail to a setting nobody named aloud, racked the second of the five weights, and checked the pawl with her thumb, all without hurry, and with the faint air of a woman doing a job she suspected had been done badly by somebody else the last time.

"Four places it can come down," said Gault. "High or low. Near or far. Stand in the chalk with your back to the rail, and tell us which, when it falls."

So there would be nothing to watch. No feet, no shoulders, no breath, no face. Only a weight on a rail behind him and the question of where it was. Cael stood in the chalk square and looked at the blank wall of the room in front of him, and felt a small, plain gladness at how well the thing had been made. It was the read and nothing else.

He had never known how to describe the read to anybody who did not have it. The Wind was a thing he did. The read was more like a thing that happened to the weather on his skin. A weight on the move pressed on the air, and the air pressed on him, a little before the weight itself could, in a thin band along the outsides of his arms and up behind his ears. It told him how heavy and which way. It had never told him why, or what anybody hoped would happen next. It was cheap and silent and gave nothing away to anybody watching, and it would not reach one inch past a pace and a half however he strained it. One month, long ago, had gone to straining it further. Every month after, he had left it to be itself.

And a fortnight ago, in a room with a key outside its door, it had told him a lie by saying nothing.

He let himself remember that for one breath. Then he set it down, because a frame was not a weight. What fell here would be a weight, and weights the read had found every single time.

"Ready," said the Mire instructor.

The pawl let go.

It came to him like the first heavy drops on a roof he was standing under: all together, from up and behind his left shoulder, pressing in along the back of that arm.

"High," said Cael. "Far side."

"High, far," the clerk agreed.

Twelve times. He called each one as it came, and in the gaps the room went on making its noises round him: the pendulum, the drip at the end of the row into its brass cup, the clerk's nib. The ninth was wrong before it had finished arriving. It did not come all together. It came the way rain comes when the wind keeps changing its mind, a light early touch and then, a beat behind, the real weight, and he had two answers and had to pick one.

"Low. Near." He turned his head a fraction. "And that's wrong. I'm fairly sure."

"Low, far," said the clerk. "Wrong."

"You are quite right to say you are wrong," said Gault. There was nothing light in it; he might have been reading a dial. "What told you?"

"It didn't arrive in one piece." After a moment Cael gave him the rest; it belonged on the record too. "A clean one is a single blow. This one arrived twice, a touch first and the weight after, and I had to choose which to believe. I think it let go slowly. That isn't an excuse. It's only what I felt."

The Mire instructor was already out of her chair. At the frame she worked the release by hand four times, slowly, her ear bent close, and at the fourth her thumb stopped on the pawl and stayed.

"Sticks at the second notch," she said. "Not every time. Once in five, near enough." She looked across at Gault with real annoyance. "It had its service before term. It shouldn't be doing this."

"Good for the rest of the morning?"

"So long as somebody's told when it sticks." She went back to her seat. "And he seems to feel it before we hear it."

Gault wrote for a long time. The clerk wrote too, on a small separate slip, and pushed it into a slot on the frame's brass housing, where it stuck out like a little white tongue. For service. Cael looked at it over his shoulder and thought how easily a careful hand on a busy morning might pull a slip like that out to read it and forget to put it back, and the work never be done. Then he thought it was not his frame, nor his busy morning, and turned to face the wall.

The last three came clean. Eleven of twelve, the clerk read out, and the wrong one the ninth, and Cael stood in the chalk with his back to the rail and noticed, with some surprise, that he had begun to like the room.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The third trial put the two together.

Rail set somewhere he was not told, weight racked, Cael in the chalk beneath it; and when the weight let go he was to feel where it came from and be out of the square before it hit the boards. Read, then move, with no gap between them for thinking in.

Eight runs, and seven times he was clear. On the eighth the press came to him a hair late, through no fault of the pawl, and he went a hair late after it, and the weight came down on the oak with a flat heavy knock a finger's breadth behind his heel. The other seven were good in a way he did not think the clerk's figures would ever show: the press arriving along his arm, his hips already going before he had told them to, the half-breath, the sideways nothing, the boards, the weight landing in a place he had just stopped being.

Somewhere around the fifth, it came to him that he was enjoying this. The realization arrived with a little cold prick behind it, like a draught under a door.

It was the room's doing; every other floor he had ever stood on had wanted something out of him, a purse or a place or a noise from a crowd or a verdict. This one wanted only to know where he went, and asked so plainly and so patiently that he could feel himself easing under it. Easy men talked. He tightened up again, on purpose, between the sixth run and the seventh, and was aware of the Ash instructor watching him do it, and kept his eyes on the wall.

Of the six, the fourth cost most, and what it asked of him was to leave something undone.

The Mire instructor racked the heaviest weight. The clerk shifted the chalk square to a pace from the rail.

"No getting out of this one," said Gault. "Too close, too heavy. Catch it on the plate."

The clerk brought the plate across on its brace and put it into Cael's hands: a round of steel with a spring behind it and a small dial in the housing, made to show how much of a blow had been held and how much had gone on through.

Feryn's fragment woke up in his right arm and reached for it.

He felt it the way a hand in the dark goes to a tool it has used before, already shaping to the grip. Since a bout he had lost fairly three years ago it had lived in him, used seldom, but always close under the skin. It did not keep a blow; it gathered it, turned it, and passed it on somewhere else. It was made for this. If anybody in the room had been marking answers right and wrong, it was the right answer to the question in his hands, and the little dial would have swung round to a figure nobody at that table had seen in their lives.

It was not on the record.

He stood with the plate and the reaching in his arm for two breaths, which was one breath longer than he had meant to, and he saw Gault see the extra breath and say nothing. Somewhere the pendulum ticked. He thought of Lira on the wash-house step: make him look. He thought of Karis in carrel eleven: it was mine before it was yours. He thought of half a page of transcript, late and thin. Then he let the reaching go, as he had let it go on a thousand other floors, and his arm was only his arm.

He braced the plain way: feet wide; the plate held out on an arm loaded from the shoulder; everything down through his legs into the oak. It was how a body with no Path takes a knock, and how he had taken every knock in his first winter on the Ironyard's planks. The pawl let go, and the weight came down the rail and met the plate, and the shock went up the bones of his forearm and stopped in the shoulder like a nail driven into a joist. Nothing in him carried it anywhere else; the shoulder had all of it. Behind the plate the spring hit the end of its travel with a dull clank.

"Held, low," said the clerk.

"Again," said Gault.

Four of them. By the fourth, his right arm had no feeling from the wrist halfway up to the elbow, and a hard bright ache had settled deep in the shoulder joint; it would be with him, he knew, to the week's end.

"Your account," said Gault.

"Four of those I can stand." Cael opened and closed his right hand in plain sight. "Eight, no. It doesn't go anywhere. The shoulder keeps it."

Every word was so. Taken together, the words were a coat cut to look like the whole man, with most of the man left at home, and he knew it while he said them. He had to hold his face very still.

The last two trials were the first two again, run cold, to see what an hour on the oak had taken out of him.

The board picked its louvres and he answered them, and the clerk's figures came back a palm short of the morning's, with the stiff beat at the end of each a hair slower. His hip had its bill by then and he did not try to argue with it. He let it show. The drop-frame he answered twelve times out of twelve, and it did not stick once.

Let the loss be written; he did not mind. That was the point of a cold run: to show what the morning had cost, honestly, so next half-year somebody could see whether it cost less. A line that hid its own tiredness would be a line he could never grow past.

He went back to the chair afterward without being told and sat, because the hip asked him to. Nobody minded. He watched his right hand on his knee until its fingers were still, and then, for the first time that morning, let himself look at the three people behind the long table as people.

The Ash instructor's book lay shut in front of her, with a finger in it at a place she had long since stopped keeping. The Mire instructor no longer looked resentful; she looked thoughtful, which on her face was nearly the same expression turned the other way up. And Gault had watched him; Cael understood it only now. All through the morning, every run and every drop and every clank of the plate, the heavy still man in the middle chair had watched him, start to finish, and looked away only to write.

Make him look, Lira had said, and he had not needed to. The room was built for nothing else, and the man in it had done nothing else, and sitting there with his arm aching Cael found it was nothing like being stared at in a corridor. It was like being counted, carefully, by somebody who meant to get the number right.

For four minutes or so Gault bent over his papers. The pendulum went on, and the funnel dripped.

Then he lifted the top sheet. By charter the note had to be read in the enrollee's hearing. Gault read it, and Cael heard the words that would stand for him on this bluff for as long as he stayed.

"Assessment of entry demonstration, assay-provision enrollee. Non-standard architecture. Execution consistent across trials. Baseline established; semester evaluation to measure against it."

Four short sentences, against three bad nights and an hour of held breath and a shoulder that would complain until the week was out. He waited to be let down by them, and was not. There was nothing wrong in any of them. Consistent across trials was the only good word the instrument knew how to say, and it had said it.

The Ash instructor signed. The Mire instructor's name came next, and under it a note on the sticking notch, initialled twice. The clerk pressed the stamp down, blotted, and closed the folder.

Dull. Exact. Stamped. Cael could not remember the last time he had been so glad of anything.

He thought of the four pages of Karis's list, every line anybody had ever written about him: the station's word in brackets, the registry's forms, the observer track, the ruling, Bracken's record with its two signatures. Most of them had been written by people deciding what he was. A few by people taking great care not to. This one had been written by a man who had not tried at all, because deciding was no part of his work, and it was the plainest line on the list, and the only one, he thought, that would read as true a year from now.

He wrote the plate up that evening at the desk by the window, with his arm on a folded shirt because it did not like to hang.

Not doing it costs little. One choice, made a thousand times before; I'm good at it.

The dear part is the man across the table. He was straight with me from the first minute, and I gave him something true with a hole in the middle of it, in his own room, for his own book, and he took it down and thanked me for being frank. I was frank. It still wasn't everything.

Bill: a shoulder until the week's end. Plus something I've no column for yet.

Quenna asked whether I could keep my hands still before people who'd enjoy seeing me hurt. That one's still open. This morning I held them still in front of a man who wants nothing from me but accuracy. I think, for the record, the second one was harder.

The instructors and the clerk were already out in the passage when Gault, folder under his arm, stopped him at the near door.

"A word before you go," he said. "Off the book. Do what you like with it."

"Magister."

"Half this faculty would give a good deal for one plain sentence about your nature." Gault said it flatly, as he had read out the crossings. "Some ask out of curiosity, some out of worry. Two of the worried ones, as I judge it, are worried for the school and not for their own skins, which is why they are worth your attention. You'll hear the question put a dozen ways before the term's out, give or take."

"Eleven so far," said Cael. "I've written them down."

"I expect you have." Gault moved the folder to his other arm. "I am not among the askers. I want you to know why. Take it for indifference and you'll misread me all year, and the work will go harder for us both." He looked at Cael directly, as he had in the first minute of the morning.

"I don't need to know what you are, Enrollee. I need my instruments and your consistency. Give me the second; the first is not my mandate."

Cael did not move from the doorway. He held the sentence carefully. He had the sense that it was the most useful thing the bluff had handed him yet, and that it could be taken two ways, and he did not want to walk off with the wrong one.

"Do you mean that kindly?" he said. "Or is it where you stop?"

Gault's face did its brief thing again, a lamp passing behind a shutter.

"It's where I stop. And the stopping is for your sake." He said it simply. "The moment an assessor settles what a practitioner is, the measuring stops. Everything after that is him proving himself right. I have seen that finish men's careers. I saw it finish one man altogether. He was a better assessor than I shall ever be. He decided early what a girl in front of him must be, and he spent four years building trials that showed he was right, and they all did. A man's instruments will agree with him if he wants it badly enough. He was simply wrong."

He pushed the door open. The passage's noise came in, feet and voices.

"So I don't decide. Twice a year, as long as you're here, I measure you, and I set down what the needles say. If the needles start saying odd things, I set that down as well, and my hand will look no different on the page. That's the whole of what I offer. Don't call it friendship. Don't lean on it as a shield." He paused. "But nothing else in this building will go on giving the same answer when somebody above me would like a different one. Good morning."

Cael went out past him into the passage, and Gault did not follow at once; he had turned back into the room to say something to the clerk, who had come back for his pens, and the door swung half to between them.

The passage was full, as it always was at the change of bell, and Cael went along it slowly, because his hip had sent its bill and his right arm would not swing. Heads turned as he went by. Two second-years stopped talking outside the records room. A girl with an armful of practice smocks flattened herself against the wall to let him pass and stared at his arm. Somewhere behind him a man carrying a stack of forms stepped out of the stream, as clerks do, to let the passage go past; Cael did not look at him, because there was nothing in a clerk with forms to look at, and because by then his whole attention had turned inward, to the conversation at the door.

He was thinking about a man who would not decide. On a hill where everybody had already made up their minds about him, he had found one man who had made not deciding his trade.

Under the plate that night he added the rest.

He doesn't want to know what I am. He wants me to be the same twice running. That's harder than being anything. It's also the first thing anybody's asked of me in a long while that I can actually give.

About the man he spoke of. Instruments agree with whoever wants them to: that isn't a story about instruments. It's a story about me, if I let it be. Every column I keep, every third entry I've been hoping for since the first. I've been the one holding the instrument all my life. I'd better be Gault's kind and not the other.

Line drawn. Two capabilities, measured honestly, on the record for good. Four free on a floor that gives. Eleven in twelve; the miss belonged to the frame. Held, low. A shoulder till the week's out.

Everything from here gets laid against it.

[Observant, controlled narration; keep status, leverage, and friendship legible beneath the travel]

The panel had been closed. By the fourth bell that afternoon, the whole bluff knew what had happened in it, and none of what the bluff knew was so.

He worked out how before supper, because working out how was the only part of it he could do anything with. Nobody in the room had talked. He was sure of that by the evening and surer by the end of the week; he went at it four separate ways and found no road out of the demonstration room that any word could have taken. What had happened was simpler and, he thought, rather worse. By charter, the plain fact of any provision-status evaluation had to go up for the whole academy to read. It went on the board beside the theater door in the administration range, among the minutes of open sessions and every other act the institution performed. Halcenvane had kept its business in the open since its charter. So a little after the noon bell, the clerk had pinned up a slip.

Entry demonstration, assay-provision enrollee: satisfied. Baseline established and filed.

Nine words. They said nothing at all about what he had done. Inside four hours, every one of the eleven stories that had followed him round the bluff since the gate had rushed in to fill that nothing, until a reader could no longer make out the wall behind the slip for the crowd of them.

He found it oddly hard to be angry with anybody about it. The slip was accurate. As charters went, it was a good one. The people who had filled the space were only doing what people always did with a space, and he had watched them do it at Greyvane, and on the road, and in the stew line on his thirteenth evening here. It was only that he had hoped, without quite admitting it to himself, that a room full of instruments might be the one thing on the bluff a rumour could not reach.

Lira brought the first two to supper.

"You broke the drop-frame," she said, sitting down opposite him with her bowl. "A Current girl in the third quadrangle has it that you laid a hand on the rail and the rail snapped." She took a spoonful. "And you refused to demonstrate at all, and sat in a chair for an hour with your arms folded, and Gault passed you anyway because he was afraid of the Compact. That's from two Iron boys outside the north hall, and they didn't agree with each other about why he was afraid."

Not one of them is so. The nearest is about the frame. It did stick, and a woman did leave her chair to look at it, so if I deny that one I sound as though I'm hiding something, and if I let it be, it grows. A notch that wanted oil and an instructor checking a pawl, and four hours later it's a legend.

Nine words. That's all the board gave them. People don't fill an empty space with what's true. They fill it with what they already had, and then they'll defend it, because now it's theirs.

So nothing I say is going to move any of this. Only what I do, where people can see it, over a long time. That's slower than a rumour. It's also the only thing that's ever outlasted one.

The porter was wiping down the Copper board the next afternoon, and Cael was sitting on the rim above him reading his own notes on the morning's practice rings, when the Iron column's best fighter came up the tiers toward him at an even walk.

There were perhaps sixty people still in the yard. The session had broken up a few minutes before, and the stone seats were emptying in the slow, sociable way they always emptied, with knots of second-years arguing about a bout and somebody calling a name across the floor. Ephram came up through all of it without hurrying. His weight rode forward on the balls of his feet, as it always did, so that even climbing a stair he looked like a man about to step into something.

For most of a month Cael had watched him from the east hall's gallery, and not once in all that time had Ephram lifted his eyes to it. It wasn't shyness; Cael had settled that early. He had seen Ephram leave four other people unlooked-at in the same way, people who plainly wanted his notice. His notice was a coin he paid out only after he had weighed what it would buy.

He had decided now, and Cael shut the notebook on one finger.

"He sent five up the bluff this year," said Cael. "Three went to faculty. One's in the library. Karis asked him who had the fifth, and he wouldn't say."

Ephram's eyebrows rose by the width of a hair. It went into the notebook that night: the first thing he had ever learned from Ephram at arm's length.

"Mine," said Ephram. "So you know what I'm working from, and what I'm not." He moved his head an inch, taking in the yard, the boards, the sunk floor, all of it. The other half have made you a fraud. Not one of either half has seen you do anything. What they've got is a law report. It tells me the Compact lost an argument about paper. He made himself sit with that and look at it. It was not shame, exactly. Whether it was gold, he did not yet know. That was the trouble: nobody did.
