Seln had not picked the question. He had only picked the answer. Seventy-two. He let the clerk give him seventy-six, coloured slightly, and took up his pen. One wrong sum, two shelves filled. By the week's end the wing had decided he was a careful man with no head for figures, and had stopped thinking about him. And behind the boy's quiet, attentive face the same small verdict had gone, Seln had been almost certain, onto the same shelf, where verdicts sit undisturbed because their owners believe they arrived at them unaided.

Almost certain. For three weeks it had looked like certainty.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

That evening, when the wing had emptied, he did something he had not done since his twenty-third day. He climbed the stair to the east hall gallery, alone, with a lamp, and walked out along it to the turned post at the west end, and looked down.

The hall was dark. The lamp put a small warm ring round him on the boards of the walk and threw nothing on the floor below at all. He stood at the post a while, and then he went along the gallery and down the stair, and crossed the dark floor to the near door, and sat on the bench inside it.

He set the lamp on the floor at his feet and looked up.

The gallery was there above him, just visible, a long dark rail against a longer dark wall. He could not see the turned post from here without lifting his chin, and lifting his chin was a thing anybody watching could have seen.

So he did not lift it. He looked straight ahead, across the floor, at the door that stood propped open against the wall to air the hall. It had glass in its upper half, old glass, a little wavy. And in the glass, small and bent and perfectly clear, lit by his own lamp, hung the gallery, and the rail, and the turned post.

He sat on the bench and looked at it for some time.

The boy had not looked up that morning. Seln had been sure of that, and had found it a comfort. The boy had not needed to. He had sat with his eyes on the floor in front of his boots like any bored student waiting for a session, and watched the gallery in the glass of a door, and seen a clerk come out of the far end of it and walk the whole length of it without slowing at the post, and without once glancing down at the only lit window in a dark street. And that had been the reading. Not that the clerk had passed. Clerks passed all day. The reading was the glance the clerk had not given, because not giving it was Seln's trade, and he had been too practised to remember that an ordinary man would have.

He had been pleased with himself for the length of the yard afterward. He remembered that, the way a man remembers the last step before a stair he did not know was there.

Twice in fifteen years someone had found him out. Both had worked for the other side; both had had ledgers and colleagues and half a year to do it in; and both had been the rare sort of watcher he had met only those two of in his life, who hunted for the gap where a man ought to be rather than for the man. He had thought well of them both. Neither had been a subject. Neither had been fifteen.

He had priced his choices on the first night, and he priced them again on the bench, with the lamp at his feet.

He could ask to be withdrawn. Somebody would replace him, a new face in a building where a covered officer had just been found, and the new face would begin a long way behind where Seln stood now, and never catch up.

He could walk into the chancellor's room tomorrow, lay his warrant on her desk, and become an open officer in a declared post. His brief allowed it. It would also make him useless by the noon bell.

Or he could go on, and watch what the boy did with what he knew.

He had gone on. The boy had done nothing whatever.

No word had gone to the chancellor; her minutes came through the wing, and Seln copied them. None had gone to Gault, nor to any instructor, nor into any petition or complaint. The boy's hours had not moved by so much as a bell. He sat in the same tiers on the same afternoons and passed the wing door twice a day at the same unhurried walk. His three friends were as they had been on the first morning. The Wind girl, whose face Seln had judged the least schooled of the four, had never once turned it toward the copying table, and a face like hers did not manage that by accident; somebody had asked it of her, and she had agreed.

And under that stillness the air of the bluff had changed for him in a way it had taken him the better part of a fortnight to put a word to.

It was not being looked at. A stare he would have caught within the hour. This was more like the sense a man has in a house at night that one of the clocks has stopped: no sound, no movement, only a certainty that somewhere in the building a figure is being kept. He was being accounted for. His comings and goings had become a column in someone's book. He knew the feeling to its roots. He had made it in other men, deliberately, as his life's work, in more rooms than he could count. He had never once sat inside it.

It had held eight days now. A frightened boy would have broken it on the second, by going stiff at the wing door, or by staying away from the gallery, or by telling a friend who told a friend. A clever boy might have held it three days, out of pride. Eight days of nothing, of walking past a found man four times a day and letting nothing show, was neither fright nor cleverness. It was a discipline. And disciplines did not grow wild. Somebody planted them.

He thought of the windowless room and the officer setting down his line like a lamp he wanted admired. He thought of the analysts and the grades above them who had agreed that what the boy was, was the question. He thought of his own sealed month on its way up the coast in a canvas sack, every word true, not one of them within a mile of that question.

None of this would be written. It was guesswork, and guesswork did not go into the product, and the product was the only paper he kept.

He picked up the lamp and went back across the dark floor, and up through the wing, and out into the night, where the river was loud with barges going down. And on the step outside, with his hand on the cold rail, he let the thought finish at last, the one he had been leaving unfinished for eight days.

Fifteen years say the file's question is the wrong question. The interesting question is who taught him to watch.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

Karis was the one who made him say what a declaration was, out loud, in carrel eleven, with the door shut and her pen waiting, and it was harder than he had expected.

"Everybody knows what it is," he said.

"Everybody knows what it looks like," said Karis. "I'm asking what it is. You've been writing no declaration in that book for two weeks as if it were a fact about him. I want to know what fact."

He took his time; she meant it.

"The Path declaration. It's the moment the Path is chosen," he said slowly. "Every Path I've seen work has one. However fast the practitioner, there's an instant when the working begins, and the body says so. It can't help it. The Path has to be paid for, and paying is a thing a body does." He held up his hand and counted. "Stone drops. The weight goes down through the feet a hair before the anchor takes. Force sets. A Force fighter's shoulders square, every one of them, even Fiske, though hers you could miss. Lira folds at the hips. Brom bites. He's been trying to stop since Ardenmere, and the jaw goes every time."

"And mine?"

"You lift your chin," said Cael. "About the width of a hair. It took me two months."

"I know exactly how long it took you." Karis looked pleased in spite of herself. "Go on."

"That's why it matters on a floor." He found he was leaning forward, the way he did when a thing he knew in his body had to be made into words. "The declaration's the only honest thing an opponent ever tells you. Everything else he can fake. He can look at your left and go right, he can breathe like a man who's tired when he isn't. But when the Path begins, it has to be paid for, and the payment shows, and he can't stop it showing any more than he can stop his heart. Every fighter I've ever beaten, I beat by waiting for that. Lira's hips. A Stone boy's heels. The instant the working's bought, you know what's coming, and you're already somewhere else." He sat back. "A fighter with no declaration would be the most dangerous person on any floor in the world."

"And he never sets foot on a floor," said Karis.

"No. He doesn't."

"So I've looked for his," said Cael. "Nineteen days. Through glass, in the lamp, in the brass on the lecture stair, from the side of my eye while I write down other people's bouts." He shook his head. "Nothing begins. There's never a moment. He's the same at the first bell as he is at the fifth."

"So you've written none."

"I've written none observed."

Karis tapped her pen on the desk, twice.

"A hole's got edges," she said. "You taught me that, about the clause. You measured the gap on the shelf and found the book that should have been in it. So don't tell me what isn't there. Tell me what shape the not-being-there has."

He sat back in the carrel's one chair and looked at the ceiling.

Then he took the binder and turned to the page that said none observed and wrote under it, without crossing anything out, because the first version deserved to be kept as the thing he had believed before he knew better.

Second version. A Path declaration is a purchase. The practitioner pays a price, all at once, in a single instant, and gets the working in return; the paying is what the body shows. Every Path I know pays that way, because it's the cheapest way to pay. But it shows. And this Path's whole trade is never showing. It can't afford one visible instant. So it doesn't pay all at once. It pays a little at a time, without stopping, from the moment he leaves his door. Not no declaration. A declaration smeared across four hours, so thin that nobody has ever seen it on him. You'd only see a smear if you already knew how wide the brush was.

He turned the binder round so that Karis could read it. She read it twice, and then a third time with her finger under it, and handed it back.

"That's not watching any more," she said.

"No."

"That's a Path." She sounded almost jealous. "That's somebody's architecture, written down from outside, by a person it was being used on. I've been trying to explain that difference to you for a year."

"I know," said Cael. "I didn't understand it till about a minute ago."

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

If he could not see the smear on the man, then he would have to find it on everybody else. A smear has to fall on something.

He already had the means: the tally, with its strict rule for what counted as a look, which for six weeks he had only ever turned on himself.

The covered walk between the quadrangles ran along a low stone rail on its east side, elbow high, where people waited for friends or leaned out of the wind to talk. At the change from the fourth bell to the fifth, some sixty people went along the walk, and four or five were nearly always leaning at that rail. Cael came along it at that hour four days in seven, back from the north hall. And on most of those days, because Cael came along it, the man from the wing was one of the leaners, in the middle of them, forms against his chest.

So Cael stopped counting the eyes that came to him. He counted the eyes that went to the rail: how many of the sixty, passing, turned their heads toward anybody leaning there or let a look rest on them. He took the count the same way every time, over the same stretch of the walk, while he crossed it.

Then he split the tally in two. Into one column went the days the man was at the rail. Into the other went the days he was not, when the leaners were four or five strangers and nothing more.

He was strict with himself about what went in. Days of rain went out, because in rain people walked fast with their heads down and looked at nothing. So did the afternoon Fiske had stopped at the rail to talk to a friend, and half the walk had turned to look at the Copper champion; he wrote that day across the top of the page, spoiled: Fiske, and threw it away whole. So did any day he crossed late, or early, or with Brom beside him, because Brom drew eyes of his own, being the size of a door.

What was left was a dull, steady sample, the same stretch of stone at the same bell on dry days, with nothing on it to look at except a few people leaning on a wall. Dull was what he wanted.

The columns took a fortnight to fill far enough to be trusted. When they were full the difference between them was not large. It never once went the wrong way.

When the man was among them, about a third fewer people looked at the rail at all.

Cael sat on his bed with the two columns on his knees and felt the skin of his arms tighten.

It was a number. Nobody had ever given him a number for a Shadow Path, at any tier, and he did not think anybody had ever held one. And the number said the man was not hidden. People still looked at that rail when he leaned on it, two of every three who would have looked in any case. The Path leaned on everybody else. It took each passer's small, idle wish to look at a few people chatting by a wall and made that wish a fraction heavier to lift, as a hand on your shoulder makes your head a little harder to turn, and about a third of those wishes were never lifted.

That was not a wall round him. It was a toll on everybody near him.

If it's a rate, he wrote, he's spending, and spending has a shape across a day. Find the shape.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He sorted the shorthand by the hour on a wet evening near the month's end, which he should have done a fortnight before, and the shape was lying in it waiting for him.

Before noon, every time, the man's places were perfect. Every gallery, every stair, every tier: the one best view, the heart of the cluster, the most of Cael's hour laid out below him like a page.

After noon they began to slip.

Not into carelessness; never that. They slipped by small degrees, and the degrees followed the clock. Three hours into the wing's day, he was still on the best view, but on the edge of his cluster now instead of in its middle. Four hours in, he would sometimes take the place beside the best one: the top of a stair from which most of a floor could be seen, when the rail beside it would have shown him all. And twice, at the end of days when the wing had kept its counter open from first bell to last, he had stood where no watcher stands: in the angle of two walls in the yard's north stair, with a single doorway in front of him, seeing almost nothing of the floor.

Cael knew that place. He had stood in places like it himself, in the Ironyard, at the end of nights when he could no longer guard every side and had chosen instead to guard the one way out.

He wrote the hours down the left of the page and the places down the right, and drew a line through them, and the line went down.

It isn't free, he wrote. Underline that. Whatever it burns, he has less of it at the fifth bell than at the first, and by the next morning he has it all back. The bend comes at about four hours. Before that he buys the best places. After it he buys what he can afford. I know that bend; it's my own ceiling. It's the evening I stop using the Wind for the good escape and start using it for the cheap one, because the hip has already sent two bills that day.

He sat back, and something in him that had been tight since the gallery let go. He had been half afraid of the man because he had never seen him pay, and a thing that never paid had no edges. Now he had found one.

Then he turned to the facing page, the column he kept for what he could not reach.

Discarded / cannot reach.

How far. I've only ever seen him at rest, in company. I don't know whether the toll reaches across a yard or only an arm's length, or whether it holds while he runs. I can't make him run.

Floors. He never sets foot on one except carrying paper, and his Path does one thing where I can see it. I'd give a good deal to see it do another. I don't suppose I will.

And under all of it: every line hangs from a single thread, the spot a man picks to stand on. Vell would call a judgment on one leg a guess wearing a ledger's coat. She'd be right, and I've no second leg to give it.

He read the column through. Then, at the bottom, smaller, he added something that was not a finding and not a gap, because it had been sitting in him since the gallery and he wanted it on paper in his own hand.

He knows I found him. He must. And he has gone on standing in his crowds every day since, on the same posts, at the same bells, keeping himself hard to see for four hundred people who were never looking. So it was never me the Path was for. It's for everybody else, so that I'm the only one who can see him, and I've agreed to keep my mouth shut. I've been trying for a week to think of a better answer to being caught. I can't.

Chapter 19 — The Bruise

[Focused, analytical narration; make each tactical choice feel earned rather than announced]

The round Current lecturer hummed.

He had hummed through the first ten minutes of every session he had ever signed for Cael. He hummed now, on the bench under the east hall's gallery, with his hands folded on his stomach and his eyes half shut, a tune with no particular shape that went up and down like a man walking over hills. Cael had stopped hearing it after the first week. Today he heard every note, because it was First-day, the seventy-fifth, two days after the council, and Lira had asked for the slot.

Brom had broken the agreement first, as Karis had promised he would, and he had come to breakfast that morning to confess it with the air of a man bringing a dead bird to the kitchen door.

"I walked into the wall," he said, sitting down.

Karis put her spoon down. "Which wall?"

"The one by the wing door. Yesterday, after the post." He looked at his porridge with deep sorrow. "I was going past, the way you said, ordinary, not looking. And I was thinking so hard about not looking that I forgot to look where I was going, and the passage turns there, and I didn't." He touched his forehead, where there was a faint pink mark nobody had noticed until now. "Went straight into the corner. Made a noise like a dropped bucket. Two second-years laughed."

"Was he there?" said Lira.

"I don't know." Brom looked up, honestly anguished. "That's the worst of it. I didn't look. I'd have had to look to know."

There was a short silence round the table.

"Then you kept the rule," said Karis, with great gentleness, "and broke a wall. That's allowed. Thank you for telling us." She picked up her spoon again. "Next time, look where you're going and not at him. Those are two different directions. It's easier than it sounds."

"It's much harder than it sounds," said Brom, and ate his porridge with the dignity of a man who has done his duty and been laughed at by second-years for it. Cael wrote the break into the agreement page that evening under its date, with Brom's own words beside it, went straight into the corner, because that was the rule under the rule, and it had worked as Karis had said it would.

"Full pace," Lira had said at the same breakfast, to her bread, when Brom had finished. "First to three. I want to see something."

"See what?"

"I'll tell you when I've seen it."

The office allowed it, as it had allowed it before, because the two of them shared a residence roster and a supervised session needed a body on the floor besides the enrollee. The Current lecturer signed without looking at either of them, settled on his bench, and began to hum. Above them the gallery held seven or eight early watchers. Cael did not look to see which post had a man with forms at it. He did not need to look. He knew.

They went to their chalk. Lira did what she always did before a bout and had done since the Ironyard, which was to touch the floor with the flat of one hand, as if asking it a question, and then stand up and roll her neck once each way. Cael had asked her about it the first winter. She had said it was so her hand would know the floor before her feet had to, and then refused to say anything else about it for two years. He had come to find it reassuring. A Lira who had touched the floor was a Lira who had stopped thinking about anything in the world except the next three touches.

Lira fought him at full pace on the timber, as she had every week since the first, because the boards here gave and returned and she had said, flatly, the first morning, that it would be a crime to waste them. She came at him low and quick off her lead foot with the Wind at her heels. He read her a pace and a half out, felt her weight go left along the skin of his forearm, and slipped right on his feet without the framework, and she went by.

On the second exchange he went to the Wind early, too early, while her feed was still a feed. He had read her weight going one way and trusted it and committed, and the half-breath closed in his chest, and the framework took him a long stride back and to the side. Lira had not gone that way at all. She had stopped, a hand's width short of where her weight had promised, and simply waited for him to arrive somewhere. When he landed she was already turning to meet him, and the beat at the back of the burst held him for its half-breath like a hand on his collar. She put her palm flat on his chest and pushed, almost gently, and he sat down on the oak.

"One," said Lira.

"Mine," said Cael, getting up. "I went on a feed."

"You did." She went back to her chalk without any comment on it at all, which was the comment.

That first fall was ordinary. He had gone too early on a dummy; it was a mistake he made perhaps once a month, and Lira had been punishing it since the Ironyard, and he deserved it. He took his chalk and rolled his shoulders and told himself to wait for the weight and not the promise of it.

The bench went on humming. Somewhere behind it a door banged in the north passage. The light lay across the boards in its long low bars and the floor breathed under his feet.

On the fourth exchange it went wrong in a way that was not ordinary at all.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

She came straight. Remember that, Cael told himself afterward: she gave him a true one. She came straight and honest down the middle of the floor, no short step, no dummy, her weight forward on the diagonal from his left, committed, the kind of feed she sold perhaps one time in ten precisely because it was true.

He read it. The press came along his left forearm, heavy and fast, and it was right. Diagonal, committed, real. He priced the burst before he reached for it, the way the Log had made him price every burst for eighteen months, and the price was fair: the second of four free on this timber, a cheap answer to a true question.

His knees softened. His hips sank. The oak took the first of his weight and gave it back, and the half-breath closed, the toll at the front, and for its length he was no heavier than the air in the room. Her whole committed weight went through the place where he had been and out the other side into nothing.

It was a perfect escape. Nothing on the floor could have done it better.

Then the landing.

He had paid it four hundred times. Every borrowed lightness came back at once at the end of a burst, a jolt up through both heels. With it came the locked beat: half a breath in which he was only a thing that had arrived, unable to turn, or reach, or do anything at all but finish arriving. Three years of trying had not taken a hair off it. Against a good fighter the whole art of the framework was knowing in advance what that beat would be spent on, so that the instant it ended he was already moving into the next thing.

He knew what this one should be spent on. Lira's weight had gone past him on the left; her recovery would come round to her right; the beat, if he used it for setting his feet square, would let him meet her coming round with his whole weight behind his hands.

Her recovery reached his skin only once the beat had him.

That was the whole of it. The read came. It came true, as it always came: her weight swinging out and round to her right, fast, where he had expected. But it came the way a letter comes that was posted late, with the event it describes already over. By the time it reached him his feet had set themselves square for the wrong thing, on their own, in the dark, and the locked beat had closed round them, and Lira was not where his feet had set for her. She had come round tighter than he had planned for, and low.

Her shoulder took him under the ribs.

He went over backwards onto the oak with all his own weight and some of hers, and the boards that were so kind to a landing beat were a good deal less kind to a whole body coming down flat. The breath went out of him in one piece. For a moment he lay looking up at the beams and at the long dark rail of the gallery, where somebody was leaning to see, and could not have told anyone his own name.

On the bench the humming had stopped.

Lira was standing over him, bent with her hands braced on her thighs, blowing hard, and looking not the smallest bit sorry.

"Two," she said.

Breath came back in a thin thread. He used it to nod.

"You saw that," she said.

"I felt it."

"It wasn't the burst. The burst was lovely." Her hands stayed on her thighs. "It was after. You set your feet before you knew where I was going. You've never once done that. Not in three years. You always know where I'm going before your feet do; it's the most irritating thing about you." She tilted her head. "Your read was late."

"I know."

"You knew before we started. That's why I asked for the slot."

He got his elbows under him. "You saw it at breakfast?"

"I saw it on the stair, after the council. You told Karis it was late on cords, and you said it the way you say things you've already written down and don't want to say twice." She straightened up. "So say the rest of it out loud, then. Not in that book, where I've got to wait for it."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He sat up on the oak. Something under his ribs on the right side was deciding whether to hurt, and coming down on the side of yes.

"It's the counting," he said. "Whatever I watch people with, the read drinks from the same cup. I've been emptying the cup into stairs and galleries since before the council. So the read gets the dregs, and the dregs come in slow." He pressed two fingers to his ribs and found the place. "Slow enough that I set my feet for where you were going to be instead of where you were. On the floor, against you, that's this." He took the fingers away. "Against somebody who doesn't like me, it's worse."

"So I see." Lira put down her hand at last, and he took it, and she leaned back on his weight and brought him up off the boards in one pull. "And it buys what?"

"The counting?"

"The counting. You've paid me two falls for it today. Karis says it took you across the shin last week. What are you getting?"

He took his time. She let him. She stood with her hands on her hips in the middle of the floor, getting her breath, while on the bench the Current lecturer pretended very hard to be asleep.

"I'll give it you like a receipt," he said. He held up a thumb. "I can walk into this hall and know which post on that gallery the Compact is leaning on, without looking." A finger. "I can walk into the yard and know which tier, and roughly which body in the knot." Another. "I know his Path costs him, and that it runs short in the afternoons, and about when." Another. "And I know the one thing that makes him walk away from a good view, which is being alone." He looked at his hand. "Nobody I've ever heard of, anywhere, has known that much about the people set to watch them. I'd have paid twice as much for it and called it cheap."

"And the other side of the receipt?"

"A beat off the read, for as long as I keep it up. Two falls, First-day, east hall. One shin, last week, on cords." He touched his ribs. "One bruise. Here. Your shoulder."

Lira looked at him for a moment without any expression at all.

Then she laughed. It came out of her short and surprised and completely real, and went up into the beams of the empty hall, and two of the watchers on the gallery leaned over to see what was funny.

"You're the only person I've ever met who'd file a bruise," said Lira.

"Somebody ought to."

"Nobody ought to." She was still smiling, which she did not do often enough for him to be used to it. "That's what makes it so entirely you." She walked back to her chalk and turned round and planted her feet. "Again. And this time don't go on anything at all. Stand there and let me come the whole way, and call me as you feel me, and I'll tell you how late you are. If I'm going to knock you over for a whole season, I want to know exactly how hard I'm allowed."

They went on until the bell. He did not fall again; he did not use the Wind again, either. He stood on his feet and let her come at him exchange after exchange while he called her weight aloud a half-second after he felt it, left, round, low, and she called back late, late, on time, late. The Current lecturer, who had begun humming again at the tenth minute out of what Cael could only suppose was tact, stopped humming at the fourteenth and watched the rest of it with both eyes open.

At the end, signing the sheet, he looked from one of them to the other, and a question came all the way up to his mouth and stopped there. Then he signed, and handed the sheet to Cael, and said only, "Ice for the ribs. Not heat. Heat makes it worse," and went out.

It was the first thing any of the eleven had ever said to him that was not about the hour.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The new week's floor issue went up on the residence board the next morning, the seventy-sixth, a Second-day, in the ordinary way.

It was the usual half-sheet in the usual clerk's hand, dated twice and initialled twice in its corner, as everything the wing put out was. Supervised floor allocation, week following. Four lines. Cael read it standing at the board with the traffic of the passage going by behind him, as he read every issue, and on the fourth line he stopped.

The office numbered its halls on paper, as offices do, though nobody on the bluff ever said the numbers aloud. Hall one was the north hall, on stone. Hall three was the east, on timber. And his Sixth-day slot, the coming Sixth-day, the eightieth, which had been hall three every week since the allocation began, said hall one.

He knew at once how it had happened. It was the trade. Nine days ago he and Brom had swapped for a single Sixth-day, his hour on the timber for Brom's later hour on the stone, one week only, on a half-sheet he had carried to the counter himself. Somebody making up the new week's issue had copied from the wrong line of the ledger, from the traded week instead of the standing one, and carried a single week's exception forward as if it were the rule. It was the most ordinary mistake an office could make. A wing that issued paper for four hundred people must make it twice a week, and mend it whenever somebody came to the counter to complain.

He did not go to the counter.

He went to his lecture instead, and sat at the back, and did not hear a word of it. He spent the whole of it with the issue folded in his pocket, deciding.

It cost him almost nothing. That was the first thing to price. If he did nothing at all, then on Sixth-day he would walk to the north hall at the second bell, find the stone empty of any supervisor expecting him, walk across to the east hall, and lose perhaps a quarter of his session to the walk and the explaining. It was a nuisance. It was nothing more.

But to somebody who was building a map of Cael's week from the paper, it was not nothing. To that somebody, the issue said that at the second bell on Sixth-day Cael would be on the north hall's stone. So a man who read the paper and trusted it would be at the north hall's best post at the second bell, among whatever crowd the north hall gathered, looking down at an empty floor. He would lose a whole session's watching, every minute of it, to a clerk's slip that nobody had reported.

Unless he read the paper more carefully than that. Unless he read it the way he read the backs of sheets.

If the issue stayed wrong until Sixth-day, then the office did not read Cael's paper any closer than it read anybody's. If it came right on its own, without a word from Cael to anybody, then somebody in that wing was reading his sheets line by line, and minded a wrong line enough to put it right unasked.

He wrote the decision down that evening before he did anything else, because a decision he had not written down had a way of turning into an instinct he could not afterward examine.

Floor issue, Sixth-day the eightieth: hall one for hall three. The trade carried forward. Leaving it. I'll say nothing to the office, the board, or anybody. If it stays wrong, I walk across on the day and lose a quarter of an hour. If it comes right on its own, I'll know who reads my paper.

He looked at that, and then wrote a line under it, because Lira had a claim on the subject.

Lira's price: if he touches my paper wrong. This isn't his error. If he touches it at all, it'll be to put it right. I think that's outside her terms. I'll tell her either way.

Then he went to bed, and lay awake for an hour, not because he was worried but because he could not stop wondering what a man who never looked at him would do with a mistake he had not made.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The brackets posted the next morning, and for a day and a half the whole bluff thought about nothing else, and Cael thought about it with the rest of them, and the floor issue sat folded in his coat.

The next sheet went up on the Fifth-day, the seventy-ninth, among a dozen others, and he nearly walked past it.

Revised issue, it said at the head, in the office's hand. Two dates in the corner, two sets of initials, and not a word anywhere about why. He read down it from habit. First line, second, third. Fourth line, the coming Sixth-day: hall three.

The east hall. The timber. His own slot, where it had always been.

He did not take it down at once. He stood in front of it with the passage going by at his back, every voice in it still arguing about the brackets, and felt something deep in his chest roll slowly over, like a fish turning in cold water, and come up delighted.

Nobody had complained. He was certain of that, because the only person on the bluff with a reason to complain was himself, and he had been nowhere near the counter for three days. The clerk who made up the week's issues had not caught it; that clerk had made the mistake in the first place. Somebody else had sat down with the ledger in one hand and Cael's issue in the other and seen the single week's trade carried into a week where it did not belong. That somebody had known it was wrong, and had known that Cael would know it was wrong, because Cael read every line of every sheet as surely as the man at the copying table read the backs. And he had known that Cael had let it stand for three days without a word.

And he had mended it.

Cael went and sat on the stair at the end of the passage, out of the traffic, with the two sheets on his knee, the wrong one and the right one, and went over it the only way he really knew how to go over anything, which was as a bout.

It had been an exchange. He saw that now. He had opened it. He had let a wrong sheet stand on the board, deliberately, and that was a feed: a little weight put forward on purpose to see what the other man would do with it.

A man who wanted to catch Cael out would have let it ride and been at the north hall on Sixth-day to see whether Cael went there. A man who did not care would never have noticed. This man had done neither. He had answered the feed without touching it. He had simply done his work correctly and on time, with his initials on it twice, as though for anybody, and in doing so he had said, as clearly as if he had stood in front of Cael and spoken: I see what you did. I am not going to pretend I didn't. And I am going to go on doing my job properly, in plain sight, whatever you do.

No touch either way. Called even. Both men back to their chalk.

Cael folded the two sheets together and put them inside his coat, and went up to the rim of the Crown yard, where he knew he would find Lira reading the brackets for the tenth time with her arms folded. He gave her both sheets and told her the rest.

She read them, and gave them back, and was quiet.

"He touched your paper," she said.

"He mended it."

"I know what he did." She looked out over the empty floor. "It's outside my terms. I said wrong. You were right to keep it." She was quiet again. Then, much lower: "It's worse, though, isn't it? If he'd moved your hall to make you miss an hour, I'd know what he was. I'd be at Withrow's door by noon. Instead he's put it right. On time. Twice initialled." She shook her head slowly. "I don't know what to do about a man who does his work properly."

"No," said Cael. "Nor do I. I think that may be the point."

He did not write anything that afternoon. He waited until night, until the window was dark and the river was loud, and then he opened the binder to the day's page and wrote two lines under everything else, and sat over them with the pen still in his hand.

He fixed it. Sixth-day, hall three. Nobody asked him to.

We're playing now. Neither of us has said so. I don't think either of us is going to.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

He eased off the counting for four days after that, on purpose, because he had promised the Log that he would, once, at a time of his choosing, and see whether the read came back.

It was harder than he had expected. The shorthand had become a habit in a fortnight. He caught his eyes going to the turned post and the brass lamp and the second landing of the lecture stair a dozen times a day, and each time took them away again. He did not count. He did not write a single dot. He let the man stand wherever he stood, and went to his sessions and his lectures with his attention on nothing but what was in front of him, and on the fourth evening he went out to the wall to find out what that had bought.

Brom was at his post. Karis was feeding him, which was a sight Cael would have paid money to watch.

Karis could not feed. She knew everything about how a feed ought to be sold, in theory, in tremendous detail, and could have written a monograph on it, and her body did not believe a word of the monograph. She put her weight into her empty feeds with such earnest honesty that Brom turned on every one of them, and she pulled her honest ones up short out of sheer politeness, so that Brom let those go by. After ten minutes he had turned on twelve of thirteen empties and let all her real ones pass, and the two of them were laughing so hard that Brom had to hold onto the post.

"You're the worst feeder on this hill," said Brom, wiping his eyes.

"I'm the most honest feeder on this hill," said Karis. "That's the trouble. I can't make my body say something it doesn't mean." She looked at Cael. "Your turn. I'm going to sit down and be a scholar."

He took her place at the post and gave Brom a dozen feeds, honest and empty mixed, and Brom turned on seven of the eight empties, and groaned at himself, and said again. Then, without warning him, Cael asked Brom to feed him instead.

Brom came at him with his big hands open. The read laid his weight on Cael's forearm, left, then round, then dropping, and every time it laid it there in time. Not early, the way it had never been early. But on time, a full pace and a half, the old comfortable margin, the room he had lived in for two years without ever once noticing it was a room.

He stopped and stood still at the post, and found his hands were not quite steady.

"Back?" said Karis, who had been watching his face instead of the feeds.

"Back." He took out the Log and wrote it on his knee. Four days off the counting. Read on time, Brom feeding, a dozen calls. One instance. Not a rule until three.

Karis leaned over and read it upside down.

"You're going to go back to counting tomorrow," she said.

"Yes."

"And the read will go slow again."

"Yes."

"And you'll ease off again in a month to see if it comes back again, so you can write two." She did not sound disapproving. She sounded like a woman checking a sum. "Can I say one thing? As your scholar."

"You've never once asked before."

"I'm asking now, because it's going to annoy you." She tapped the binder on his knee, the shorthand section. "All of this. The galleries, the stair, the rail on the covered walk, the curve. It's beautiful work. It's the best thing you've ever done. And every line of it is the same instrument. Where a man stands, written down by you. You've measured it from a lot of different places, and on different days, and you've had me hold the pencil once or twice while you counted. But two hands on one instrument is still one instrument." She sat back. "You need a second leg under it. Something that doesn't come from where he stands."

"I know," said Cael. "I wrote that down."

"I know you wrote it down. I'm saying it out loud, so it's true in two places." Karis smiled. "That's what you've been teaching all of us, isn't it? Lira's been at you for a week about it. Say it, don't just file it."

Brom, at the post, groaned. "Are you two going to feed me or not?"

"Not," said Karis serenely. "We're going to sit here and be insufferable."

And they did, the three of them, along the coping in the last of the light, while Brom turned on nothing at his post and laughed at himself, and down across the river the grey coats changed at their lamp, on the bell, two and two.

Chapter 20 — Eleven Seconds

[Focused, analytical narration; make each tactical choice feel earned rather than announced]

The brackets went up two days before the floor sheet came right, at the first bell on the seventy-seventh morning, on the long board under the Crown yard's north stair. Cael was there before the porter had finished pinning the corners, because he had not come to read the brackets. He had come to watch people read them.

The sheets themselves he could have copied in a quarter of an hour. There were three of them, one to a column, ruled in Bracken's office in a clerk's careful hand. Down each ran the names in order, a number to the left of every one, and to the right a long row of blank squares, one for every session between now and the final, waiting for chalk.

Copper ran to ninety-one names. Two hundred and nine practitioners on the bluff could have put their names to it, and a few more than half had looked at what a season cost them in hours and bruises and missed lectures, and decided not to pay. Iron ran to sixty-three of its hundred and thirty-eight. The last sheet, headed Silver, held nineteen, gathered from the Bronze and Silver tiers together, all that the top of Halcenvane had been willing to put on a wall. The thinness of that last sheet, Cael thought, was the whole reason a school like this one stayed a school like this one. By the second bell the figures were in the binder.

Then he leaned on the rail of the north stair, a little above the board, and watched.

They came in ones and twos at first, and then in a steady stream, between the bells. Every one of them did the same thing first. He saw ninety-odd people do it that morning and not one failed to: they found their own name before they looked at anything else, with a small fierce hunt of the eyes, as if somebody might have left them off. Then, having found it, they did one of three things, and the three things told him more about the bluff than a month of corridors.

Most read upward. Their eyes went from their own name to the names above it, slowly, one at a time, and their lips moved. He could see them counting: four places up, the most the rules allowed a challenge to reach, and who was standing in those four places, and how they had looked on a practice afternoon. Those had come to climb. Some read downward instead, from their own name to the names below it, and their shoulders went very slightly up as they did it. Those had come to hold what they had. Cael noted, with real interest, that nearly all of the downward readers stood in the top third of a column, and that most of them were older, fourth-years and fifth-years. Holding was a thing people learned to want late.

And a few, a very few, did neither. They read the whole column at once, top to bottom. Then they turned and walked away.

In the Copper column he counted five of those all morning.

One was Lira. She came at the second bell with her hair still wet from the wash-house and read the ninety-one names in the time it would have taken him to read nine, and walked off toward the north hall without looking round, and he knew better than to follow her yet.

Another had been there before him, at the board's left end, quite still, her hands clasped at the small of her back. She went down the Copper names slowly, line by line, the way a quartermaster goes down a list of stores. Force Path. Copper Rank Eight. Fiske. Her own name stood at the very top of the column, with two seasons of results behind it in Bracken's files, and beside it, alone among the hundred and seventy-three names on all three sheets, a small brass stud pressed into the sheet like a button.

Cael had asked Bracken about that stud in his second week. Every other mark on the bluff's paper explained itself; that one said nothing, and he had not liked not knowing what it said.

"Holder," Bracken had said, without looking up from a ledger. "The name with the brass beside it holds the crown and is defending it. Fiske has had the stud two seasons. The porter puts it in himself. He's very particular about it. He polishes it."

Fiske finished reading, and stood a moment longer, and then went away along the bottom of the tiers with her hands still behind her back. She had not looked at her own name at all, Cael realized. She had found it first, as everybody did, and then never glanced at it again. She had read every other line on the sheet instead.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

He found Lira's name where he had stopped expecting to find it, and read it three times to be sure.

Twenty-two. Lira. Wind. Copper Rank Two. Transfer.

Twenty-second. The clerk had told her the foot, and he had not been wrong: in the ladder book, where names went down in the order they signed, she stood on the sixty-fifth line, the last. But the ladder book was not the bracket. Twenty-second of ninety-one.

The reason was pinned beside the sheets, on a half-page in Bracken's own small upright hand, headed Seeding, for anybody who cared to read it. Hardly anybody did. Cael did. A bracket was drawn only from the names that had paid to enter the season; the rest of the ladder book stood aside until next year. Names that had fought last season were seeded first, in last season's closing order. Of last season's Copper names, twenty-one had paid this season. Every other name went in below those twenty-one by formal rank, and then by the order of signing.

Cael stood and did that sum twice. Nearly every name that had not fought last season was a first-year, and nearly every first-year carried a fresh Arbiter's Rank One. Lira's paper said Rank Two. The one figure on her certificate that had ever helped her had lifted her over seventy people at a stroke and set her directly beneath the last of the old names.

Her paper and her place were two different measures, and only one of them would outlast the season. Copper Rank Two was her classification, written on her certificate by an Arbiter and changed only by an advancement evaluation. Twenty-second was her seed, a standing the ladder could move every six days and would wipe clean at the season's end.

He found her an hour later in the north hall, on the stone, alone, running her evasion sequence at a walk, which was what she did when she was angry and did not want to break anything.

"Twenty-second," he said from the doorway.

"I saw." She did not stop walking. "Read it before you were awake."

"It's six. From twenty-second, if you win every bout you're allowed and every one counts, it's six to the top. Not sixteen. You counted from the ladder book. The ladder book was the wrong book."

Lira came to the end of the sequence and stood still, looking at the floor.

"Rank Two," she said. "That's what did it, isn't it? I read the half-sheet. The new names go in by rank." She laughed, but not as if anything were funny. "Two years I've been trying to get out from under what that paper says I am. And the first time it's ever done me a single kindness, it's because it's wrong in my favour by one rank instead of five." She rolled her neck. "Six. I'll take six. I'll even say thank you to it, once, out loud, here, where nobody can hear." She did not say it. "There. Done."

"There's a draw first," said Cael. "The first three sessions are drawn, not challenged. The half-sheet says so at the bottom. Every name gets paired once against somebody from a different part of its column, so the column can have a look at itself. The results go in the record. They don't move anybody."

"I read that too." Lira picked up her towel. "I've drawn a Stone Path. Ninth. Nyle."

Cael had Nyle already. Everybody on the ladder was in the binder by now, one page each, and Nyle's was one of the fuller ones because Cael had watched him twice on practice afternoons out of pure liking. He was a third-year, Copper Rank Five, broad through the shoulders with a settled, comfortable stance, a dozen wins across two seasons in Bracken's files.

Stone was a slow Path to gather, and Nyle had learned, the way the best Stone fighters did, to make the slowness look like patience, so that an opponent waited for him when he ought to have been moving. A Stone fighter's weight could not bluff. It was the working itself, so whatever it promised, it meant, and the craft of the Path lay entirely in timing: bring it down at the instant that hurt most, and never mind who saw it coming. He breathed out through the gather, low, so that you could hear it from the tiers.

He's good, Cael had written the night the draw went up. He'll be gone in under two minutes. I don't think anyone has told him.

He did not say so to Lira. She did not need anything said to her. She had read Nyle's page over his shoulder at breakfast without asking, which she did with every page in the binder that had her name near it, and had handed it back and gone on with her bread.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Her bout was the season's second session, on a bright still afternoon, and the tiers were three-quarters full, which was a great crowd for the second session of anything. A good many of them, Cael guessed, had climbed the tiers for a look at the girl from the little school in the north, the one with a flag on her paper and a circuit behind her that nobody here could check.

He sat high on the east side, where he always sat. In the curve of the brass lamp, without looking for it, he saw a small figure high on the west side in a knot of five, with something pale against its chest. He put it out of his mind. He had promised the Log four days without counting, and this was the first of them.

Lira and Nyle went down into the sunk floor and to their chalk. The adjudicating instructor read the terms aloud from the table, first to three clean touches, any exchange the floor could not split called even and run again, and the second instructor stood off at the edge with his hands loose for safety. The noise of the yard did what it always did at that moment. It thinned and went away, and there was only the floor.

Nyle began his gather.

It was correct. It was what every Stone fighter on the bluff would have done against a smaller, quicker opponent: start the weight moving early, slow and heavy, and make her choose a side before he had to. Whichever side she chose, he would land on it. The yard had seen that gather beat the Copper column a dozen times.

Lira chose a side.

Cael felt it go before he saw it: a fold low in his own hips, a held half-breath closing in his own chest, three years of having her architecture in his body pulling at him from forty feet up like a hand on his sleeve. Her first burst went left, and meant it. He saw Nyle's gather begin to swing to meet it, the great honest weight leaning toward where she was going to be. She was not there by the time it leaned. The landing beat caught her in the open a pace and a half to his left, locked for its half-breath, and Nyle could not use it; his weight was still on its way to the place she had left. When the beat let go of her she stepped in under his reaching arm and laid her flat hand on his ribs.

"Touch," said the table. "Wind. One."

Three seconds, Cael thought. One burst. His own hip told him the price, low and plain: the half-breath at the front, the jolt at the back, the line from crest to knee that would start to write itself out tonight.

Back to chalk. Nyle had seen it. He began the gather again, but shorter, holding more weight back, so that if she went left again he could come round without leaning. It was a good answer. It was the right answer to what she had just done.

She did something else. She went straight at him, and halfway there went right, short and quick, and the right was real too, and his held-back weight was held back on the wrong side. Two bursts. The touch landed on his leading shoulder from behind and to the side while the landing beat still had her by the collar. She had used the beat as a place to stand still and reach from.

"Wind. Two."

Six seconds, near enough. Cael's hip had stopped being a promise and become a fact.

On the third exchange Nyle did not gather at all. He stood with his weight down and his hands up, very still, and waited for her to commit first, which was the bravest thing he did all afternoon and the only thing left to him.

She committed. She showed him left on her feet alone, a half-step with no Wind in it, and his weight leaned after it. Then the third burst took her right, and the instant its landing beat let go of her the fourth began, with no gap at all between the end of one and the start of the next, which Cael had never seen anybody do and could not have done himself. The third had put her inside his reach. The fourth was a short one, a burst no longer than a stride, that left her standing at his back on the side of his front shoulder, with every part of his stance facing the place she had been.

Then she touched the back of his front knee, just as all his weight arrived on that leg. It was hardly a strike at all. The knee simply folded, and Nyle went down heavily and well, onto his hip and shoulder as he had been taught. The safety instructor's hand was up before he landed.

"Wind," said the table. "Three. Bout."

Eleven seconds. Cael had counted them in his own breath without meaning to, from the table's first word to its last, the walks back to chalk left out. Three exchanges. Four bursts. And his own hip, forty feet up and three years away from where it had first learned this, ached with each of them in turn. It knew the whole bill: toll at the front, jolt at the back, and the hot line from crest to inner thigh that would be written out on her by suppertime and still legible at breakfast. She had known that price at breakfast. She had read Nyle's page over his shoulder and decided, between two mouthfuls of bread, what the bout was worth to her, and she had spent precisely that and kept the rest.

Then the yard did something he had not expected.

It went quiet.

He would fill two pages with it that night. Behind him the two Iron girls who had been arguing all afternoon stopped in the middle of a word. A first-year on the row below had both hands raised to clap and did not bring them together. The law lecturer who slept on the fourth tier every practice day was awake, and sitting up, with his hat in his lap. Two rows down a Copper fifth-year shut her notebook, slowly. For perhaps four seconds some eight hundred people on stone made no sound at all.

It was not the hush of people who have been impressed. Impressed was loud, a roar and a stamping. Cael had heard this other quiet twice before, both times in the Ironyard, both times on nights when something happened on the boards that the crowd had no place in its head to put. Every person in that yard had been handed the sheet that morning and had believed it, as you believe a printed timetable. They had trusted that ninety-one names had been put in their right order by people who knew. And now, in eleven seconds, in front of all of them, the sheet had been caught out about one name, beyond any argument, and every one of them knew it at once, and not one of them could have said what it was they knew.

It was the sound of a category failing.

Then somebody high on the north side began to clap, and the rest took it up a beat late and a little too loud, and the yard was itself again, slightly ashamed of having been anything else.

Nyle sat up on the floor, and shook his head, and laughed, and let Lira give him a hand up. By the sheet he was the ninth-best Copper practitioner on the hill, and Cael did not doubt it; he had watched him earn it. By the sheet Lira was the twenty-second. Both figures were honest. Neither of them had been watching.

Down below the long board, where the results clerk was already reaching up with his chalk, Fiske had not moved. She had not moved for the whole of it, and she did not clap now. She stood with her hands at the small of her back and looked across the floor at Lira, who was standing alone in the middle of it with one palm pressed flat to her own thigh and her face showing nothing at all. And Fiske dipped her chin, once, a very small movement, made to nobody. It was the nod you give a guest you have been laying a place for, year after year, without ever knowing whose face would be in the doorway.

Then she turned and went back to the sheet, as if to make sure nothing on it had changed. Nothing had. That, Cael thought, was rather the trouble.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Brom was drawn for the third session. Nothing about his bout resembled hers, and Cael would come to think he had learned more from it.

His draw was Merrick: Shield Path, Copper Rank Four, fourteenth on the sheet, a fourth-year with a long face and a careful way of putting his feet down, as if every floor he stood on might have been laid by somebody who disliked him. He was no fool. Cael had a page on him, not a long one, but every line of it said the same thing in a different way: Merrick did not do what you expected, and he did not do what he wanted; he did what you could least afford.

And the whole cohort knew about Brom's seam. That was the thing Cael kept coming back to, on the east side of the tiers with the binder on his knee. It had been a private flaw once. Wray had found it at Greyvane with her own two hands, the gap in Brom's redirect between the read and the turn, and it had cost him nothing there, because nobody at Greyvane had been quick enough to get into it. Then Ephram had found it in three sessions on the east hall's timber, and spent a fortnight showing everyone else where it was. By now half the Copper column could have drawn it on a slate.

Hitting an Iron Skin hard was a fool's game, and Merrick was no fool. He fed him instead.

On the first exchange he came in with a short, cheap strike, committed enough to look real, light enough that turning it would buy nothing, and Brom turned it, as Brom turned everything. Merrick went past him a stride off balance. Brom's open hand came down on his back.

"Touch. Iron Skin. One."

The tiers around Cael stirred, pleased. They liked Brom. Everybody liked Brom.

Cael did not stir. He had seen Merrick's face as he went back to his chalk. It was not the face of a man who had lost a touch. It was the face of a man who had paid a copper for a look at the goods.

The second exchange was the first again, twice over: two more cheap feeds, each arriving with just enough weight to make the turn the obvious answer and so little that the turn won nothing. Brom turned on both, honestly, with his whole body, as Rooke's post had not yet taught him not to. And then, on the third feed, Merrick did not feed. He waited for the turn to begin, saw Brom's weight go out to meet a strike that was not there, and stepped into the gap behind it.

His hand landed flat and clean along Brom's jaw.

"Shield. One each."

The third exchange went the same way, faster, because Merrick no longer needed the first two feeds to set it up. One cheap strike, one turn, one gap, and the second touch: harder this time, though Merrick had not meant it to be, a strike that caught Brom's head while it was still coming round from the turn. Brom's head went round further than a head goes on purpose. On the east side somebody said "Oh," quietly.

"Shield. Two to one."

One more, and the bout was Merrick's.

Brom went back to his chalk slowly. He stood on it with his hands at his sides and his head down, and for a moment Cael thought he was simply hurt and gathering himself. Then he saw Brom's lips moving, very slightly, the way they moved on the east hall's floor when he was counting, and understood that Brom was not gathering himself at all. He was thinking.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

On the fourth exchange Brom stopped turning.

He did not announce it. Nobody but Cael, and perhaps three people in the whole yard, would have known what they were looking at. Merrick came in with his cheap feed just as before, and Brom did not turn on it. He did not turn on anything. He simply stood and took it, square, on the forearm, with Iron Skin hardening under the blow as it always had and not one ounce of his weight going out to send it anywhere.

There was a dull flat sound, like a mallet on a wet post.

It was not a touch. The table did not call it. A strike taken on a set, hardened guard was not clean; it had arrived exactly where Brom had decided it would. But it had cost him. Cael could see the cost from forty feet away. Iron Skin hardened on a fuel neither of them had ever managed to name, though they had both tried, and the fuel ran out, and it ran out faster under blow after blow with nowhere to send them. The turn had always been the thing that paid the hardening back, by passing the force along. Without the turn every strike stayed where it landed, and Brom had to hold it there himself.

Merrick fed again, puzzled, and Brom took it again. A third time, and the third was not a feed at all but a real strike, full weight, to test whether the big man really meant it. He did. He took that one square too, on the forearm and into the shoulder, and Cael saw the guard come up a fraction slower afterward than it had before. He heard Brom's breathing go short and hard and rationed, like a man climbing a long hill at the end of a long day.

Three strikes, flat, at the full price, with no return on any of them. It was the dearest way an Iron Skin practitioner could spend a minute, and Brom spent it like a man paying a debt he had decided was fair.

Merrick stepped back, and looked at him, and Cael watched him think. There was no gap any more, because there was no turn to open one. The only way left to Brom's body was through the front of it, and the front of it had become a door.

So Merrick did what a clever man does when his trick stops working. He assumed it would start working again. He came in with a feed, and then, sure that the old habit must come back if he only gave it a moment, he committed to the gap a fourth time, his whole weight going into the place where Brom's turn had always left him open.

The turn did not come. The gap did not open. Merrick, all his weight committed, arrived at a shoulder that ought by every rule he knew to be swinging out of his way, and found it standing where it was, set and hard as a gatepost.

He bounced. That was the only word for it. While he was still finding his feet Brom's open hand came down on the side of his neck.

"Iron Skin. Two each."

The fifth exchange was ugly and short. Merrick did not feed; he had nothing left to feed with. He came in carefully, at the front of the door, looking for a way through it, and Brom stood still and let him look and took one more on the forearm, flat, with his breath sawing. Then he put his hand on Merrick's breastbone the moment the strike had spent itself.

"Iron Skin. Three to two. Bout."

The yard applauded, warmly, the way it applauded things it had not followed but liked the look of. Most of it would have forgotten the bout by supper. Cael had a page and a half on his knee before Brom was off the floor, and at the top of it, underlined twice, the only three words he was sure of: ugly, expensive, intelligent. The yard had seen the first two. The third was the whole of it. It had been an ugly, expensive, entirely intelligent win, made by a man who had stood in the middle of a bout he was losing and put down the best thing he owned because it had become the thing they were beating him with.

Brom came up the steps out of the sunk floor slowly, carrying his left arm close, with a dark line coming up along his jaw where the second touch had caught him. He sat down on the bench at the floor's edge and put his head back against the stone and shut his eyes.

Rooke was in front of him.

Cael had not seen him come down. He had not seen him in the yard at all. He was simply there, narrow and grey in his dark coat, standing in front of the bench with his hands loose at his sides and his weight even on both feet, looking down at Brom, who opened his eyes and found him there and did not move.

Rooke looked at him for the time it takes to draw three breaths and let them go. Then he spoke, in the same flat voice he used for everything.

"Again. Slower. Watch yourself."

He turned and went back the way he must have come, up the south steps, without hurrying and without looking round.

Brom sat for a moment longer. Then he leaned forward and began patting his coat, which lay on the bench under two other people's, and went through every pocket, and finally found what he wanted in a tear in the lining: a pencil worn down to the length of a thumbnail. He unwound the wrap on his right wrist, the right one, which had nothing on it, not the left with Rooke's long sentence inked on the inside where only he would ever feel it. On the outside of the cloth, where anybody passing could have read it, he wrote four words, pressing so hard Cael could see the pencil bend.

Cael did not go down to him. He watched from the bottom of the tiers, and then went up and out and back to the quadrangle with the binder under his arm, and found that he was turning it over the whole way, and the next day, and for most of the week.

The ink had been chosen. Brom had carried that sentence about for days before he wrote it, and had put it on the inside of the cloth on purpose, where it would press against his pulse and nobody else would ever see it. It had been a keepsake.

This was nothing like that. This was four words in pencil, on the outside, written on the spot by a man with his head still ringing who did not trust himself to remember them as far as the gate.

In two years Cael had seen Brom keep every sort of thing in every sort of way, in his hands and his feet and his tally book and the long patient memory of his body. Not once, until today, had Brom needed paper to hold a thing for him.

Chapter 21 — Instruments

[Focused, analytical narration; make each tactical choice feel earned rather than announced]

There was a first-year on the third practice ring who would not stop.

It had been raining since the morning, a thin grey rain that made the chalk run and the boards slick, and the tiers were nearly empty. Cael was there because he was always there. The first-year was there because, as far as Cael could tell, she had decided the season was going to be won by whoever turned up on the days nobody else did. She was a Current practitioner, small and wiry, with her hair plastered flat to her skull, and she had fought four practice bouts that afternoon and lost three of them. Between bouts she stood under the eaves of the north stair, wringing water out of her sleeves, watching the next pair with a ferocious attention, and then she put her name on the slate again.

Her fifth was against a Blade second-year a head taller than she was, and Cael watched it from the empty fourth tier with the rain running off the brim of his hood.

She lost the first touch in about the time it took to blink. The Blade boy came in long and straight and she rode his line the way Current fighters were taught, going along the force instead of against it, and the boards were wet, and her back foot went out from under her on the chalk. She sat down hard. The instructor at the table said "Touch, Blade," without lifting his eyes from the register. She got up. She did not look at the table, or at the tiers, or at anything but the Blade boy's lead foot.

The second touch was hers. It was not pretty. She went in low, deliberately short, on the wet board where her own foot had failed her, and when he came long and straight again she did not ride his line at all. She let it go over her shoulder and came up inside it with her palm on his breastbone, so close he could not have struck her if he had tried. The boy blinked down at the hand on his chest as if somebody had put it there while he was not looking.

He took the third and the fourth, cleanly, because he was a year older and a head taller and simply better, and the bout was his three to one. She shook his hand. Then she went back under the eaves of the north stair and wrung out her sleeves again, and stood with her eyes on the next pair, and Cael saw her mouth moving as if she were saying something over to herself so as not to lose it.

He did not know her name. He wrote her down by her smock and her Path and the touch she had taken off the wet board, went short where she slipped; used the slip, and then, because he was curious, went to look for her on the sheet.

She was seventy-fourth.

He did the sum on the steps, roughly, in his head, and then did not believe it. So he went down to the long reading room under the law range and did it properly, on paper, with the session calendar from the board by the theater door and a copy of Bracken's half-sheet on seeding laid beside it.

The ladder's rules he already knew by heart. A challenge went up the column, four places at the most, and a win took the loser's place. So the quickest any name could climb was four places in an afternoon, every afternoon, against the highest name it was allowed to reach, without a loss.

The calendar was the part nobody had put beside the rules.

It gave a Copper name a bout about once in six days, when the pairings fell kindly. From the posting to the final was a little over a hundred days. Seventeen bouts at the very most, then, and the first of the seventeen was the drawn bout, which counted in the record and moved nobody on the sheet. Sixteen that could move a name. And that was for a name that was never injured, never deferred, never left standing on its afternoon without anybody to fight.

He put the first-year's number in. Seventy-fourth. To reach the four names that would fight the final she needed to climb seventy places, four at a time, which was eighteen wins in a row.

She had sixteen bouts.

He sat and looked at it. He went up the column a line at a time to find where the arithmetic opened again, and found it at sixty-eighth. From sixty-eighth, a perfect season would just reach the final. From sixty-ninth and every line below it, no season could. Twenty-three names at the foot of the Copper sheet, a quarter of it, could not reach the crown even if they never lost a bout from the posting to the last day. They had been unable to reach it since the porter pressed the first pin into the board. Nothing had shut them out but a calendar and a rule, each of which, taken alone, was perfectly sensible.

And every one of the twenty-three, so far as he could tell, was out on the rings in the rain, fighting for it.

He did the sum again from the other end, slowly, then took it two floors up to carrel eleven and laid it on the commentary Karis was reading.

She read it with her finger under each line. She checked the calendar against the copy in her own notes, and the half-sheet against her memory of the half-sheet, which was better than the half-sheet. Then she turned the paper over and did the whole thing herself on the back, in her quick small hand, and came out where he had come out. She sat back and looked more annoyed than he had seen her all term, which from Karis was the highest praise a piece of work could get.

"Twenty-three," she said.

"Twenty-three. There's a girl in a Current smock fighting on the third ring in the rain right now who's seventy-fourth."

"It isn't malicious."

"I know it isn't."

"Somebody drew up that calendar years ago, for a shorter column. Somebody else wrote the four-place rule for another reason entirely, and probably a good one. Nobody's ever laid one on top of the other." She tapped the foot of the sheet, where the twenty-three were. "The people it shuts out are all down here. Nobody down here has been taught how to do this sum. And nobody up at the top has ever needed to."

"Somehow that's worse."

"It almost always is," said Karis, already writing. "Can I keep this?"

"It's yours. I made a copy."

"Of course you did." Her pen did not stop. "Is anybody going to tell her? The girl on the third ring?"

Cael thought about it.

"I don't know," he said. "If somebody told me there was no way through, I'd want to know. And then I'd go out and fight anyway, to see." He looked at the sum. "I think she already would. I think that's why she's out there."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

There was another way to read the same sheet, from the top down, and that was the way the rest of the bluff read it.

Cael took it to Bracken, because it was a matter of record, and Bracken was the record.

The registrar looked up from the same bare desk in the same bare room with the expression of a man who has been stopped halfway down a long column and would like to be told the interruption is worth the column. Cael asked him whether the season's standings decided the tournament squad.

"No," said Bracken. He laid his pen down square to the desk's edge. "They are evidence. They are admissible. They are not a verdict. I would be grateful if nobody in your hearing confused those three words. Nor a standing with a rank. A standing is this season's chalk. A rank is what the registry has written on a certificate, and the registry does not read our wall." He folded his hands. "Next year this academy will contest the qualifying season for the Continental. The chancellor has said so in an open address; it is on the record, so I may repeat it. A squad will be chosen. The people choosing it will read this season's closing standings among a great deal else. A strong season will not put a name on that squad. A weak one will very probably keep a name off it." He picked his pen back up. "Your friend from the north stands near the foot of a column she plainly does not belong in. If she climbs, it will be noticed. If she does not, that will be noticed too. That is all I may tell you, and rather more than I ought."

It explained the upper ends of the boards, which had puzzled Cael for a week. The Iron column and the thin Silver sheet fought every session with a kind of grim care, as if each afternoon were being written into a book that would be read aloud next year. That was what each afternoon was. The names near their tops were not fighting for a circlet in a glass case. They were fighting to be read.

And it threw a hard new light on Fiske.

He watched her that week on a practice afternoon, fighting a nervous first-year as a courtesy, which the Copper holder did once a session by custom. She was not fighting him to win; she had won before the first exchange. She was fighting him to show him something. She let him come, and come again, and on the third time put her small flat push into the boards an inch in front of his lead foot, very slowly, so that he could feel where it had gone and why he had stumbled. Then she told him in a few quiet words what she had done, and walked him back to his chalk, and did it again a little faster.

She was the best Copper fighter Cael had ever seen. Her certificate said Copper Rank Eight, and had said Rank Eight for two years. Rank, like tier, was a word an Arbiter wrote on a certificate after an advancement evaluation; no bout on any ladder could add a number to it, and while her paper said Copper, the Copper bracket was the only bracket she could fight in. No registry had written a word about Fiske in two years, because nobody had asked one to. Lira had worked out in a wash-house, over a pair of ruined shirts, why nobody had asked.

That left her the crown and nothing else. She had reached the top of the Copper sheet as a first-year, and had been standing up there ever since like a woman at the top of a stair with no landing. The only thing the ladder still had to offer her was a circlet she had already worn home twice.

Cael began her page that night as he began everybody's, with rhythm and weight and breath. By the end of it he found he had stopped writing about Fiske at all. He was writing about the cage.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He went to every session after that, all of them, not only the ones his friends fought in. Copper and Iron afternoons, the Silver sheet's rare bouts, the practice rings in between. A dozen Paths fought somewhere on the three sheets, and by the fourth session every one of them had its page. He did not expect all of them to be right by the end of the season, and he wrote that on the first page too.

The Iron afternoons had Ephram, and Ephram had a rail.

He would not have called it a court. He came to the yard when the ladder told him to, fought, and won, without making anything of it; he was Iron Rank Six and the highest-ranked enrollee on the bluff, and he carried it like a man carrying an umbrella on a day it was not raining. But between his bouts he stood at the lower rail on the west side, and five or six of Rooke's cohort stood round him. When a bout on the floor ended he took it apart for them, exchange by exchange, in a low even voice he never raised, and the circle of people within hearing grew a little every afternoon, because people had learned to stop talking when he started.
