Eight days after the pin came the fifteenth session, and for a week beforehand there was nobody on the bluff who did not know what it meant.

Lira sent her challenge up to the top line on the morning the cards were made, in her own hand, on the clerk's slip: her name, the arrow, and the name with the brass stud beside it. She did it before breakfast and told nobody, and by the time the three of them came into the refectory, half the room had already read the board.

On paper it was a challenge upward of a single place, the only kind there was, from the second line of the standings to the first. Underneath that it was the seeding of the final, since whoever held the top line at the season's close fought her semifinal on the earlier day and came to the final rested. And underneath that, it was a thing Cael found he could only say plainly in the observation notebook, on the night before, at the foot of three weeks of pages headed Fiske.

Tomorrow is the first time all season either of them meets somebody the ladder didn't hand her. Everyone else Fiske has fought this year, the bracket built for her. Everyone Lira's fought, the bracket built for somebody else. Tomorrow neither of them is what the paper says, and both of them know it, and they're the only two people on the sheet who do.

Lira found him in the north hall that last evening, after his hour, while he was rolling the cords. She had been running the sequence at half pace on the stone, the short fourth after the half-step, over and over, and she stopped and stood with her towel and asked him one thing.

"How long does she collect?"

"A minute and a half," said Cael. "The same as the first day. Near enough every time. Both her bad openings fall inside it."

"Every time?"

"Four bouts since you sent it. Four pages. A minute and a half, and then the doors start closing." He looked at her. "Why?"

Lira did not answer. She folded the towel in half and in half again, precisely, and hung it over her shoulder, and he saw her lips move once, as Karis's moved before a clause, on a number.

"Go to bed," she said. "You look worse than me."

He had watched Fiske, Force Path, Copper Rank Eight on a certificate two years old, fight four times since Lira's decision, as Lira had wanted him to. Four pages. On every one of them the same thing: a minute and a half of collecting, two bad openings, and then the floor closing behind her opponents like doors in a long corridor, one after another, until there was nowhere left to stand. Fiske never struck anybody. She put her force into the boards where they were about to be, and they arrived on it, and stumbled, and found her hand on them.

On the evening before the bout, crossing the covered walk, Lira and Fiske passed each other under the north stair, in front of the board where both their names stood one above the other.

Cael was ten paces behind and saw it; neither of them stopped walking.

"Fifteenth," said Fiske.

"Fifteenth," said Lira.

That was the whole of it. Fiske went on toward the halls with her hands at the small of her back, and Lira went on toward the residence with her weight on the ball of her right foot, and neither looked round.

The next afternoon the yard was full to the rail.

Cael had never seen it full, though he had seen it crowded, for Nyle and for the Shield fifth-year, with people standing at the backs of the tiers. This was something else. Every tier on all four sides was packed from the lowest step to the rail at the top, and people sat on the steps of the north stair and stood in the archways and leaned out of the windows of the lecture range opposite. The faculty box on the north side had every seat taken and three people standing at its back. The standings clerk, who sat at a small table by the long board for every session of every season, was standing up.

Withrow sat in the west gallery, upright and white-haired, with two people from Ostrand on either side of her whose coats Cael priced, without wanting to, at about a year of residence fees apiece.

He counted, because he could not help counting crowds, the Silver-sheet enrollees he could see on the tiers. Twelve. There had not been more than two at any Copper bout all season.

He did not look for the man with the forms. Twenty-five days now he had kept his eyes off the man. But the brass hood of the lamp hung where it always hung, at the edge of his eye. In its curve the upper east tier lay in afternoon shade, and in the shade, third in a knot of six, a small figure stood with something pale against its chest.

He looked away, at the floor, where the porter was chalking the ring for the last time, slowly, with the face of a man who knew that he was being watched by more people than had ever watched him do anything.

Lira was on the bench at the floor's edge with her towel round her neck and her eyes shut. Brom sat beside Cael on the east tier, very upright, as he sat in church. Karis was on Cael's other side with the grey notebook open on her knee at a fresh page, and she had written the date at the top of it and nothing else, and her pencil was not moving.

Fiske came down the north steps into the sunk floor without hurry, and went to her chalk, and looked at the door frame before she looked at the door.

The adjudicating instructor stood at the table and read the terms in a voice that carried to the rail. A challenge upon the holder's line. Four exchanges, each on the table's glass, each to the cleaner touch or called even. The bout to the practitioner holding more touches at the close of the fourth. A drawn bout to leave the holder where she stood.

The glass was turned, and the sand began to run.

"Begin," said the table.

Chapter 29 — Four Exchanges

[Measured, public-facing narration; hold the spectacle at a human scale]

Karis wrote one line for each exchange. Cael read them afterward on her grey page, four lines in her small upright hand, and found that between them they told the whole bout more truly than his six.

One. L. spends nothing. Why?

Before the word, Lira did what she had done before every bout since the Ironyard: crouched at her chalk, laid the flat of one hand on the boards, stood, and rolled her neck once each way. Fiske, across the chalk, kept her hands clasped behind her and studied the boards between them.

At the table's word, Fiske gave ground.

She always did; Cael had four pages that said so. Her art lived in arriving early, at the place another fighter was about to be, and she could not arrive early anywhere until she knew the fighter, so for the first stretch of every bout she was only learning, and learning made her clumsy. She stepped back off her line in the first breaths, and then again, nearly over her own chalk. Two openings, just as the pages promised, and on the tiers a hundred people sat forward at once.

Lira let both of them go by.

She did not even look at them. She stood on her chalk after the word, quite still, with her weight on the ball of her right foot. Then she began, at a walk, to run her evasion sequence.

Cael knew it the instant he saw the first step. Everybody who had ever trained beside her knew it. It was the drill she ran on the north hall's stone at half pace whenever her hip would let her do nothing else: nine movements, always in the same order, a step left and a check, a turn, two steps right along an arc, a fold and a rise, round and back to where she began. She had run it ten thousand times. She ran it now on the yard's boards in front of eight hundred people at the pace of somebody showing a child how to tie a knot, with no Wind in it anywhere, and when she reached the end she began it again from the start.

Fiske watched it.

Cael watched Fiske watch it, and felt the back of his neck go cold. Lira was teaching her. Step by step, slowly enough for anyone to follow, she was laying out the order her feet liked to go in and the places they liked to go, and the woman across from her, who lived on knowing where people would be, was taking down every word. He saw Fiske's head tilt a hair at the turn. He saw her weight shift a hair toward the arc before Lira reached it, the second time round. The third time, Fiske's eyes were on the place where the fold would come before Lira had begun the step that led to it.

Lira tested her guard twice in passing, a hand going out low, a hand going out high, with nothing behind either. They were only part of the drill.

The sand ran down, and at the table every eye went to the glass.

"Even," said the instructor. "No touch. First exchange."

A groan went round the tiers like wind through standing corn, the noise of people who have paid for a fight and been shown a dance. Behind Cael somebody said distinctly, she's thrown that away. Down on the south tier the cohort sat in their dark knot and looked at one another and did not seem sure.

"Why?" said Karis, beside him, very low. The pencil sat idle where the line ended.

"She asked me last night how long Fiske collects." Cael kept his eyes on the boards. "I told her a minute and a half. So she gave her two minutes. She gave her everything she wanted to know, and every bit of it was true. That's her sequence. That's what she does when she's left alone."

Karis's gaze went from him to the page and stayed there, and the pencil did not move again.

Two. F. closes the doors. F. one.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Fiske took the second exchange, and took it the way a locksmith takes a door.

At the word, Lira went into the sequence again, at speed now, the first step left and the check. Fiske was already there. Not at Lira. At the place the step after the check would have gone. Her declaration went into the boards there, short and flat, without any show at all, and the boards there turned to something no foot could trust, a smooth hard slickness lying over the oak like oil on a stair. Lira saw it and broke off the turn.

Fiske had already shut the arc.

A second declaration, three beats after the first, into the place the sequence went next. Lira broke off again, and the third went down behind her, into the stretch of floor the fold would have brought her through, and in a dozen heartbeats there was nowhere on the boards that the sequence could reach. Lira stood in a narrow patch of honest wood with oil on three sides of it, and every edge of the patch had been drawn by Fiske, from the copy Lira herself had handed her a minute earlier.

Cael found that he was gripping the binder hard enough to bend its board.

He had charted Force on five floors. Nobody he had charted could have done that, and she had not hit anybody. She had read a page and closed it, line by line, faster than the girl who had written it could turn over.

He wrote it down, honestly, on Fiske's page and not Lira's, because a page that only ever praised his friends would have been no better than a letter home.

She isn't fighting Lira. She's fighting the drill Lira showed her. She's right about every step of it, because every step of it was true.

Lira went for the last open side on her own feet, quick and low, and Fiske was there before her. Her flat hand landed on Lira's shoulder.

"Force. One."

On the tiers a long breath went out, and somebody behind Cael said there, in the satisfied voice of a man who has seen a picture straightened on a wall.

"One to none," said Brom, from Cael's left. His voice was very quiet. "Two left."

"She needs both," said Karis. "If it ends level, Fiske keeps the line."

"I know," said Brom. "I'm only saying two is a lot."

Lira walked back to her chalk. At the turn she glanced down at the slick patches already fading from the boards, and then, for an instant, across at the place behind Fiske where nothing had been closed.

Three. L. runs the sequence and lies at four places. F.'s fourth goes into the floor. One each.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

At the word, Lira went into the sequence again.

The same first step left, the same check, and Fiske put her declaration into the place where the turn came next, as she had in the second exchange, and Lira's turn did not come. A burst came instead, the first Wind of the bout, and it took her not round the turn but straight past it, a stride beyond where the sequence had ever gone in ten thousand runs, onto clean wood.

Fiske's force lay on the oak behind her, a slick patch on a stretch of floor nobody was standing on.

The arc next. Fiske shut it, from the copy, a beat early, exactly right. The second burst took Lira out of the arc's middle in the wrong direction, inward instead of out, toward Fiske, which the drill had never once done. Fiske's force went down on the arc's far end and found nothing on it.

Then the fold.

The fold was where the sequence always paused, a half-breath down and up. It was also, Cael saw with a shock that went through his own hip, where a third burst would end if a fighter had taken two before it: the exact place the cohort's plan had marked, the third landing, the beat when a Wind fighter on this sheet stood locked and spent in front of a fresh opponent. Every fighter in the Copper column knew that beat now, Fiske among them. Her third declaration was already going down under it.

Lira burst into it. Then, from inside the last of the landing beat, she took a half-step.

It was nothing. A shift of one foot sideways, short, with no Wind in it, so small that most of the yard never saw it and those who did thought she had slipped. It moved her a foot, and Fiske's third went into the boards a foot from Lira's heel instead of under it.

The fourth burst came from there, from a place nobody counting landings would ever have stood to wait.

Cael felt all four go in his own leading hip, forty feet up. Four held breaths, not one returned; the last she paid for with breath borrowed from tomorrow. Four landing beats, four half-breaths locked in place, every one of them standing still in front of the one woman on the bluff who could hit a still thing before it knew it was still. And the hip. From the tier he watched the leading side take the load, and take it, and take it again, and the line it was drawing down her thigh was one he had drawn in himself at two bursts and never dared carry to four.

All four went to a single purpose. She had run her own sequence, the true one, the one she had shown Fiske, and lied with it at four places. Four times Fiske's force had gone where the copy said the girl must be. Four times the girl had gone somewhere else, not by any trick of her weight or her lean, but because the burst did not come out of her weight or her lean at all.

Fiske's fourth declaration was building.

Cael saw her see it: shoulders squaring, the force gathering, and the place it was for already empty. She stopped it. A Force practitioner can stop, if she will pay everything she has built to do it, and the force has to go somewhere when she does. Fiske sent it down. It went into the oak at her own feet with a flat, wrong crack, like a beam splitting in a roof, and eight hundred people drew one breath at once.

Lira's hand was on Fiske's ribs before the sound had finished.

"Wind. One each."

Four. F. stops placing. L. walks in. L. two to one.

Neither of them had anything left to stand behind, and both of them knew it.

Fiske could not read the girl any more. Whatever she had been reading had stopped meaning what it said, and she knew it. Cael watched the knowledge settle into the line of her mouth as she walked back to her chalk. So at the word she did the only thing left to a champion whose instrument has been broken over her head in front of her whole hill. She stopped placing. She built, and committed, and came straight at Lira with a plain heavy delivery, the Force that every other Force fighter on the sheet had always used.

Not one bout all season had she fought like the rest of the column. Now she did, and from her, even so, it was frightening.

Four bursts gone, the whole of her ceiling. If one remained, it would be slow, and short, and paid for all week. Cael sat on the tier with his hands locked on the binder and did the sum and came to that number just before Lira came to the moment of needing it.

She did not need it.

She stepped in on her own feet. Not the Wind's feet: the feet a foundry floor at Ardenmere had given her over two winters, when she had been younger and poorer and had learned that a burst you can't pay for is a burst you haven't got. She went toward the delivery at a slant, so that its edge caught her across the left shoulder instead of its whole weight across the chest. It hit her hard; her knees dipped and the last of her breath went out of her in a short hard sound. She came up out of the dip with no distance left between them at all, inside Fiske's recovery, with her palm flat on Fiske's breastbone.

Four seconds. Close and graceless, and as plain as a signature.

"Wind," said the table. "Two to one. Bout."

The yard came apart.

Not slowly, as it had after Nyle. It went up all at once, every tier, so that the noise of it hit the lecture range opposite and came back off the stone. In the faculty box a grey-bearded member of the law range had stood up and was clapping with his hands over his head like a boy at a fair. Cael was on his feet without having decided to stand. Brom beside him had both fists pressed hard against his mouth. And Karis, on his other side, sat perfectly upright with the pencil in her fingers, writing nothing, with tears running down her face that she did not appear to have noticed.

Down on the boards, Lira stood where she had touched, her hand still half raised, until the safety instructor walked out and laid his own hand very gently on her arm.

In the west gallery Withrow had not stood. She sat as she had sat all afternoon, upright and white-haired, with her two Ostrand guests on their feet on either side of her, clapping. She was not watching the floor. She was watching their faces, the way she always watched the faces beside her on these afternoons, and from the east tier Cael saw her turn her head and say something short to the woman on her left, who nodded slowly, twice, and took a small book out of her coat and wrote in it.

And in the brass of the lamp, high on the east side, in the shade, a small figure with something pale against its chest had not moved at all, through any of it. Cael saw that without looking for it, and let it go.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

It took Cael most of a quarter-hour to get down through the crowd on the stair. When he reached the floor's edge he found them both still there.

Lira sat two steps up from the boards, bent over her knees, taking her breath back a mouthful at a time. The leading leg was folded under her at an angle he did not like, and she had not tried to stand. She was keeping her face entirely empty of that, and of everything else, in front of the boards.

Fiske had a cup of water in her hand. She crossed to the step and stood over Lira.

By the long board, threescore people found the chalk suddenly fascinating.

Fiske spoke first. "You gave me a false first exchange."

Lira raised her head.

"I gave you a true one. You just assumed it was all of them."

Fiske's face changed.

Cael knew how a beaten champion's face went. This was not that. Cael had watched that one all season, on Fiske's opponents, and knew it to the eyelid. This was what he had seen once before and failed to name: at the board in the first month, the transfer with the flag, Fiske with a towel round her neck, standing two breaths longer than the words needed. That afternoon he had failed to name it. He read it now from four paces away, entire, and wondered how he had ever missed it.

It was relief. Both times, it had been relief.

"There's a form," said Fiske. "For an advancement evaluation. The registry sends an Arbiter if the form goes up. It wants one signature that isn't mine." She turned the cup in her hands. "Two seasons I've sat on top of that sheet, with Rank Eight on my certificate. Two crowns. Every bout on this hill worth having. The porter polishes the stud beside my name on Fourth-days. And in all that time nobody has picked up the pen. Not because anyone decided not to. Because nobody ever had a reason to. I was winning. Why would anybody send the winner away?"

Lira said nothing. Every bit of her attention was on Fiske.

Fiske looked down at her. "So win it. Win the crown. Then make them look at you. It's the looking that matters — it was always the looking. The crown's just how you force it."

Fiske drank, and then studied what was left in the cup.

"I didn't know how. I thought if I won enough, it would turn into a reason on its own. It doesn't turn into anything. They chalk it up, and once a thing's chalked up, people feel they've dealt with it."

Her gaze went past Lira to the long board. The brass stud still sat beside her name, a line lower than it had sat at noon. Until the final, it was still hers.

"Six weeks," said Fiske. "I'll see you in the final."

"You will," said Lira.

She held out her free hand. Lira looked at it a moment and took it, and Fiske did not pull her up by it, as a lesser fighter might have done in front of the boards to make a show of being gracious. One shake, and she let go.

Fiske walked away along the bottom of the tiers, cup in hand. Round the board, the onlookers began all at once to discuss the weather.

Lira stayed on the step a while longer. Then she put a hand flat on the stone and pushed herself up, slowly, in two stages, and Cael kept his own hands where they were. In front of the boards she would have refused his help, and he had known that since the Ironyard.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

That night Brom did his fourth exercise of the week at the post behind the second quadrangle, by lamplight, because Karis had found him at supper and said the date aloud.

Cael fed him. Karis had the coping, the lamp and the grey notebook. And Lira, who should have been in bed with her leg up, sat on the coping beside Karis with her leg out straight along the stone and a wet cloth folded over the hip, and watched Brom hold and shift and hold and shift, forty times, with his heel trying to lift on every one and being set down again by main force.

On the thirty-first, without any warning, she said it.

She said all of Fiske's words in order, about the form and the signature and the stud and the pen, and the four sentences in the middle, and the board, and six weeks. She said them to the dark beyond the lamp in Fiske's flat voice, as though setting down something she had been asked to carry across a room. It took her the better part of a minute. She did not drop a single word. Brom stopped holding, and Cael stopped feeding. Nobody wrote anything down while she talked; Cael had learned that much at Ardenmere, in the first month, and had not forgotten it.

When she stopped, the lamp hissed.

"All of it?" said Cael.

"All of it. She said each thing once. There wasn't any show in it." Lira moved the cloth. "I've heard people say true things before. Plenty. I've never heard anybody put down a thing they'd had to carry by themselves for two years. She'd been carrying it around looking for somebody who could take it off her."

"And it was you."

"It was the first time anybody on that sheet was able to." She said it without any pride. "That's an ugly thing to find out about where you live."

Karis had the pencil out. "May I write it down? Exactly as you said it."

"You can write it down exactly if you never call it the file. Not once. Not to anybody."

"I won't," said Karis, and wrote, and didn't.

Lira looked out at the dark where the ferry landing was, and the two grey coats under their lamp, on the bell.

"And now I like her," she said. "I've no idea where to put that."

"Nothing," said Brom.

He was still at the post with his forearms up and the sweat running into his eyes, on the thirty-first of forty, with Rooke's sheet folded in his back pocket and a row of Karis's ticks on it, and a row of small crosses in his own hand beside them for the days he had wanted to stop and hadn't.

"Karis files everything. That's Karis being a good sort." He set his heel down hard and shifted his weight. "Thirty-two. Feed me, Cael, before my arms forget what they're for."

Cael fed him. Karis, between ticks, turned back two pages in the grey notebook and held it out across the coping to Lira, open at the four lines she had written on the tier.

Lira read them by the lamp, and Cael watched her eyes go down the page and stop at the first line, at the question mark, and stay there.

"Why," said Lira.

"I didn't know," said Karis. "Not then. Cael told me on the tier, and I still didn't really know till the third." Back came the notebook; Karis frowned at her own question mark. "I wanted to cross it out after. I thought it looked stupid. Then I thought it was the most honest thing on the page, because it's what eight hundred people were thinking, and I'm the only one who wrote it down."

"Leave it," said Lira. "It's a good question. Fiske asked it too. For the whole minute and a half." She shifted the wet cloth on her hip and looked at Brom straining at the post, his heel lifting and being forced down. "She just didn't get the answer till it was too late to use. Neither did you."

"Did you know?" said Brom, through his teeth, on thirty-five. "Before the word?"

"I knew what I meant to do." Lira considered. "I didn't know if it would work. You never know that. You only know if you've built it so that if it doesn't work, you'll find out early."

"That's Rooke," said Brom.

"That's the foundry," said Lira. "Rooke just says it in fewer words."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

It was very late when he opened the Log for the session. The river was loud below the window and the lamp turned all the way up.

He put the fragments first, as he had at the head of every session entry since Ardenmere, one line to each.

Five confirmed fragments. All five as they were.

Then one line he had been carrying in the second column for most of three weeks, and now, with a certain ceremony, ruled through and copied into the first.

Iron-adjacent read. Off the counting four days, back to full: three times running, four days each time. Then under load at the post in hall three, seventeen days rested, on time and true when everybody else in the hall was a beat behind. Confirmed. The watching and the read drink from one well. Four days fills it.

Then the bout. He found he did not want to write it as he usually wrote a bout, exchange by exchange, because Karis had already done that in four lines and done it better. He wrote what it had been instead.

Fifteenth session. Two to one on the final's terms; second line to first on the standings. Nine and nothing on the season now: nine bouts unbeaten, none lost, the opening bout drawn by lot among them.

Every exchange took one more pretence off. In the first, Lira showed Fiske the truth about herself and nothing else. In the second, Fiske believed it and was right to. In the third, Lira used the same truth to go somewhere it couldn't have told anybody. By the fourth there was nothing left to show or believe, only two people, and Lira's feet had been made on a foundry floor.

What the third one cost her, in my own hip's language. Four bursts, all borrowed against tomorrow. Four half-breaths stood still in front of the one fighter on the bluff who could have used any of them. A hip I'd guess at three days before it lets her walk, and then the semifinal on top of it. A left shoulder that took the edge of a Force delivery so she wouldn't have to give up a hand's breadth of distance.

What it bought. The top line and the earlier semifinal, so a day's more rest before the final. And a woman who's held the crown two years walking across the floor to give her the one honest thing anybody on this hill has said aloud since we came up the road.

And the other column. On the morning after the final, Bracken's sheet will still say Copper, Rank Two, in the tier column beside her name. Fiske has already said what the crown is for, better than I could. I'll only write down the word for it. The crown is a lever.

He read it through. One thing had lain under all the rest of the day, waiting. He gave it the foot of the page, in a smaller hand.

At the fifth bell, most mornings, she's at the board alone. She's been going for weeks and never mentioned it. The morning after the tenth, I came up the north stair and found her there in front of six and nothing, standing square on both feet with her breathing held level, which is how she stands when a thing is costing her.

I went back down without speaking. I keep going back over it. I think I was right to. I'm not certain, and I want the not-being-certain on the page. The day I'm sure I know when somebody wants to be left alone is the day I've started deciding for people what they need. I've spent my life being decided for. I know what it's like from the inside.

He blotted the page and closed the Log and sat a long while with his hands on its cover, listening to the river.

Somewhere along the passage, through the thin wall, he heard Lira laugh once in her sleep, short and surprised, and then go quiet.

Chapter 30 — What Seln Keeps

[Patient, strategic narration; let alliances and costs accumulate without melodrama]

The conclusion had come to Seln on the bluff road, on the ninth night after the pin, somewhere on the third bend going up. He had just watched the courier's clerk drop his third report of the fortnight into the canvas sack by the fish steps, and he was climbing home in the dark with nothing in his satchel at all.

He had not gone looking for it. He did his best thinking the way a mill grinds, slowly and all the time, with the stones turning whether anyone was watching them or not. On the third bend the stones had stopped, and there it was on the floor of his mind, finished, like flour.

He found nothing wrong with it, which was what made him uneasy. Sound conclusions arrived as things he had been working toward. This one arrived as a thing he had been walking round.

So on the tenth night he fastened the shutter of his room on the staff corridor, turned the lamp down to a bead, and went over the argument one step at a time, as he would have gone over somebody else's.

First step: the service depended not on its officers being honest but on its files being complete, because officers were posted, promoted and buried while the file outlived them all, and a gap in it was therefore a slow trap. One day a reader with better access would come at that stretch from another side, see one man's product go quiet just where things got interesting, and ask him why.

Second step. Gaps were always found; he had spent two years of his youth at a long table up the coast finding them. When one was found, the officer's whole defense was what he had known, and when; silence alone could sometimes be explained, but silence with nothing kept behind it left a man only his word, and he had twice watched what a covered man's word was worth at an inquiry. It was worth the paper it was not written on.

So: paper. Not product, nothing that would ever go down the river, but his own, in his own keeping, dated, so that on the worst day of his working life he could put his hand on a page and say this is what I saw, and this is the night I saw it. If that day never came, he was out a few sheets.

The logic held, and the further thought waiting behind it he left standing in the dark where it was: a man who sent everything down the river would never need a drawer of his own.

Not one of his four hands would do for this. What he wrote it in was a fifth thing, a private shorthand grown out of the cramped hand when he was young in the field, and no other living person had ever been taught it. Any trained reader could have cracked it over one pot of tea. It had been made for landladies.

At his last posting but two, a landlady doing his table had found a page of it, and turned it face down again very gently. All that week, from the way she said good morning, he knew she believed she had seen a lonely man's diary. The words ran to ordinary lengths. Little words seemed to fall where little words fall. And the lines sloped downhill toward the right-hand margin, as a tired man's lines do late at night, which was the touch he was proudest of. Nobody who reads a tired man's diary upside down reads it twice. They are too sorry for him.

He headed the page with the Third-day of the pin, ten days late, and set the afternoon down whole. He had never needed notes for what he had seen; the service valued that in him above his Path.

Range: six feet.

Interval: shorter than the return.

Heading: in.

The third word held him longest. Every evasive framework he had ever watched did one thing above all others, and that was carry its owner out of trouble. A Wind boy who went in, across a live delivery, had been given a framework and then decided for himself which way to point it, in a third of a second, when nobody would have blamed him for being somewhere else.

Contact: guard forearm, the thin edge of the fold. Placed, not found.

Force: not shed. Grounded. Through him into the boards.

Wind did not do that. Iron Skin families did. Two components, at the least, inside one breath. The brief had a category for that, and he had known which, before the forearm came down.

Then, because this was not product, he did what product forbade and wrote what he thought.

One. The wing measured a floor. The floor was chosen.

Two. He knew the noise the core makes when it is about to lock. He has never worked that post. Yet he knew to a heartbeat how long it ground. Every machine in every room gets weighed and costed as he walks in, and the habit is so old it has stopped charging him.

Three. At the north door the third-year asked him what happened, and he answered him truly and left the important part out, in about the time it takes to tie a boot, with nothing rehearsed. Grown officers, trained for it, fumble that. With him it is not a skill. It is a reflex. Somebody made it one.

He sat back. Then he leaned forward and added a last line, which was not about anything he had seen.

Nobody builds that at fifteen unless somebody has been coming for him since his Kindling.

The key to the small case lived in the hollow spine of a treatise on harbour dues, which nobody in any posting had ever taken from a shelf. He shook it into his palm and got down on the floor. The draught under his door ran along the boards and up both sleeves, and his knees, which had lately begun to hold opinions about floors, gave him this one in full. Out came the large case, and from under its shirts the little one: old, brass at the corners, its leather soft as a glove. He opened it between his knees.

He folded the pages to the size of a letter and laid them on top.

What lay beneath them he did not lift or count. None of it had been wanted in years. A locked case is worth exactly as much as nobody's knowing what it holds, and the habit of not looking is part of the lock.

He locked it and slid everything home. Then, still kneeling, he took from his satchel four carbons he had drawn from the wing's drawer at locking-up, which nobody else ever opened.

One was from his first month on the bluff. The rest were the three he had walked to the fish steps since the pin. He laid them in a row on the floorboards.

Subject's routine unchanged. Four supervised floor hours weekly. Attends every ladder session. Associates unchanged. Private notation continues.

Retaining pins: warden's schedule paid for out of reserve; replacement under way. Registrar assembling charter documents. No inspection notice seen.

No undisclosed capability observed.

That last sentence stood on every one of them. On the first it had been true. On the three since, it was the sentence the posting existed to send, and its absence would have been read before anything else on the desk it reached.

He gathered the four up, shuffled them, and laid them out again face down. Then he turned them over one by one and tried to tell, from the pages alone and without the dates, which had come first.

He could not.

Long ago, at the long table up the coast, he had taught a room of new auditors what that meant. A live situation moves. Coverage that does not move for a whole term means either the situation has died or the man has stopped following it. He had chalked it on a board, and been rather pleased with the way he put it.

He put the carbons back in his satchel in their proper order. He knew how they would look to a reader with better access. He had known it on each of the three nights he walked them down the hill.

He had filed them anyway. He knew that as a fact, and it was true, and he went on. Then he turned the lamp out and slept without trouble until the second bell.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Two and two, on the bell.

Cael wrote it in the margin of the observation notebook, under the date, as he had written it every evening and every morning since the pin. He was sitting on the coping of the wall behind the second quadrangle in the grey before breakfast, with his coat buttoned to the throat and Karis's marbled log open on the stone beside him. Down on the river street the relief had just walked up to the ferry landing, two grey coats coming and two going. They had nodded to each other at the change, and the two going had turned for the town without looking back.

Eleven days.

He had promised himself a change would show in four if it was going to. It had not shown in four. It had not shown in eight. At the foot of the bluff road it had been the same, on the same bell. One of the coats coming on there walked with a stiff left knee that Cael remembered from the morning of the pin, so even the roster was unchanged. There had been no new face in the residence quadrangle and no extra pair on the covered walk. Bracken would have heard of any visitor to Withrow's door by supper and told Karis by breakfast, and Bracken had heard of none.

He did not know yet what to make of it. He had decided, in the second week, to know nothing until he had a reason, and he was holding to it.

Under the date, below the standing line for the five confirmed fragments, he made the other entry he had been carrying.

Compression, recovery: four mornings, not two. One instance, under a heavier load than any I've measured. Amend the column in pencil.

The arm lay on the stone beside the notebook. The bruise along the outer bone had gone from black to yellow to nearly nothing. The hum had not come back. Twice he had pressed the bone hard with his thumb in the dark, to see whether it would, and it had not.

Footsteps came along the top of the wall, uneven, a long step and a careful one. Lira sat down on the coping beside him with her leg stuck straight out before her and a heel of yesterday's bread in her hand.

"Two and two," she said.

"On the bell."

"I saw from my window." She tore the bread in half and gave him the smaller half. "I don't know why I come out here, if I can see it from my window."

"Because the window can't tell you it's nothing."

"Neither can you." She ate. The hip had let her walk on the third day, as he had guessed it would, and this morning she had stopped pretending it was not there. By Third-day she meant to be back in hall one at a third of her pace, running the sequence on the stone with a face like a locked door. The shoulder that had taken the edge of Fiske's last delivery had come up purple. She carried her satchel on the other side now and had not once mentioned why.

Below them the sound of a mallet started up from the far side of the second quadrangle, where Brom's post stood. It was too early for the post. Then a voice that was certainly Karis's said a number, and the mallet stopped.

"He's doing them before breakfast now," said Lira.

"Nine boxes," said Cael. "Four a week since the Tarn bout, and the first four all in one night. He did the ninth last night, and Karis didn't even have to come and find him."

"Did she come anyway?"

"She came anyway. She stood there and said the date. He says it's the most frightening thing that happens to him all week."

Lira almost smiled. She looked down at the ferry landing, where the two new coats had settled under their lamp, and she was quiet.

"Top line," she said at last, as if trying the words for fit. "Three days on the top line of the Copper standings. I keep going to the board to check it's still true."

"It's still true."

"I know it is. I'm not checking the board." She brushed the crumbs off her knee. "Six weeks, she said. Fewer now. Some mornings I'd like it to be tomorrow and some mornings I'd like it to be never." She stood, slowly, in her two stages. "Don't put that in anything."

"I won't."

"I mean it. Not even the coat-notebook."

"Not even that," said Cael, and she went off along the wall toward breakfast with her long step and her careful one, and he sat a while longer and wrote nothing at all.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The pen in the assessment wing's end office was chained to the counter by a length of fine brass chain, and it scratched. Cael had signed for things with it perhaps thirty times. He knew where it caught, a third of the way through any downstroke, and he had learned to lift for it.

He had also learned not to come between the second and third bells. In that hour the desk clerk took her breakfast in the little room behind the office with the door ajar and a newspaper, and the porters were down setting the frame, and the counter was minded by whoever sat nearest it. By some trick of the wing's furniture, that was always the copying table. He had worked it out in his fourth week and put it in the shorthand. Since then he had done his signing at the fourth bell or after.

This morning the board had left him no choice. Hall three's posts had their new pins at last, and the east hall's floor hours had been put back as they were before the pin, and the revised sheet had to be signed at the counter by the third bell, in the wing's own wording. He was in the end office before the second bell had finished echoing off the quadrangle, with the chained pen in his hand. Across it, Seln turned the sheet to face him without raising his eyes from it.

"Third line. The clerk countersigns."

He signed, lifting for the catch.

It was the first thing Seln had said to him in thirteen weeks. The last had been at the copying table on his fifty-first day: east and north halls, four a week, a warning about notices from halls. There had been no word since, and a great deal else. A floor sheet corrected that nobody had asked to have corrected. A gallery. A stair-head. A rail. Afternoon after afternoon of a man standing at precisely the right distance from a boy who never once let his eyes stop on him.

Seln took the sheet back and squared it on the wood. The tray of forms at his elbow stayed where it was.

"Your training requirement will take coursework," he said, to the sheet, in the level voice the counter used for everything at that hour. "Under the clause. Supervised coursework counts as evaluable contact. It's written in your file. I processed it."

Cael waited.

"Gault's putting a unit on the back half of term. Field assessment." A mark in the ledger. "Observation, position, presence. Once a week to the close of term. Most of the places will go to second- and third-years who mean to be assessors. Provision enrollees may sit."

"On a floor?"

"In a room in this wing. It isn't a combat unit. Rooke won't have it on his boards."

Through the clerk's door came the small dry sound of a newspaper turning. In the passage two first-years had lost their lecture room and were blaming each other for it.

"Who takes it?" said Cael.

"I do." The pen in Seln's own hand moved once more in the ledger. "Gault approves the syllabus. Gault doesn't attend."

The signed sheet went face down under the countersign block.

He said it to the sheet. "Your file says you watch things well. The course would tell us if the file's right."

The wing's carbon sets came in threes, held at the corner with a pin: a top sheet for whoever asked, a second for the wing's own drawer, and a third, faint and grey, for the file that went away. Cael had handled a hundred of them. He read the sentence the same way, top to bottom, in about two seconds, before the clerk's newspaper turned again.

The top sheet was for anybody. A member of staff had offered an enrollee a place on a course, at a counter, with a rule and an authority and a reason. Repeated by anybody within earshot, all four of them, it would sound like nothing whatever.

The second sheet was what it gave. For thirteen weeks he had watched this man across halls, from forty feet, past the shoulders of crowds. Now he was being offered eight feet, a table's length, in a room, signed and countersigned under Gault's own approval. Shadow, taught by somebody who used it. And the man would be talking.

The third sheet was the faint one, and it was the one that mattered. Seln knew precisely what eight feet of him was worth; nobody alive could have priced it better. He had spent fifteen years making himself a man no one could get near. Now, in the dullest hour of the day, he had drafted a lawful pass into his own range, made out to the single person on the bluff who could find him.

Whether that pass was the finest snare the Compact had ever laid or no snare at all, he had not been able to decide since the gallery, and he was not going to decide it at a counter.

Only the top sheet had been spoken aloud, so the top sheet was the only one he could answer. If either of them so much as glanced at the other two, it would be the worst mistake of the term.

"Sign me up," he said.

"Sheet's on the residence board from tomorrow." The next form was already in Seln's hand. "Put your name down like everybody else."

Cael put the copy inside his coat. The door was six paces.

On the threshold his feet stopped.

He had not told them to. It lasted half a second at the most, the hitch a foot gives in the dark at the top of a stair when it has counted one step too many. Then they carried him out into the passage. He was cross with himself about it until the evening, and some way past.

Behind him the chained pen scratched on. Through the clerk's door a page turned. Anybody in the wing who had been asked would have said, quite truthfully, that an enrollee had signed for a floor sheet and left.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He did not tell the others at breakfast.

A thing that was going to be decided was read to all three at once, with the door shut, before anything was done about it. Breakfast was a long table and sixty people. So he ate, and listened to Brom describe exercise nine in a voice of deep injury, and said nothing. Karis looked at him once across the bread and then down at her plate, and he saw her decide not to ask.

After breakfast he had an hour before the lecture. He spent it walking.

He went the length of the covered walk and back, past the board. Lira's name stood on the top line with Fiske's brass stud a line below it. The porter had chalked the date of the final in the corner the week before, very small. He went down the north stair and stepped over the third step without thinking and then, a moment later, thinking. He went out through the arch and along the edge of the yard and stood for a while at the rail above the river. A barge went down with its long note and its two short ones, and was answered from the bend.

He was trying to work out what he wanted. He did not like the answer.

He wanted the room. He wanted it the way he had once, at fourteen, wanted the reference room at the community hall at home, all those shelves nobody else read. He wanted to sit at that table and hear the man say anything at all about where people look, and why. He wanted it badly enough that he could feel himself, already, beginning to build the reasons it would be safe.

That was the thing to be careful of. He knew it from the minute in Karis's notebook, and from the night after it, when he had argued both sides of a question with himself in the dark and won every time. A want did not come to you looking like a want. It came looking like an argument. It brought its own reasons along with it, ready-made, and laid them out in a neat row.

So he made himself argue the other side as well, the way the minute had taught him, and found at the rail, with some irritation, that a trap and an honest offer would look exactly the same from the counter: the dullest hour, a voice built to be overheard, a form and not a favour.

Jask went past behind him on the way to the Force hall, with his collar up and a book under his arm. He lifted a hand. Cael lifted one back. Jask had turned his dial to the wall for every set now, and had told nobody why, and had moved up two lines on his ledger. He walked the way a person walks who has stopped being the story.

There was one thing Cael did know, and he had known it since the coping at dawn, and the room in the wing had not changed it.

Eleven days. Two and two.

He went to the lecture, and took notes on the drainage of practice floors, and did not hear one word in three. Near the end of the hour he looked out of the lecture range's window and saw a man in a plain wing coat cross the far corner of the north quadrangle with an armful of ledgers. The man walked at the quiet even pace he always walked at, along the one stretch of the quadrangle where nobody else happened to be looking.

Cael did not let his eyes stay. He wrote the date and the bell in the margin and nothing more, and bent his head back over the drainage of floors.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Hall three had its posts back.

They stood along the north wall where they had always stood, four iron columns with their padded heads, and the new retaining pins shone in the collars like fresh nails in an old fence. The chains were gone. The floor warden had fitted every pin herself over two long evenings, so the Ash instructor told him at the bay's edge, and had made each Force third-year who used the posts that week watch her do it, and then made them each say the plate aloud before she let them near a dial.

"All of it," said the Ash instructor. "Core and pin. In front of their friends." She signed his sheet against her knee, in her small stooped way, and gave it back. "Half of them sulked. The other half will be alive at forty. Footwork, then four, then the landing. I'll be here."

He did his footwork first, on the timber that gave and returned under him, slow and then not slow, down the length of the bay and back. Then the Wind-adjacent bursts, up to the ceiling the timber allowed. He took four, the four the oak gave him for free, and felt the floor hand back its share on each landing and the hip take the rest. The landing beat came where it always came, the half-breath of being set in place like a peg in a hole. Three years of trying to shorten it, and it had not given him a hair.

At the far end of the hall the door opened and a porter put his head in, looked for somebody who was not there, and went away again.

Cael was halfway into the third set when he found where he was standing.

He had come out of the second landing and drifted, without deciding to, a few steps toward the wall. He stood now just inside the angle of the north wall and the end post, in the strip of floor that the door's opener would reach with his eyes last of all, after the instructor and the bays and the windows. He had not chosen it. His feet had chosen it, while the rest of him was thinking about a counter.

He stood there long enough to be sure. Then he walked out of it into the middle of the floor, where anybody coming through that door would see him first, and finished the set in the open, all four bursts, under the high windows, in plain view of the Ash instructor and two Stone first-years waiting for the next bay and anybody else in the building who cared to look.

"You went for the wall," said the Ash instructor when he came off the floor. She had kept her eyes on her book, as far as he had seen. "Halfway through the third. Something on the wall?"

"No," said Cael. "Something in my head."

"Leave it in your head on my floor," she said, mildly, and turned a page.

He wrote it down that evening before supper, sitting on his bed with the observation notebook, because it was the kind of thing that turned into an argument if you let it go unwritten past dark.

The man offered me a place in his unit this morning. I said yes. I have not yet told the others; that is tonight.

Before I tell them, the want, in my own hand, so it can't come back later in a hat: I want that room. I want it more than I've wanted anything on this bluff since the gate list. My feet went looking for the place a man by the door would see last, in hall three, in the middle of a set, without asking me. That is what wanting it looks like from the outside, and I would rather the three of them heard it from me than worked it out from where I stand.

He read it over, and left it, and went down to supper with the page folded inside his coat, where it rested against the copy of the floor sheet Seln had turned face down under the countersign block, two pieces of paper about the same morning that said nothing at all alike.

Chapter 31 — Both

[Patient, strategic narration; let alliances and costs accumulate without melodrama]

Lira locked the door and put the key in her pocket, which was how every one of these evenings began now, and sat on the arm of the settle with her bad leg along the cushions.

Cael read them the counter.

He read it from the observation notebook, word for word, because he had written it word for word on the walk back from the wing before it could soften in his head. He gave them the sheet and the chained pen, and Your training requirement will take coursework, and Gault and the unit and the back half of term, the room in the wing and Rooke's boards; then Who takes it? and I do, and the file sentence, and his own three words, and the board where his name would have to go up among everybody else's. He read the half-second at the door as well, since to skip it would have made the evening's first lie. Then he turned the page and read them the other entry, the one about his feet in hall three, and what he wanted, in his own hand.

Nobody said anything until he had closed the notebook.

"No," said Lira. "Don't go in that room. Not for anything."

She said it to the cold fireplace, with her arms folded, and then shut her mouth on it and looked as if she would very much have liked that to be the end of the evening.

It was not, as all four of them knew perfectly well. Since the Fiske bout Lira had taken up a habit none of them had seen in her before: when she had said a thing hard, she turned straight round and argued the other side of it, as hard as she could, to see what was left standing. She said it was what Fiske had done to her in the second exchange, and that it had been the most useful thing anybody had done to her all season.

So after a moment she unfolded her arms.

"Right. The other side." She looked at the ceiling. "He's offering it in public, on a board, with Gault's name on the syllabus and every second-year who wants to be an assessor in the same room. You can't be quietly anything in a room full of second-years. If he wanted you on your own, that's the last place he'd put you." She stopped. "And you'd learn something from the only man on the bluff who could teach it, which isn't nothing. I'd have walked a long way at your age for a teacher like that." She looked down at Cael. "I still think no. I just can't make it as big as I'd like it to be."

"That's honest," said Karis.

"It's irritating," said Lira. "Your turn."

Karis sat with both palms pressed flat either side of the grey notebook, which was how she stopped her hands from helping her think.

"I'm going to give you my position," she said, "and then I'm going to tell you why you shouldn't trust it, because I don't, and I'd rather say so here than at the fourth bell with nobody to say it to."

"Go on," said Cael.

Karis took a breath, the short sharp one she took before reading a clause aloud to a room that would rather not hear it, and he saw her decide, as she always did, to put the part that made her look worse at the end, where nobody could say she had hidden it.

"Position: it breaks nothing in the minute, because you didn't arrange it and you didn't go near him. The offer came over a counter, by the route any clerk would use, and the right it rests on is printed in your own file. Every rule you wrote is standing." She paused. "Now why I don't trust that. I want it. Not on your account; on mine. I've wanted to sit in a room with a working Shadow practitioner at a table's length since the first page you wrote about him, and I want it the way I want a missing volume, which is badly and for my own sake. And I caught myself, about halfway through you reading it out, building the case for yes. I'd got two good reasons laid out before I noticed the want they were standing on." She turned one hand over. "So whatever I say tonight, mark it down. Mark it down a long way."

"How far?" said Brom, from the floor.

"Further than you'd think. I'll tell you if I see myself doing it again."

Brom was sitting under the window with his back to the plaster, as he always sat, with Rooke's sheet open on his knee and Karis's nine ticks along the top of it in pencil. He was running his thumb down the fold in it, slowly, as if he were trying to smooth out a crease that had been put there with an iron.

"He's not recruiting you," he said.

"You don't know that," said Lira.

"No. I don't." Brom looked up. "But if that's recruiting, it's the worst I've ever seen. My grandmother hired people all her life, clerks and factors and yard men, and the way you do it is you make it easy, and you make it quiet, and you make it feel like their own idea." He tapped the sheet. "He's done the opposite of every one of those. Your name goes on a sheet in the residence passage, where three hundred people walk by twice a day. You have to sit in a room with eight others who'll talk about it at supper. Wanting a boy near you on the quiet, you'd never in your life ask him to sign for it where the whole house can read it. If he wanted you, he'd have left you an easy way to refuse. He's left you a hard way to accept."

Nobody had anything to add to that, and Lira looked at Brom with an expression of mild betrayal, and then at the fireplace again.

"I hate it when he does that," she said.

Brom only nodded, comfortably, and went on smoothing the crease.

Cael waited until the barge on the river had finished its long call and the answer had come back from the bend.

"The course isn't what I keep coming back to," he said.

"The coats haven't changed."

He laid Karis's marbled log open on the table between the four of them and turned it so that it faced the room. Eleven days since the pin, in her small hand and his scrawl and once in Lira's square capitals. Every change at the ferry landing and every change down at the road's foot, the bell, the faces where faces could be told apart, a tick for on time.

Row after row of ticks. There was the pie, crossed out, and the cart in the road, and the dog, all from before the pin, and after the pin not one cross, not one face that was new, not one change by so much as a minute, only the same small upright tick, bell after bell, down the whole of the page and on to the next.

"Here's what I know about the Compact," he said. "It answers paper with people, because people are all it has ever had to spend. Somebody writes something interesting at the bottom of the coast, and it goes up, and somebody reads it, and what comes back down is coats. More of them, or different ones, or closer. I've seen it every time anything about me has gone up." He touched the first row. "The registry's district office is half a morning down the river. Had the pin gone up whole, the river would have brought me an answer by now. Not a letter, either, but a man."

"So nothing went up," said Lira.

"Something went up; it must have. Sending nothing for a fortnight would leave a hole in his product that a clerk could see from the door, and he doesn't make holes clerks can see." Cael looked at the column. "But the afternoon wasn't in it, or not the part that matters. He watched me stand in front of a locked post and take an Iron-tier return on my arm and send it into the floor. And today there are the same two men at the landing that there were the morning before. One of them still has his stiff knee."

Karis had stopped writing, and sat looking at the column of ticks with her pencil held a little above the page.

"That's one observation," she said.

"It fits your reading. Other roads run through it too. I want them on paper, numbered, so that later we can lay what we thought beside what turned out to be so." She drew a line under the date and wrote a figure one. "One. It's lying in a tray somewhere, under other trays. Clerks have trays; so do the people above them. Two. It went up and somebody decided to change nothing while an inspection might be coming, because moving coats is the kind of thing an inspection notices. Three. It went up whole, and he's been told to stand where he is and keep watching." She wrote a four, and stopped, and then wrote beside it. "Four. It went up, and it was written so that a reader who wasn't in that hall would find nothing in it to act on. All of it true, and nothing in it to see."

The fourth line held Cael's eye.

"That's mine," he said. "That's the same as mine."

"It isn't. Yours says he left it out. Mine says he could have put it all in and still made it say nothing. Those are different men." She set the pencil down. "I'm not arguing with you, only putting the other roads on the page."

Karis looked at the pencil in her hand. "Now the part that isn't work, once only, and afterwards you'll all have the decency to forget it."

"I told you that before the season. It was a warning then, and it's been the first article of my trade for as long as I've had one." She squared nothing in particular on the table. With Karis, that stood in for a sigh. "Eleven days isn't a finding. I know that better than anybody in this room. But this is the first thing I've ever put in a notebook that I can't make go into that sentence, turn it how I like. I hate that. I'd rather tell you tonight, while it's still sticking out, than after I've sanded it down to fit."

The room was very quiet. Down on the river a barge called once, long, and nobody answered it.

"Thank you," said Cael.

"Don't thank me. I've told you it's unprofessional." But her mouth had gone tight in the way it did when she was pleased with something and refused to show it. "Write it down. Somewhere I don't have to look at it."

Lira had listened to all of it with her chin on her fist. Now she reached over and turned the marbled log round to face her, and ran her finger down the rows the way she ran it down the standings, looking for the line that did not belong.

"I'd like to meet the man with the knee," said Brom from the floor. "All these days, and I feel I know him. I could pick his walk out of a crowd at the fair." He thought about it. "I'd buy him a pie. He looks like a man who's never once been bought a pie."

"You can't buy a Compact watcher a pie," said Karis.

"Why not?"

Karis opened her mouth, and closed it again, and looked at the column of ticks, and for once in Cael's experience could not find the clause.

"Then there's the part nobody wants to say," said Lira, "so I'll say it."

She swung her leg down off the settle and sat forward.

"If you sit in that room, you sit eight feet from him once a week. Earnest, in his own work, close: that's your rule two, and you wrote it." She meant the minute they had all signed in this room a month before, whose second rule allowed a reach only inside an engagement the man began himself. "If it's ever going to happen, that room is where it's likeliest." Her eyes stayed on Cael's and did not leave them. "So I want it written now what happens after. So they wrote it, the four of them, at the common room table, in the last hour before the residence lamps went down. Karis said that was how you could tell it was good.

One. If it happens: eight days of nothing the wing can measure. No floor time hard enough to make a note, no demonstration, no supervised intensity. Ask Gault's office to defer my training for fatigue. That's true, and they give it to anybody who asks.

Two. The three of you are told before, which is now, and within the hour after, whatever the hour is.

Three. This week, while I'm well, Karis measures me. Then there's a before to hold up against an after. Last time we had only the after.

Four. If any of the five slips past the line we draw tonight, everything halts — deferral, unit, the lot — and I say it out loud to Karis and Lira, in plain words. I don't write it in the Log and sit waiting for someone to ask.

"What's tolerable?" said Brom.

They argued that for a quarter of an hour.

Lira wanted nothing tolerable at all: one wrong thing, anywhere, and stop. Karis said that would stop him on the first morning, since last time had begun with two misfires before breakfast, and that a rule nobody could keep was only a way of feeling safe. Brom wanted to know what counted as wrong, and whether a slow burst was wrong or only tired, and whether the read going a beat late counted, since it went a beat late every time Cael had been counting anything. Cael wanted the line drawn where last time had ended, and said so, and Lira said that was just the kind of line a person drew when he meant to walk right up to it.

"Within the hour," said Brom at one point, reading part two upside down. "Whatever the hour is. What if it's the fourth hour of the night?"

"Then you get woken."

"Wake Karis first," said Brom. "She's nicer about it."

"I'm not," said Karis, still writing. "I'm only quieter."

In the end Karis wrote it in under the fourth part in her own hand: Tolerable: one misfire in any session, self-correcting. Anything more, or anything that does not correct, or anything in the read: stop.

Cael signed it, and then held the pen out, and the others signed under him, Karis neatly, Brom slowly and with his tongue between his teeth, Lira in her square capitals that took up two lines.

He read it again, aloud, to the end, I don't write it in the Log and sit waiting for someone to ask, and she listened to the whole of it with her eyes shut.

"Right," she said, and stood, in two stages, and unlocked the door. "That one I'll hold you to. The others are Karis's." She went out, and they heard her uneven step go along the passage and her door shut.

"She means that," said Brom.

"I know she does."

"No," said Brom. "I mean she's going to lie awake tonight saying it to herself. That's what it costs her, you going near him. She'd rather you'd never seen him." Rooke's sheet went back inside his coat, along its old crease. "She signed anyway. Write that down too, somewhere."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

He opened the Log at his window at the ninth bell, with the shutter back and the river loud in the dark below, and the fresh-signed sheet laid in the back board beside Karis's minute, where he would see the four signatures every time he turned to the end of the book, whether or not he wanted to see them.

He wrote the standing lines first, as he always did: five confirmed, and the forearm's amendment to the recovery column. Then, for a while, he sat with the pen lifted and did nothing, because he knew what the next entry was going to be and was not sure he would like it.

It came out whole. That hardly ever happened.

He watched me stop Iron-tier force with a Copper baseline and his desk stayed quiet. Eleven days of the same two coats at the landing say so. This morning he offered, at a counter, to teach me his own Path across a table. Either it's the best trap the Compact ever built, or the man they sent to watch me has started watching them. Karis says instruments don't change sides. Karis has never met this instrument.

He left it as it stood. Then he wrote the working out underneath, because a conclusion with no working under it was only a thing you had decided to feel.

For a trap: he cut the door into his range himself, it costs the Compact nothing, and written down it's a clerk with a syllabus. Against: the same two coats, day after day, and Brom's point, which I've tried and failed to break, that whatever the man lets me have I must claim myself, publicly, in ink. A trap wants to be walked into. This was a door made so I could walk past it.

What I think, put here so I can be shown wrong later where everybody can see: for thirteen weeks he has been careful around me. This morning, I think, he was careful on my behalf. Careful for me. I haven't one piece of evidence for that preposition, and it's the only part of today I'm sure of.

What I'll do: sign the board, sit in the room, and learn the Path, if he teaches it.

What I won't do is let a single morning shift how I read him, since he still draws the Compact's pay, a man who says nothing can begin saying something on any day he likes, and a column of ticks at a ferry landing is a very thin floor to build on.

So: both. I read him as an officer, and I sit in his room anyway.

He stopped there. Then, because it was the kind of entry that would be easy to leave unwritten until it was too late to be honest, he turned to a fresh page and wrote the last part in advance.

If the day comes when I take something from this man, it will be a day he made possible. He'll have spent a whole term making it possible, and nobody will have asked him to, and he can never be told. That isn't a detail of the cost; it is the cost, nearly all of it. It won't feel like a cost on the night but like something else, and I'll want to call it by a kinder name. So I'm writing it here, tonight, while I can still see it plainly. Read this first.

He blotted the page and sat looking at it, and then took the pencil and, at the head of the page, in small capitals, wrote READ FIRST.

There was one more thing, and it was not about the debt. It was about Karis's fourth road, which had been sitting in him since the common room like a stone in a shoe.

Karis's fourth road: one man hides a thing by leaving a hole, the other by filling the hole with so much truth that nobody looks down. I don't know which he is, only that either is better at paper than I am, and I've been working at paper since I could hold a pen.

He closed the Log on that. Through the wall, along the passage, he heard Lira's floorboard go, once and then again, the long step and the careful one, as somebody walked to a window and stood there. Then nothing, and he did not knock. Brom had been right about what it cost her, and the least he could do with a thing that cost her was not make her talk about it at the ninth bell.

At the first bell next morning the wing's round copying hand appeared on the residence board.

Field assessment (staff unit). Weekly, from Third-day, the sixth bell, the long room off the assessment wing. Observation; position; presence. Open to second and third years; provision enrollees admitted on the training requirement. Places: twelve. Sign below.

Cael was there before breakfast, before he could find a reason to be there after it. The passage was empty except for a first-year reading the lost-property list with the absorption of a man reading a will. He took the pencil off its string and wrote his name on the first line, Cael, and under it assay provision, as the cards did, and put the pencil back.

Karis was waiting for Cael in the second-quadrangle wash-house afterward with the grey notebook, a lamp, a wooden rule a foot long, and the expression of great purpose she wore for any task that would produce a column of numbers nobody else would ever think to want, and which she would be able to look at in a month and know something by. Brom's sandbags hung from their beam in the corner where they had hung since the third week, three of them in a row, light, middle and heavy, with the knotted cord and the peg.

He sat on the upturned tub. She held the rule upright by its top end, with its foot between his open finger and thumb, and let go without warning. He caught it, and she looked at where his fingers had closed and wrote down a number, and did it again and again, a dozen times in all, and wrote a number each time.

"What does it tell you?"

She made him count his breath for a minute by the wash-house's clock, at rest and then after twenty steps up and down the yard stair, and wrote that. She made him take the middle bag on the forearm, the way he did in the mornings, and asked how many he would get to before it went, and wrote down his guess before he began, and then wrote down the true count beside it, which was eleven, and which was the same as his guess. "Good. You're honest about that one, at least."

"I'm honest about all of them."

"You round," said Karis. "Up when it's the Wind and down when it's anything that hurts, and you've done it since Greyvane, and I've got it in a column." She closed the notebook. "Tomorrow, the read at the post with Brom. The day after, the Wind on the stone, with Lira, at a third. And then I'll have a before."

"And Ember?"

"Ember stays off the floor; we agreed that. I'll take it from your own account, and I'll trust it, because it's mine and I'll know if you've rounded it." She picked up the lamp. "Go to bed. You look like somebody who's been carrying a sentence about all day."
