Cael went up early. He sat at the window with the lamp low and did not write anything for a long time, and the weight behind his eyes had grown into something with corners. He had not stopped minding his edges once all day, not even when the counsel read the name and every other part of him had wanted badly to go somewhere else.

He wrote that down, short.

Bumps: none. Even at the table. The hold doesn't care what kind of day it is. That's the first useful thing I've learned about it that isn't a cost.

Told Lira I'm frightened. She was right. It's smaller now it's said.

Across the dark second quadrangle there was a lamp still burning on the ground floor of the administration range, in the window of the registrar's outer office. While Cael watched, a cohort boy came across the flagstones from the direction of the halls with a stack of paper held flat in both arms, as carefully as Brom had carried the basket, and knocked at that door with his elbow. It opened, and closed behind him, and a little later he came out empty-handed and went back the way he had come, and came again with a second stack.

Cael counted four trips before he put the lamp out, and he did not write them down, because some things are better kept as a picture.

Chapter 39 — Filing-Grade

[Dry, precise narration; sharpen the institutional pressure through exact detail]

On the morning after the reading the door of the registrar's back room stood open, and Cael, waiting at the outer counter with a request slip of Karis's, could see straight through it into a kind of weather.

There was paper on every flat surface in the room. It lay on the long table in squared stacks and on the window seat in fanned ones, and on the floor along one wall in a row of open boxes, each with a card propped against its side. Three of the registrar's clerks sat at the table with their sleeves pinned back, writing. A fourth stood at a slope desk by the window copying from a heavy volume, with a librarian at his elbow who checked each line as he finished it and pressed a small brass seal to the foot of the page. The room smelled of lamp oil and new ink, and nobody in it was talking.

Karis was on her knees beside the row of boxes with a card in her teeth.

Bracken came out to the counter himself, wiping his fingers on a rag that had long since given up any hope of being clean. He took Karis's slip, stamped it and gave it back, and then, because Cael did not leave, he waited.

"I'd like to help," said Cael. "If there's anything. Carrying. Copying. I write a fair hand."

Bracken considered this with the full seriousness he gave every request at that counter, which was one of the things about him Cael had come to depend on.

"You write a very fair hand," he said. "And there is nothing in that room I can let you touch. Not one sheet." He folded the rag. "Every document on that table is about you. If a delegation counsel ever finds that the enrollee carried his own file, or copied a line of it, she will spend a whole morning asking what else he carried, and she'll be right to. Your hand on any of it makes all of it weaker."

"Then what can I do?"

"Be dull," said Bracken. "Go to your lectures. Train in your hours and sign for them. Hand your work in on the day it's due, and not a day early, because early is interesting. Don't put your name to a single sheet the calendar didn't ask for." He leaned his forearms on the counter. "Strong files are made of dull months, Enrollee. Give me a dull month."

"There are fifteen days to the evaluation."

"Then give me fifteen dull days," said Bracken, "and I'll write them up as a month."

He said it without a flicker, and it took Cael a moment to understand that the registrar had made a joke, and another moment to understand that he had made it on purpose, for Cael's sake, because the boy at the counter looked as if he needed one. Cael nearly laughed. Through the open door, Karis took the card out of her teeth and propped it against a box, and he saw that it read, in her small hand, 41 pages — tabbed — DO NOT RE-SORT.

"The argument's already won, though," he said. "Karis won it at Greyvane. Your counsel sealed it before I ever came up the road. What's left to build?"

Bracken did not answer at once; he took the second pen from behind his ear, looked at its nib, and put it back.

"An argument persuades a person. A file survives a person leaving the room." He said it plainly, as he might have said what bell it was. "Miss Karis persuaded me. My counsel persuaded the chancellor. Both of those were people. In a week there will be a room full of strangers on this bluff, none of whom were persuaded of anything, and some of whom would rather not be. A file has to work on them. It has to work if Miss Karis is in her bed with a fever and I'm at the bottom of the river. That's what's being built in there." He nodded at the door. "Not a better argument. Something that stands up with nobody holding it."

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Over the next four days Cael watched it being built, from the counter and the passage and once, by invitation and with his hands kept firmly in his pockets, from the back room's doorway. He understood it the way he understood a fight he was not in, by its decisions.

The first decision was that nobody should ever have to trust Karis.

Her chain of proof ran through thirty-odd volumes, from the founding schedule that held the clause to the charter article that took it into Halcenvane. At Greyvane she had built it out of her own transcriptions, careful ones, in her small upright hand, and Bracken would not use a single line of them. For every link in the chain a clerk went to the actual volume, in whatever library held it, and copied the passage whole. Then the librarian who kept that volume read the copy against the page, word by word, and sealed the foot of it. Where the volume was not on the bluff, a letter went down the river by the first coach to the house that held it, asking for a copy under that house's seal. A dated note of the asking went into the box in its place, so that even the gap was on paper. That protected against the first thing a hostile reader would say, which was that the whole chain rested on one girl's handwriting. By the end of the third day there was not a word of Karis's handwriting anywhere in it. She had stood at the table and watched the last of it go, and Cael had watched her face, and it had not looked like loss.

The second decision was harder, and he would not have thought of it himself. It protected against the next thing a hostile reader would say: that Karis had found what she wanted to find.

At Greyvane, Karis had spent eleven weeks proving a negative: that the clause had never been repealed, by searching every place a repeal could have been recorded and finding nothing in any of them. She could have done the search again with her eyes shut, which was why she was not allowed to. Bracken took a clerk from his own office who had been away on leave for most of the term and had never seen a page of her notes. He gave him the list of places a repeal would have to be recorded, and put him in a separate room on the floor above with the door shut. He worked alone up there for four days. On the evening of the fourth he came downstairs with his findings tied in string, and Bracken laid them on the long table beside Karis's, and the two searches by two people who had never compared a word reached the same nothing in the same places.

Cael was at the counter when the clerk came down. He was a thin young man with spectacles and a bad cold, and he carried his bundle in front of him with both hands, like a dish he expected to be blamed for. Karis was at the long table, forbidden to speak to him about anything but the weather, and she kept to it with a kind of ferocious exactness.

"Is it still raining?" she said.

"It's stopped," said the clerk, and put the bundle down, and fled.

Bracken laid the two searches side by side on the table and went through them place by place, his finger moving down one and then the other. Karis stood beside him and did not touch either. At the end Bracken said, "Same," and nothing else, and wrote one line in the index. Karis read the clerk's last page twice and then went out into the passage and stood with her forehead against the cold wall for a while.

The third decision was about the standardization directive, all forty-one pages of the order that had swept away the old terminology. It protected against a reader who knew only the four pages everybody quoted, and would say that a repeal might be hiding in the rest. So the whole of it went into the file, all forty-one pages, copied and sealed. The four passages where the old words were replaced by new ones were tabbed with green paper. At every place in the text where a clause repealing the assay provision would have had to stand, if one existed, a narrow white slip was pinned with a line in Bracken's hand saying that nothing stood there.

The last decision was the index, and Bracken wrote it himself. It protected against the plainest danger of all, a reader too tired or too hurried to find the one sheet that mattered.

It was a numbered list of every sheet in the file. Beside each number stood one line, never more, saying what that sheet proved and nothing else. There were no adjectives anywhere in it, and nothing that argued. Cael read the first page of it over the counter, upside down. With it, a delegation counsel with a sore back and no patience could find the sheet that carried the whole matter inside a minute and a half. She would not have to ask anybody on the bluff for anything.

On the fifth afternoon Karis tested it. She did not ask anyone's leave. She simply took the clerk with the cold, who had never seen the file's contents and had only searched for the absence of one thing, and sat him down at the long table in front of the first box with the index on top. Then she turned over the little sand-glass she used for timing her own reading. "The question," she said, "is whether this enrollment rests on a clause that has been repealed. Find me the sheet that answers it." The clerk ran his finger down the index, stopped, turned to the number, lifted out a sealed copy of a schedule with a white slip pinned to its margin, and laid it in front of her. Karis looked at the glass. A little under half of it had run. She turned it back over and wrote the figure in her notebook, and did not say anything at all, and Cael, from the doorway with his hands in his pockets, thought it was the most satisfied silence he had ever heard.

That night it went into the Log, with Hesk's pen, under a heading of its own.

How the registrar fights: he takes everybody who built the file out of it, me included, and builds for whoever walks in tired.

Everything that ever went wrong for me went wrong on a sheet of paper that nobody could check. This is the same weapon, held the other way round.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

On the fourth evening he found Karis on the floor.

The clerks had gone. The back room's lamps were down to two, and she was lying flat on her back on the boards between the row of boxes and the long table, with her feet up on an empty box and her hands folded on her stomach. Her fingers were black with ink to the second knuckle. There was a long smear of it along her jaw where she had pushed her hair back with the wrong hand.

"Are you hurt?" said Cael, from the doorway.

"I'm resting." She did not open her eyes. "Bracken said I could stay till the lamp-man comes. Come in, if you keep your hands in your pockets. He'll know if you don't. I don't know how, but he'll know."

He came in with his hands in his pockets and sat on the window seat, which was the only surface in the room without paper on it.

"The clerk's search came back," said Karis. "You heard."

"I heard. Same places. Same nothing."

"Same nothing." She let out a long breath at the ceiling. "Do you know what that file is now? It isn't mine. That's the whole point of it. At Greyvane it was mine. I'd dug it up, and people believed it partly because I was standing there ready to answer for it. Take me away and you took half the reason they believed. Bracken's spent four days taking me out of it. One link at a time. Every place my hand was, there's a seal now, and a librarian's name, and a clerk who never met me." She opened her eyes. "I could fall off the bluff tomorrow and the enrollment would hold without me."

"That's a grim thing to say about a good afternoon."

"It's the best thing anybody could say about an afternoon," said Karis, with great firmness, and closed her eyes again. "I've been waiting all my life for a piece of work that didn't need me. Do you know how tired you get, being the only person who can explain a thing? At Dellenmoor I wrote a paper on drainage tithes when I was fourteen, and for two years every time anybody wanted to know about drainage tithes, they came and found me. Not the paper. Me. The paper was right, and nobody read it, because it was easier to ask the girl." She lifted one inky hand off her stomach and let it fall back. "This is the other kind. This one won't need the girl."

Cael sat in the window and looked at her lying among the boxes, and found that he did not want to say anything that would spoil it.

"I wanted to help," he said instead. "Bracken wouldn't let me touch a sheet."

"Of course he wouldn't." Karis sounded faintly scandalised. "You're the subject. The subject doesn't carry his own file. That's the first thing anybody learns." Then, more gently, still with her eyes shut: "You're doing the other half. The dull half. You'll have done the harder one, if you manage it. I couldn't be dull for fifteen days if you paid me. I'd find something."

"I'll find something," said Cael. "I'll find it in the library and write it in a notebook nobody will ever read."

"That," said Karis, "is dull. Good."

The lamp-man came at the ninth bell, and stood in the doorway with his pole, looking at the girl on the floor with her feet on a box, and decided, visibly, that he had seen worse. When Cael helped her up she left two black fingerprints on his sleeve and did not notice, and he did not tell her.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

What he had found in the library, by then, was nine names out of eleven.

It was quicker work than he had feared. The Compact printed its findings, every chartered house was bound to keep a set, and every finding named its panel at the foot. Halcenvane kept them in a long bay on the library's second floor, bound by the year in brown cloth, with an index at the back of every volume that nobody had touched since it was printed. He went through a dozen years of indexes in two afternoons, writing names on a slip as he went, and then went back to each name and read whatever it led to.

Delegation counsel had a long run of findings on enrollment basis behind her, and a habit, plain once he had read six of them in a row, of attacking where a document came from before she ever asked what it said. He wrote that on her page and underlined it, and thought of Bracken's librarians and their brass seals, and felt better than he had all week.

The three clerks were names in lists of attendance and nothing more, and so were three of the four riders of the escort. The fourth rider's name was nowhere at all. Cael spent half an hour on him before deciding, with relief, that he was simply too new for his name to have travelled anywhere yet, and that a man who rode beside a carriage would not be the one who mattered.

Then the records officer.

Havel.

He did nothing at all but look at it.

He had met Havel twice. The first time was at Ardenmere, in the Unranked District, on a cold bright morning at the pump step, when a young assessor in a well-fitted grey coat and boots too new to have creased had come across the square with a credentials case held close against his side. He had read his questions off a form in a careful level voice. At the end he had asked one more question that was on no form, about why Cael had stayed at one address, and he had written the answer down at a slant across the page, in a hand that had suddenly stopped filling in a form. When Cael offered him a pear, something had crossed the young man's face that looked like wanting one, and he had not taken it.

The second time was at Greyvane, in the hearing room. The same man had sat at the end of the delegation's table with a recorder's case open on his knees and a little brass sand-glass beside him, turning the glass every quarter of an hour and writing down every word that anybody said, including all of Cael's.

Now he was records officer on an Archmarshal's manifest, which was another grade, and a grade above the last one.

Cael wrote on the page, at the top, Havel, and under it, after a while: He keeps going up a grade, and he keeps turning up wherever I am. I've never decided whether that's chance. I'm not going to decide tonight.

He showed the page to Lira at supper, folded back so that only Havel's lines showed, and she read it with her spoon in her other hand.

"The pear one," she said.

"The pear one."

"You told me about him the same night. You said he wanted the pear and wouldn't let himself." She gave the page back. "And then he sat at Greyvane and wrote down every word you said for the whole of the hearing, and never once looked as if he liked or minded any of it."

"That's him."

"Careful men go up," said Lira, and went back to her soup. "That's all going up is, mostly. Somebody notices you've never once been wrong in writing." She considered that. "It doesn't tell you what he's careful for."

He wrote that under the rest, because it was the better question.

The senior evaluation seat was the last of the nine, and he already knew her name before he found it.

Assessor Ilsev.

The library held six of her findings. He read all six through on the second afternoon, and then read them again that evening, although he had known by halfway through the first reading that he would not need a second. She had sat the senior evaluation on him the year he Kindled, in a district office with a wall so thin he had heard the next room's clerk sneeze. She had sat the senior seat at Greyvane. In all six findings she did one thing, over and over, with a kind of quiet ferocity that did not show until you put them side by side. She read the text she was given all the way to the end, and went where it went, even when the room did not want to follow.

At Greyvane the text had gone in his favour, and she had followed it there in front of a warden, and he wrote that down. Underneath he wrote that a woman who followed text wherever it went would follow it against him just as readily, on the day it went that way. He could not tell, from six findings, whether she was the gravest danger on that list or the best hope on it.

Probably both, he wrote. Probably those aren't different.

That left one name.

He went looking for it on the third afternoon with the slip in his hand and the whole of the long bay to himself. He went through all twelve years of indexes, carefully, the way he would have counted a crowd, and then he went through them again. Then he went down to the main floor and asked the duty librarian for the general catalogue, which covered the whole library and not just the findings, and went through that.

There was nothing.

It was not a thin file. A thin file is a shape; it tells you that someone was there and did little. This had no shape at all. No panel had ever been printed with him on it. He had signed nothing the library owned: not a finding, not an opinion, not so much as a note on procedure or a circular to the house.

In the end he went and found Karis, because Karis read faster than he did and wanted things less.

She came up to the long bay with ink still faint on her knuckles and went through every index he had been through, and the general catalogue after them. Then, without being asked, she went through the visitors' books for the last forty years, which were kept in a press in the corner and smelled of mice. It took her most of the evening, and she came back to his table with three slips.

"Three," she said. "In the whole library. A list of the officers present at a dedication, eight years ago, down the coast. A list of seats at a dinner given for a retiring magistrate. And a list of those who stood witness at a swearing-in." She laid them in a row. "Every one of them is his name in a list. Not one of them is a word he said."

"So he doesn't write."

"He writes. Of course he writes." She sat down across from him. "Assessors' work ends up in print. That's why Ilsev is on our shelves six times over. His doesn't. It goes into drawers that only open for people a long way above us, and we'll never see the inside of one. I can't find what he thinks, because nobody below that desk is allowed to read it."

"Then I can't build a page."

"No," said Karis. "You can't build a page."

He took a fresh sheet out of the observation notebook and wrote the name at the top of it, and sat looking at it for a long time with the library going dark round them. Karis did not hurry him, and somewhere below the duty librarian was walking the floors with her keys, closing the presses one by one.

At last he wrote one line under the name and left the rest of the page empty.

Every opponent I've ever had, I read on paper before I read them on the floor. Every one. The shelves have nothing on this one. I'll have to read him standing up.

Karis read it upside down across the table, which she did with everything, and did not pretend otherwise.

"Standing up," she said. "On a tier somewhere, I suppose, when they come up the road."

"Wherever there's a clean line."

She was quiet for a little, turning one of the three slips over and back.

"You go thin when you read hard," she said. "You know that. It's in your own ledger, in your own hand. Reading, thinking, anything that takes all of you. That's when the hold slips, because the hold needs a corner of you, and when you read hard you don't leave any corners."

"I know."

"The day those carriages come up, you're going to want to read every soul in them at once, with everything you've got." She laid the slip down. "Take Lira with you."

"Why Lira?"

"Because she'll be watching you, and not them," said Karis. "Somebody ought to be."

He did not argue. He wrote Lira at the foot of the empty page, small, under the one line, and closed the notebook, and they went down together through the dark stacks to the stair, where the duty librarian stood waiting with her keys and an air of great patience.

Lira found it first, which was fitting, since half of it was hers.

She was standing in front of the main board under the covered walk's north arch when Cael came through at the change of the second bell on Fifth-day, with her weight on the good hip and her hands in her coat pockets, quite still among the people going past. She was not reading, because Lira never read a thing twice; she read it once and had it; she was doing sums.

"Look," she said, without turning round. "They've put us next to each other."

All season the left half of the main board had belonged to the Copper column, ninety-one names long in the porter's white paint, with Lira on the top line and the brass stud on the line below it, beside Fiske. The right half was where notices went to be ignored. That morning somebody from the wing had taken down a warning about lamp oil and a lost glove and pinned up a single printed sheet in their place, so that it hung level with the season's dates, a hand's breadth away.

Lira read the left margin aloud for him in a low voice, as though he could not read it himself, which was her way of saying it mattered.

"Copper column. Semifinals: the ninth and the tenth of Reaping. Final: the Crown yard, the nineteenth. Panel: three faculty. Witnessed."

Then the printed sheet.

"Delegation of the Guilds Compact. Arrival: the twelfth. Sittings on the records: from the twelfth through the fifteenth. Review of facilities: the fourteenth. Faculty interviews: as the delegation directs. Observation of provision-status evaluation: reserved. The twentieth of Reaping."

She stopped, and they both looked at the two columns.

"They overlap," said Lira. "A whole week. They'll be here for my semifinal's aftermath, and Brom's, and the final, and you." She took one hand out of her pocket and laid a fingertip on the printed sheet, lightly, on the word reserved. "That's you."

"That's me."

"It doesn't say your name."

"It doesn't need to," said Cael. "There's only one."

The last time a pinned sheet on a board had carried a date that was about him, it had been at Greyvane, in a narrow passage with a draught in it, and the date had been a hearing. His name had been printed out in full above it in the registry's square type, and he had been fifteen. He had stood in front of it and understood that a system had written him into its calendar without asking, and he had thought at the time that nothing a board could say would ever be worse.

He looked for that feeling now, honestly. It was not there.

Neither date on this board was aimed at anybody. The final's had been chalked into the margin since the brackets went up, by a registrar who had never heard of a notice. The evaluation's had been on the wing's wall since the first week of term. The delegation's clerks had drawn up their own dates in some office far down the river, out of a register of charter visits. They had not had the least idea that a foundry girl and a boy who had been taken apart on purpose were going to fight for a crown in the middle of their stay. Ordinary people at ordinary desks had done their ordinary work, and the dates had fallen where they fell.

And his own line on the printed sheet was not a summons. It was the procedure he had signed for on the day he enrolled, on its posted day, before its panel, against his own baseline. The only thing the delegation had added to it was a chair at the rail.

"You've gone quiet," said Lira.

"I was checking whether I mind."

"And?"

"I don't," said Cael, a little surprised. "Last time a board did this, it was a summons. This is a calendar."

Lira looked at him sideways, then nodded, and took her finger off the sheet.

"Good," she said. "Then I'll mind for both of us. Mine's on the ninth."

That night, at the window, the board went into the Log. One part of the entry had been waiting for him all day, ready-made, and only needed setting down.

Last time the Compact came to an academy for me, they sent a warden with a challenge. This time they're sending an Archmarshal with no stated business at all. Coss I could read in a week. I don't know what reads an Archmarshal.

He let that stand for a while, and then went on underneath, more slowly.

Three men told me the same thing inside a day, in three different rooms, and none of them asked the others first. Gault at the long table: my wing changes nothing. Rooke under the north arch: keep doing it, it's as boring as it sounds. Bracken over his counter the next morning: give me a dull month. Not one of the three is fond of the other two. One instruction between them. Hold the ordinary. Stand still while they come.

All my life, people with seals have told me to take up less room. These three told me to stay exactly the size I am. They meant it. I think they're right.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The bluff's temperature went up for three days, and it went up in small ugly ways, as the temperature of a place does when it is frightened and cannot say so.

The first sign was a rumour. It started in the Iron bracket the day after the reading and had worked its way down to the Copper benches by supper: the inspection had been asked for. Another academy, jealous of Halcenvane's season, had written to the Compact to complain about the provision enrollment, and this was the answer. By the second morning the rumour had grown a name. It was a river academy two days downstream, which had lost three good Stone students to Halcenvane the year before and had never forgiven it. By the third morning there were people in the refectory who could tell you who had signed the letter, and what colour the wax was.

"There isn't any letter," said Karis, at breakfast, with the marbled book open beside her bowl. "A complaint from one house about another goes to the regional office and comes back as an ordinary visit with two officers and a ledger. You don't get eleven names and an Archmarshal for a quarrel about Stone students. Nobody who knows anything believes it."

"Nobody who knows anything is spreading it," said Lira.

"That's the trouble with rumours," said Brom, through bread. "The people telling them never know anything. That's how you can tell they're rumours."

The second sign came at Bracken's counter, on the afternoon of the second day.

Cael was in the queue with a library request of Karis's. Ahead of him stood two second-years from the law range, a tall one and a short one, who had plainly come together so that neither would have to ask alone. When the short one reached the counter he laid both hands flat on it.

"Registrar," he said, "we wanted to ask. If the delegation found against an enrollment, say a provision enrollment, would the enrollment be suspended? While they decided? Before there was a finding?" He went a little pink. "We're asking about the law."

Bracken looked at him over the top of the counter.

"No," he said. "Not by a delegation and not by the chancellor. An enrollment stands until a finding is filed against it and answered in the proper forum, and then it stands until that forum rules. That is the law, and you may cite me." He made a small note on a slip, which might have been anything. "Is there something else you'd like to ask me?"

There was a pause in which it was clear to everybody in the queue that there was, and that it was not about the law.

Bracken did not wait for it, but looked past the two second-years, down the queue, to Cael.

"Enrollee," he said. "Miss Karis's request. Box nine of the founding-era copies, up from the store by the fourth bell." He held the stamped slip out across the counter in the voice he used for every slip he had ever handed anyone, a voice with nothing in it at all. "Initial it, please."

When Cael stepped up and initialled it, the two second-years stood aside to let him, and looked at him, and looked at Bracken, who had already gone back to his ledger. Then they went out together without saying anything more, and Cael understood that he had just watched the registrar answer the question under the question, and answer it with a stamped slip about a box of old copies.

The third sign was a first-year.

He was a Mire boy, young even for a first-year, with ink on his collar, and Cael met him in the covered walk on the morning of the third day. The boy stopped dead in front of him. He looked at Cael's face for a little too long, as if he had been told a great deal about it and was checking the description against the original. Then his eyes went down and up once, quickly, and he walked on with a small frown. He had worked something out, and Cael would never know what the sum was, or what it had come to.

It was the fame problem again, come back in a new coat.

Cael had lived with it since the bridge. Every person on the bluff had come up the road already carrying some version of him: the boy from the transcript, the boy who had beaten the registry, the boy whose people had given him up. Not one of those versions had ever been tested against anything that mattered. Now something that mattered was coming up the road in carriages, and all over the bluff the versions were being taken out and turned over in people's hands, to see whether they would hold.

The looks came back, nearly as many as in the first month, in the refectory queue and on the lecture stair, and people watched him cross the second quadrangle in case he did something unusual in the middle of it. None of that touched his edges; their eyes were their business, and the hold was his. Being stared at did not make the rent any heavier. It only made it lonelier.

Gwen, alone of everybody on the bluff, took it at face value.

She found him in the library on the second afternoon, at the long bay where he was working through the findings, and sat down opposite without being asked, with her green scarf trailing and her decorated notebook open at a fresh page.

"Is it true," she said, in the whisper she believed was quiet, which carried to the end of the bay, "that an Archmarshal is coming up the road to watch you?"

"An Archmarshal is coming up the road," said Cael. "With ten other people. To inspect the academy."

"And watch you."

"And observe a provision-status evaluation, which is in the scope."

Gwen considered this, and wrote it down word for word, which took her some time, and then drew a very small eye at the end of it.

"That's a yes," she said.

"It's a yes," Cael admitted.

"I asked my aunt once what an Archmarshal was. She's an assessor, at the Fenmark station. She said she'd met one in thirty years, at a dinner, and he'd asked her to pass the salt, and she'd never been so frightened of a sentence in her life." Gwen looked at him with frank interest across the table. "Are you frightened?"

"Yes," said Cael.

She looked surprised, and then pleased.

"Good," she said. "Everybody else says no, and they're all lying, and it's very tiring." She closed the notebook. "Seln says on Third-day we're going to count how many people look at a person who's frightened and how many look at a person who's pretending not to be. I'm going to put you in the first column. Is that all right?"

"That's all right."

"I'll draw you an eye," said Gwen kindly, and went away.

On the third evening the space round him at the refectory's long table was wider than it had been since the first week, though nobody had decided to leave it. A boy had sat a seat further along than he might have, and then a girl a seat further than that, and the gap had made itself.

Jask sat down in it.

He did it on purpose, with his tray, without asking, and without looking at Cael while he did it. He was the third-year from hall three who had stood under a locked core with a jammed pin while Cael came across the open boards toward him. Since then he had been careful, in the way of a person who does not want to be the story, never to be seen with Cael more than anybody else was.

"They've put my dial back," said Jask, to his soup. "The one on the post. The warden's new pins came. It turns smooth now. You can feel every stop."

"That's good," said Cael.

"It's very good. I've moved up two lines on my term sheet." Jask ate some soup. "My mother writes and asks if I'm being careful on the floors. I tell her the floors are being careful now." He tore a piece of bread in half. "I'm not sitting here for any reason. I'm sitting here because it's the end with the bread."

"Understood."

"Good," said Jask, and ate his bread, and talked for the rest of the meal about nothing at all, about dials and stops and the price of boot leather in Ostrand, in a steady unremarkable voice that carried as far as the people on either side of them and not one seat further. When he had finished he took his tray and went. He did not look back. By the time he reached the hatch the gap at the long table had closed behind him, because a boy who had been sitting a seat too far along had moved up into it to get at the bread.

Cael wrote one line about it that night, on the page with Jask's name, which until then had held only the pin.

Sat in the gap at supper on purpose and said it wasn't on purpose. Doesn't want to be the story. Was a better friend for ten minutes than most people manage in a year.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

On the fourth morning Withrow spoke to the whole of Halcenvane in the lecture range's great hall. Karis timed it by the clock over the east door, and it took twelve minutes.

The hall had benches for six hundred, and Cael guessed five hundred in it: faculty in the front rows, then every year of enrollee in rising tiers behind them, more people than he had ever seen in one room on the bluff. He stood at the back by the east door with Lira and Brom, where the latecomers stood, and he had decided beforehand not to read the room. A hall of five hundred was the kind of crowd that pulled all of him outward into the reading of it, and he had a hold to keep. So he gave himself one thing to watch, and chose the clock.

Withrow walked out to the front without anybody announcing her and stood there with nothing in her hands.

"I'm told that clock runs two minutes slow," she said. "I'll be done before it notices."

A ripple went along the tiers, not quite a laugh.

She gave them the three differences first. They came in the order her counsel had used round the long table, and no more dressed than they had been there: early, and nobody had said why; large, eleven where two would do; and at the head of it, an officer of a rank that did not come to academies. She did not dress any of it, and she did not soften it either. She laid the three things out in front of five hundred people like three stones on a table and let them look.

"Now," she said. "What follows from that? For you, nothing new. I have no instruction to give you that I haven't given every week this term. Go to your lectures. Sit your assessments on the days they fall. Fight your bouts when your names are posted. That's all." She let it settle. "If any of you is tempted to put on a show for our visitors, a cleaner floor, a quieter refectory, a better face, don't. They will see it. They're made to see it. A house pretending to be itself is the commonest thing an inspection finds, and the easiest. A performance is the one thing an inspection can truly see. Give them nothing to see but Halcenvane."

Cael did not look at the tiers, and did not have to. Even with his eyes on the clock he felt the hall go down. Down along the benches shoulders came off ears and backs found the backs of benches, with a long low rustle like a field after the wind drops. A boy in front of him who had been perched on the edge of his seat for six minutes sat back with an audible breath.

"One thing more," said Withrow, "and I'd sooner it came from me than from a passage. I took a provision enrollment into this academy. I took advice before I did it, and I read the law myself, twice, and I think the basis is sound. I still think so. If the delegation rules otherwise, it's my ruling they're overturning, not anybody else's, and I'll stand at the front of this hall and tell you so with my own mouth." She looked once along the tiers, slowly, from one side to the other. "Nobody else here carries my decision. Least of all a sixteen-year-old."

She went out by the side door, the way she had come in.

The clock over the east door had moved twelve minutes, and for a moment the hall did not move at all. Then it did, all at once and in the ordinary way, with the scrape of benches and the rising noise of five hundred people deciding where to go next.

In the faculty rows Rooke stood up with the others. He did not clap, because nobody was clapping, and he did not frown, and not once on his way to the side door did he turn his head toward the back of the hall. Cael watched him go the whole length of the aisle. He was fairly sure, by the end of it, that the not-turning had been decided in advance, as the kindest thing a narrow grey man could do for a boy in front of five hundred people.

Lira had her arms folded and her weight on the good hip.

"She said it to everybody," said Lira, low. "So nobody can say it to you."

"Yes."

"I think I'd fight for her," said Lira, with faint surprise, as though she had found something unexpected in a pocket, and pushed herself off the wall.

Ephram met him on the lecture range stair on the way out. He came up it, against the crowd that was going down, and stopped one step above Cael on the second landing, so that people had to go round them both on either side, and slowed, and listened. That was how Ephram did everything, and Cael had stopped holding it against him.

He was the top of the Iron column, a lean Blade fighter with a kit bag over one shoulder. In the second month, in the Crown yard, with sixty people hearing it, he had said a thing, and all season he had kept to it. Greyvane, he had said, had needed the assay boy to be real; Halcenvane did not; and he would make up his mind at the semester evaluation and not one day sooner.

"Cael," he said. "A minute. I'll be quick."

"Go on."

"In the second month I told this yard I'd hold my opinion till your evaluation. I've held it. People have tried to talk me out of it in both directions all season, and I've held it." He shifted the kit bag. "But I said it about a panel of three and an empty gallery. That's not what it is now. Now there'll be an Archmarshal in the gallery. So I'm altering my terms, here, out loud, where people can hear me do it, because that's where I made them. And the alteration's in your favour." He looked round at the stair, at the thirty or so faces slowing on it. "Anybody looks good in an empty room."

Somebody above them laughed, briefly, and stopped.

"You'll be watched by the most senior person any of us is ever likely to stand under the same roof with," said Ephram. "If you are what that transcript says, all of us will see it, in daylight, with the best witness in the Compact sitting at the rail, and no one will ever be able to say it was arranged. If you're not, we'll see that instead. I'd sooner see. Whichever it is."

There was no warmth in it and no malice; it was the voice of a fighter reading out a rule he happened to approve of.

"So would I," said Cael.

He meant it, and it showed, and Ephram looked briefly and visibly put out to have been agreed with in front of thirty people. He opened his mouth to add a condition, found he had none, gave a short nod, and went on up the stair with his kit bag, against the stream, to wherever he had been going in the first place.

Brom watched him out of sight.

"He changed his mind out loud," Brom said. "In public. On a stair."

"He didn't change his mind. He changed his terms."

"Same thing, for him." Brom rubbed his jaw. "I've watched him in the cohort hour all season. He's never once said a thing he couldn't stand behind with a crowd looking at him. It's the most annoying thing about him. I think it might also be the best." He considered. "I'm going to tell Rooke. Rooke'll say noted."

That night Cael opened the page headed Ephram and wrote under the last entry: Altered his own terms in public, on the stair where he could be heard doing it, and said the alteration was in my favour. Owns his opinions like tools, and puts them down where people can see.

Then, because it was true:

I'd like to be able to do that. I'm not there yet. I still alter mine in this notebook, where nobody has to watch me be wrong.

Chapter 41 — Complete, Consistent

[Dry, precise narration; sharpen the institutional pressure through exact detail]

Seln had read four of Assessor Ilsev's findings on the road up from his last posting, in a coach with a broken window, out of the habit of reading whatever he could find about anybody who might one day read him. He had shut the volume knowing one thing about her for certain. She went through what was put in front of her from the first line to the last, at the same pace throughout, and she did not want anything from it while she read. A reader who wanted nothing was rarer than a clever one, and harder to be read by.

So on Seventh-day afternoon, when the requisition came, he tried to read his term the way she would.

It had come up from Ostrand in the noon bag under the wing's seal, and it had crossed the copying table on its way to Gault, as everything sealed did.

To the assessment office of the receiving institution: compile, under one covering index, the whole of this term's monitoring product on any enrollee held under provision, and keep it sealed against the senior evaluation seat's call.

He had laid it in Gault's tray between a query from the bursar and a letter about chalk, and finished the afternoon's floor allocations to the last line. At the third bell Gault had set it back on the copying table with one word pencilled in its margin: Proceed.

The compiling was an afternoon's work at most, since every sheet was his own. He did it at the copying table in full view, with the desk clerk at her ledger six feet off, because nothing in it wanted a closed door.

Most of what he had sent down the river that term was carpentry: calendar extracts, floor issues, lists of associates, and that went at the back, as appendices. In front of it went the product proper, which came to six filings. He laid the six side by side along the edge of the wood, squared each to the last, so that the whole term lay under his hand at once.

Then he read them, as Ilsev would, from the first word to the last, with a finger moving under each line, and no hope in the reading at all.

Coverage established.

Subject's routine is disciplined and unremarkable. Trains under supervision… Extensive private notation habit… No undisclosed capability observed.

No undisclosed capability observed.

Enrollee present at bay edge… Response consistent with documented baseline.

No undisclosed capability observed.

No undisclosed capability observed.

Every sentence in the six was true, and every filing was whole in its form, with its appendices in order and its date and initial and its walk down the hill to the fish steps.

He thought of it as a ledger, because he had been trained on ledgers, and on one side stood the subject. In a single year the boy had produced an adjudication, a transcript that half the continent had paid six silver marks to read, and a designation on his file graded well above that of the man sent to watch him. On the other side stood a full term of embedded coverage by an officer with a clean record. And at the foot, where the total went, there was nothing at all.

He knew the words a reader would write under that. He had written them himself, once, at a long table up the coast, under a colleague's stack that had looked very like this one, and the colleague had been brought home inside the month.

Complete, consistent, and containing nothing.

Nobody needed to suspect anything to write that. The sum wrote it.

He looked at the six for the space of a few breaths, while the desk clerk murmured forty-one and wrote it down, and then he made up the file.

He tied each filing to its own appendices with pink tape, oldest first. He wrote the covering index in the upright, plain hand that he kept for product and used for nothing else: each sheet by its heading and its date, one line apiece. He put no note on it anywhere, because a note is the start of an argument, and an argument is something a reader can take the other side of.

He added nothing, took nothing out, and left the exception report shut. Near its end stood a word he had once weighed for four seconds, and he did not open the report to weigh it again. Nothing in the bundle was false. Nothing in it was the whole of anything. At the fourth bell Gault's clerk took it from him across the counter with the rest of the day's paper and pressed the wing's seal into the wax over the tape, and locked it in the holding cabinet, where it would wait four days for the delegation.

After supper he read the floor allocations on the covered walk's board, which he had written himself, as if they were news, and went up the staff stair at the pace of a man going to bed. There was nothing for the small case tonight. He sat on the bed's edge for a while, listening to the river under the bluff, and then he put the lamp out.

What he kept, he kept.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Cael went to the east hall's gallery at the fifth bell, as he did most days, to watch Rooke's cohort, and found that Rooke had rearranged the floor.

All season the cohort hour had run the same way: Rooke set pairs at the four marks on the timber and walked between them. Once in an hour he called a pair out into the middle and took one of them apart in front of the rest, slowly, with a few words, so that everybody could learn from the taking-apart. Brom had been taken apart in the middle of that floor perhaps thirty times since the first week, and Merrick had done a fair share of the taking.

Today there were only three marks in use, and Merrick was not at any of them. He was at the far end of the hall, at the wall bars, with a junior Shield fighter for a partner, working panes. Brom was at the near mark with a Blade second-year. Between the two ends of the hall there was perhaps forty feet of empty timber, and every few minutes Rooke walked slowly down the middle of it, checking that it stayed empty.

Halfway through the hour Merrick turned his head to look down the hall at Brom. He did it once, briefly.

"Back to the bars, Merrick," said Rooke, without raising his voice and without seeming to have looked. "You'll see him on the tenth. Neither of you learns the other on my floor this week. If you want to study him, you've had a season." He stopped at the empty middle of the floor. "So has he."

Merrick turned back to the bars, and somebody in the cohort laughed and was looked at, and stopped.

Cael watched Brom work.

The Blade second-year fed him short strikes, cheap ones, the kind Merrick had always fed him, and Brom stood under them and did not turn. He took them on the forearm and the shoulder, square, with his weight set, and the instant each one landed he went forward through it, hard, while the struck side was still hard. That was Rooke's repair, the one the nineteen exercises had been built to make: stop finishing the absorption. Drive while you're still iron. For two years Brom had taken a strike, finished taking it, softened, and only then countered, and in the gap between the softening and the counter there had been a stall that every good fighter on the bluff could find.

The stall was still there. Cael could see it from the gallery, if he watched for it: the smallest hitch, a fraction of a beat, between the landing and the going. But he could only see it because he knew to look for it, and because he was forty feet up with nothing to do but look. Down on the boards, inside an exchange, the Blade second-year never found it once.

Twice in the hour Rooke came and stood at Brom's mark and watched three exchanges without saying anything. The second time he said, "Again," and Brom did it again, and Rooke said, "Better," which from Rooke was a speech, and went away.

Cael wrote three lines in the shorthand on the edge of his lecture notes.

Brom: the stall is a hitch now, not a gap. From the gallery: findable. On the floor: not, in an hour of trying.

Merrick: had a season to find it, and will have something new.

Rooke: kept them forty feet apart. On purpose. Fair to both.

Merrick passed him on the gallery stair afterward, coming up toward the north door as Cael was going down. He was a long-faced fourth-year with a careful way of setting his feet, as if every floor he stood on had been laid by somebody who disliked him, and he stopped two steps above Cael and looked down at him with an expression of grave courtesy.

"You'll be on the tier on the tenth," he said. It was not a question.

"I'll be on the tier."

"Tell him something from me, then." Merrick considered. "No. Don't. He'd only think it was a feint." He went up one more step, and stopped again. "You know he looks for you before every bout? Up at the tiers, before the word. I've watched him do it all season. He finds you, and then he starts."

"I didn't know that," said Cael, which was true.

"I'd sit somewhere else on the tenth, if I were his friend," said Merrick. "Somewhere he has to look for." He went on up the stair and through the north door without waiting to see how that was taken.

Cael stood on the stair for some time before he wrote a fourth line under the other three, and did not like it any better for having written it.

Merrick: has been reading Brom by reading where Brom looks. Has he been reading me too?

Lira had her leg up on the chair when he came to her door after supper, with a wet cloth folded over the hip and the window open on the river, and she did not get up.

"Sit," she said. "Not on the bed. Brom sat on it this afternoon and now it's a hammock."

He sat down on the boards against the wall, the notebook on his knee. It was a fat notebook by now, and three weeks of it, in the back, were headed Fiske.

Lira looked at it and looked away.

"I know what's in that," she said.

"Everything I've seen her do since the first month. Every bout. Every opening, and where she placed, and how long she collected before she did." He laid a hand on the cover. "She'll have changed. She's had a month. But the shape of how she changes is in here too. She changes in a particular way."

"I know," said Lira. "That's why I don't want it."

He waited.

"Think about what she's got," said Lira. She did not look at him; she looked at the river. "She's got all of me now. The first time, I showed her my sequence for a whole exchange, step by step, so she'd learn it, and she learned it. Then I lied with it four times and she watched me do that. Then I walked in on my own feet and she watched that too. She knows I've four bursts on a good day and that the fourth is paid for out of tomorrow. She knows I can move my landing a foot with a half-step, because she watched me do it in front of eight hundred people. She knows where I learned to walk." Lira moved the cloth on her hip. "Last time she had a page about me with a hole in it, and I went through the hole. There isn't a hole now. She's had a month to sew it up, and she's the best on this hill at sewing."

"So you want more, not less."

"No. That's what everybody thinks, and it's wrong." She turned her head and looked at him at last. "If I go in carrying your pages, I'm carrying more than I can use. I'll be watching for the things you saw, and while I'm watching for them I'll be slow. She'll be ready for everything I brought last time. Good. I'm not bringing it. I'm going in with less than she thinks I've got, and I'll find out what's left when I'm standing on the boards. That's the only way to beat somebody who knows you completely. You stop being the person she knows."

His hand stayed on the notebook.

The old want came up in him, strong and familiar, the want that had built every page in the book: to give her everything, every pattern and tell and number, and send her into the yard armoured in it. He felt it come up and recognised it, and saw clearly, perhaps for the first time, that it was his want and not hers, and that giving her what he wanted to give would be a way of fighting the bout himself from the tier.

He took his hand off the notebook.

"All right," he said.

Lira looked at him, surprised.

"That's it? All right?"

"It's your bout. You know what you need better than my pages do." He put the notebook down on the floor beside him, out of the way. "How many bursts have you got?"

"Enough," said Lira.

"That's not a number."

"No," she agreed, and nearly smiled. "It's an answer, though. I'm not giving you the number either, because you'll sit on the tier counting, and I'll feel you counting, and it'll be like having a clock in my hip." She shifted the cloth again. "The hip's fine. It's tight. It's been tight since the foundry. Tomorrow it's going to hurt, and the day after tomorrow it's going to hurt more, and then it's going to have nine days, and that's how it's going to be. Nobody's to talk about it."

"Nobody will."

"Brom will. He can't help himself. He's going to look at it at breakfast like it's a sick dog." She lay back on the floor and closed her eyes. "Tell him not to."

"I'll tell him."

Lira lay looking at the ceiling for a while.

"If I win tomorrow," she said, "and Brom wins the day after, then on the nineteenth I fight him in front of an Archmarshal."

"Yes."

"Fiske told me to make them look." She said it slowly, laying the words out one at a time to see how they sat together. "Win the crown, she said, and then make them look at you. The crown's only how you force it. I've been thinking about that for a month. I thought she meant the registry. Somebody at a desk in Fenmark with my flag in a queue under forty other flags." She turned her head on the floor and looked at him. "And now the most senior pair of eyes in the whole Compact is coming up our road on its own feet, and it's going to be sitting in the gallery on the nineteenth whether I like it or not, and it isn't coming for me at all. It's coming for you. I'm what happens to be on the boards while it's here."

"Does that make it worse?"

"It makes it funnier," said Lira. She did not laugh. "All my life I've wanted the people with the stamps to look at me properly, just once, instead of at a number on a card. And when they finally send the biggest stamp they've got, it's to look at somebody else, and I'm the fight it watches while it waits." She closed her eyes again. "I'm going to give it a very good fight. That's all. I'm not going to think about whether it sees me. If it's any good at its job, it will."

They sat for a while without talking, while a barge went past below, low in the water.

"She'll be good tomorrow," said Lira, with her eyes shut. "She'll be better than last time. I want her to be. If I'm going to beat her, I don't want to beat a tired one." She was quiet. "She's the only person on this hill who's ever told me the truth without wanting anything for it. I'd like to give her the best bout she's ever had. Then I'd like to win it."

Chapter 42 — One Very Long Minute

[Dry, precise narration; sharpen the institutional pressure through exact detail]

On the morning of the ninth of Reaping the registrar's outer office smelled of hot wax, and there were four boxes on the counter.

Karis had asked him to be at the registrar's counter at the second bell, and had not said why. So he was there, standing at the dark wood with nothing in his hands, for the last minute of a piece of work. It had begun in a Greyvane carrel in the third week of a term, and it had been finished, in its final form, in six days in the room behind this one.

The boxes were plain grey pasteboard, the kind the stationer in Ostrand sold by the dozen, with brass corners and a cloth hinge. Three of them were already closed and tied with white tape, and on each lid in Bracken's hand was a single line: a number, and the words Enrollment basis, and the number of the box. The fourth stood open. Bracken was laying the last sheets into it from a stack at his elbow, one at a time, squaring each against the one below with the side of his hand.

Karis stood at the far end of the counter. She had her grey notebook clasped against her chest with both arms, and her knuckles were still faintly blue from four days of ink.

Nobody spoke, and the senior clerk at his high desk had stopped writing and sat with his pen lifted.

Bracken laid the last sheet, which was the first page of the index and went on top, so that whoever opened the box would see it before anything else; then he closed the lid. He took the white tape from the reel, measured it against the box without looking, cut it with the small knife from his waistcoat pocket, and tied it in a flat registrar's knot that would undo with one pull and with nothing else. Then he took the pen from behind his ear and wrote on the lid, 4 of 4, and under that, smaller, 311.

He set the box on the shelf behind him with the other three, and turned them all a little, so that the lettering faced the room.

"Three hundred and eleven sheets," he said. "Every link in the chain copied from its own volume and sealed by the person who keeps the volume. Two searches for a repeal, by two people who never compared a line, finding the same nothing in the same places. The whole of the directive, all forty-one pages, tabbed where it matters and marked where a repeal would have to be. And one index. A reader who wishes us well will find what she needs in about forty breaths. A reader who wishes us ill will find it in about ninety, because she'll check everything twice on the way." He put the pen back behind his ear. "Whoever on that delegation asks to see the provision gets the shelf, in the order it stands, and a clerk to carry it across for them."

He looked at Cael then, as though only now noticing that the enrollee was standing at his counter with no business there at all.

Cael stayed where he was.

"Tell him the rest," said Karis, from the end of the counter. Her voice was not quite steady, and she was cross with it. "The part you told me."

Bracken looked at her, and then at Cael. Whether the rest was a thing a registrar said aloud in his own outer office, in front of his own senior clerk, took him a little while to decide. Then he decided.

"The rest," he said, "is that neither of us is needed now. Miss Karis found the clause. I filed it. Neither of those things carries any weight now. The shelf carries it." He straightened the four boxes again, though they had not moved. "That's what a defense is, Enrollee, when it's finished. It isn't a speech. It's a thing that goes on being true in a room where nobody who built it is standing."

The senior clerk lowered his pen to the page and began, very quietly, to write again.

Cael went out into the covered walk and stopped by the first pillar, because he had to stop. The sentence had gone into him somewhere under the breastbone and was still going.

He had been fourteen in the Denvash certification hall. A clerk behind a long counter there had written a word about him on a form, in about the time it takes to sneeze, and the word had followed him into every room he had entered since. It had stood there talking about him long after the clerk who wrote it had gone home to his supper. That was what files had always been, to him: true in rooms he was not in, kept by people who had long since gone home, and impossible to question or to stop.

Bracken had just taken that machine and turned it round and pointed it the other way.

He stood by the pillar for perhaps a minute. Then Karis came out of the registrar's office behind him with her notebook still clasped to her chest and her eyes very bright, and walked straight past him without stopping.

"I'm not crying," she said, over her shoulder. "Don't write that I was. I've got something in my eye from the wax."

He did not write it. He wrote, that evening, Bracken closed the file. Karis has something in her eye from the wax, which was not the same thing at all.

The Crown yard was full by the fourth bell, and it was a different kind of full from the fifteenth session.

That afternoon, a month back, the yard had come to see a champion tested. Today it had come to see a question answered, and the question was harder. Everybody on the tiers had watched Lira take the top line by lying with the truth, and everybody had gone home and thought about it, and most of them had come to the same sum Cael had: that a trick like that worked once. Fiske had had a month to learn it, and whatever Lira did today, she could not do that again.

Cael sat in his usual place on the east tier, a third of the way up, with Brom on his left and Karis on his right, and did not count the crowd. He had made himself that promise at breakfast. In a yard this size the counting would take all of him, and the hold would go, and he had a hold to keep. So he gave himself the boards and nothing else, and let everything outside the chalk look after itself.

Fiske came out first. She walked to her chalk at the north end of the boards with her hands clasped behind her back, as she always did, and stood there looking at the floor between the two marks the way a carpenter studies a frame. Her face was perfectly calm, and she had fought nobody on the top line for a month, and she looked, Cael thought, rested.

Lira came out a few breaths after. She walked to her chalk with no hurry at all and crouched and laid her hand flat on the boards, and held it there a moment longer than usual, and stood up.

"She's favouring it," said Brom, under his breath. "Already."

"Don't," said Karis.

"I'm only saying."

The safety instructor stood at the table beside the sand-glass, and Withrow sat in the west gallery, upright and white-haired, alone this time. In the faculty box the grey-bearded man from the law range was already leaning forward with his elbows on the rail.

At the word, Fiske did not give ground.

That was the first thing, and the whole yard saw it and made a sound, a low surprised breath, the sound of a familiar tune going wrong in the second bar. All season Fiske had opened every bout the same way, stepping back off her line to buy herself a minute of learning, but she had nothing to learn today. She took one step forward instead, and put her first declaration into the boards at once, a yard to the left of Lira's chalk, flat and fast, and the patch of oak there went slick.

Then a second, a yard to the right.

Lira did not burst. She walked. She went forward between the two slick patches on her own feet, at an ordinary pace, straight down the one lane Fiske had left open. Cael saw instantly that the lane was a lie. It ran straight at Fiske, and it got narrower as it went, and the third declaration was already going down across the far end of it.

Lira saw it too, a step later than he did. She stopped. She stood in a narrowing strip of honest wood with Fiske's slick on both sides of her and across her front, and every inch of the strip had been drawn, in eleven seconds, by a woman who knew where Lira's feet liked to go and had simply removed all of those places before Lira got there.

"Burst," said Brom, very low. "Burst, burst."

She did not. She went sideways on her own feet, short, toward the last open edge. Fiske was already there. Her flat hand touched Lira's shoulder before Lira's foot had settled.

"Force," said the table. "One."

On the tiers the breath went out of eight hundred people at once, and somebody behind Cael said, satisfied, well, that's that.

Karis wrote one line in her notebook. Cael read it upside down: One. F. needs no minute now. L. spends nothing.

"Why won't she burst?" said Brom. "Why didn't she—"

"Because she's counting," said Cael. "She's got so many, and the hip's got so many, and they're not the same number. She won't spend one on an exchange she can't win."

"She's one down."

"I know."

The second exchange was over almost before it had begun.

At the word, Lira burst.

She did not burst away from anything. There was nothing yet to burst away from; the boards between them were clean, because Fiske had not had time to put anything on them. She burst straight forward from the chalk at the word itself, one half-breath of Wind, and the landing beat set her down two strides from Fiske, on clean oak, before Fiske's first declaration had finished gathering.

Fiske had seen it coming, of course; she had seen everything coming all season. But seeing a thing coming and having somewhere to put a slick floor in front of it are not the same. Lira had come in before there was any floor to close. Fiske turned the half-built declaration into a plain short delivery instead, and it caught Lira on the outside of the left arm, hard, and Lira's right hand was already flat on Fiske's ribs.

One burst gone. She had come in at the word with the cheapest burst there was, the one with no evasion in it, and it had bought her a touch. But Fiske had seen it, and Fiske would not let it work twice.

Karis wrote: Two. L. goes before there is anything to go round. One each. That door's shut now too.

Lira walked back to her chalk and did not look at the hip, because looking at it would have told the north end of the boards everything.

It was not bad yet: only the old line, crest to inner knee, lit up thin and bright from the one burst, the way a wire lights when you run too much through it. She could carry that; she had carried it on the foundry floor for two winters with a ladle of slag in her hands. What she could not carry was not knowing what came next, and she did not know, and neither, she was fairly sure, did Fiske.

Fiske was at her chalk with her hands behind her back, looking at the boards.

She knows everything I showed her, Lira thought. She's got the sequence and all four lies. She's got the half-step. She's got the walk-in from the foundry. She stood on her chalk and let Fiske look at her. She gave her nothing to read: no lean, no shift, no breath held too long. It cost. She stood anyway, and watched Fiske's eyes, and saw them go to the places on the boards where Lira had always liked to go, the arc on the left, the fold, the turn, one after another, like a clerk checking that every door on a corridor was locked.

Then Fiske began to close them, one by one, without waiting.

That was new. Last time Fiske had placed where Lira was going. Now she was placing where Lira might go, all of it, every likely place on the boards, before Lira had chosen any of them. A patch on the left. A patch at the fold. A patch where the turn would have come. It was expensive, since every declaration cost Fiske something, and she was spending them like a woman throwing coins into a well. But every one she spent made the floor smaller.

Lira waited until there were three places left, and then two.

When the ring closed to the size of a hearthrug she burst out of it. The hip took it. Something in the hip went bright and hot and stayed that way.

Two, she thought. That's two.

Fiske looked at her across the boards, and Lira saw her count it too.

They spent the rest of the glass like that. Fiske closed and Lira waited; Fiske closed again and Lira slid one foot an inch on honest oak and Fiske had to decide whether the inch meant anything. Neither of them came near enough to touch, and up on the tiers somebody began a slow handclap and was hushed by the people around him. "Even," said the table. "No touch. Third exchange."

One each, and one even. One to go.

Lira walked back to her chalk on a leg that had begun, very slightly, to argue with her about which way was down.

The arithmetic of the fourth was simple, and everybody in the yard knew it. If the fourth ended even, the bout was drawn, and a drawn bout kept the holder on the top line, and the holder was Lira. Fiske could not wait. Fiske had to take it.

Which meant, Lira thought, standing on the chalk, that for the first time in their two bouts Fiske was the one who had to come.

So let her come. Don't burst. Don't run anything. Make the floor hers and stand in the middle of it, and make her walk across it.

At the word, Fiske made the floor hers.

She did it quickly and completely, with a kind of terrible patience. A patch, and a patch, and a patch, closer each time, round Lira in a slow spiral, until Lira stood on a square of clean oak about the size of a table, with Fiske's slick on every side of it, gleaming faintly in the afternoon light like ice on a pond. There was no way off it on foot. A burst would take her off it, and Fiske knew how many bursts the hip had left, because Fiske could count as well as anybody, and the answer was one, perhaps, and a bad one.

Then Fiske stopped.

She stood at the edge of her own slick, a long stride away, with her hands loose at her sides, and she waited.

Lira understood. Fiske was not going to come across the oil to her. She had built a cage and put Lira in it and now she was going to wait at the bars for Lira to spend the last burst getting out, and then hit her in the landing beat, where everybody in the Copper column now knew a Wind fighter stood still. And if Lira did not burst, Fiske would wait until the sand was nearly gone and then come, at the last moment, when there would be no time left for anything but whatever Lira had kept.

It was the right plan, and Lira would have made the same one.

The sand ran.

It was the longest minute she had ever stood through.

She stood on the table of clean oak and did not burst. The hip burned. It had gone past bright now into something dull and deep and wide, a heat that filled the whole socket and spread down into the thigh, and it wanted, every moment, to be shifted. She did not shift it. Any shift was a lean, and a lean was a word, and Fiske was reading every word. So she stood on it, square, the way she had stood at the board at the fifth bell for three weeks with her breathing held level, and let it burn.

On the tiers the noise had stopped, and eight hundred people sat without moving. She could hear the sand. She could hear, from a long way off, a barge on the river giving its long note, and nobody answering.

Fiske waited. Her face did not change. But Lira, watching her eyes, saw them go once, quickly, to the glass on the table, and come back.

That's your tell, Lira thought, with a strange clear calm. You've never had to watch the sand before. You've always won before the sand mattered.

With perhaps ten breaths left in the glass, Fiske came.

She came straight, as she had come at the end of their first bout: one plain heavy delivery, built and committed, the Force that every other fighter on the sheet used, coming across her own slick on feet that knew where the oil lay. There was nowhere to go from it. Lira could not step back; behind her was slick. She could not step aside; slick. She could burst, and land, and stand still in front of the one woman on the bluff who hit still things best.

She went forward, onto the oil.

Not with Wind. On her feet. She stepped off the edge of her clean square onto Fiske's slick on purpose, the leading foot first, and let it go.

The casting floor at the foundry had been greased with tallow at every shift change, so that the moulds would slide, and every apprentice who had ever worked it had gone down hard on it in the first week, and every one who stayed had learned the trick. You did not fight a slick floor. Fighting it was what put you on your back. You let it carry you, low, with your weight over your knees and your arms loose, and you steered with the ball of the foot and you stopped yourself with the other one, where you chose, on something that held.

Lira let it carry her.

She went in under Fiske's delivery low and sliding, faster than any step, and the delivery went over her shoulder with a noise like a door slamming in a high wind. She had perhaps a body's length of slick and then Fiske's own feet, and Fiske's own patch of honest oak where she had been standing to build. Lira's back foot found the edge of it. She stopped herself there.

The stop went through the leading hip like a nail.

It did something in there she had never felt it do. Something gave, deep and sideways, with a small sound she heard inside her own head rather than with her ears. Her right hand was already moving. It landed flat on Fiske's ribs, under the arm, inside the recovery, as Fiske's weight was still going forward over the place where Lira had been.

"Wind," said the table, into the silence. "Two to one. Bout."

She did not hear the yard come up. She heard it afterward, a wall of noise from every tier at once that hit the lecture range and came back. In the moment she heard nothing but her own breath, and felt nothing but the floor under her right hand, because she had gone down on one knee on the oak at the edge of Fiske's patch and could not, for the moment, get up.

Fiske was standing over her, and her face had changed.

It was not a beaten face, of which Lira had seen plenty. It was the face Fiske had worn on the step a month ago, when she had said all the things she had carried for two years, and Lira had known then what it was, and knew now.

"You didn't run it," said Fiske. "Not once."

"You'd have shut it."

"Every step." Fiske looked down at the slick going dull and dry on the boards around them, fading back into plain oak. "You stood still for a minute in my yard. Nobody's ever done that."

"It's not your yard," said Lira, from her knee. "Not today."

When Fiske held out her hand, Lira took it, and Fiske did not pull. She only held it steady, so that Lira could use it to stand, and Lira used it, and stood, and found that the leading leg would take her weight if she asked it politely and not otherwise.

"The nineteenth," said Fiske. "I'll be on the tier for it. I haven't sat on a tier for a final in two years. I'm told you can see everything from up there."

"You can't see the far mark from the east side," said Lira. "Sit north."

Fiske considered this gravely, as she considered everything.

"North," she said, and let go of Lira's hand, and walked away along the foot of the tiers with her hands clasped behind her back.

It took Cael most of a quarter-hour to get down to the floor. When he got there Lira was sitting on the bottom step of the east tier with the leading leg straight out in front of her. Cael thought about Merrick's advice all morning, and in the end he sat where he always sat.

It had taken him most of breakfast to see it properly. Merrick had stood on the gallery stair two days ago with his grave courteous face and told him that Brom looked for him on the tier before every bout, and found him, and only then began. Then Merrick had advised him to sit somewhere else, somewhere Brom would have to look for him.

It had sounded like kindness, and Cael had carried it about for two days as kindness. It was only at breakfast, watching Brom eat porridge with the steady attention of a man stoking an engine, that he turned it the other way up and saw the shape underneath. If Cael sat somewhere else, Brom would look up at the usual place before the word and not find him there, and then he would look for him. He would look for perhaps two breaths, perhaps four, and every one of those breaths would be a breath in which Brom was thinking about the tier instead of the boards. Merrick had not offered advice. Karis's three columns: growth, control, five. Asked me where they fought. They don't. For once the hiding and the honesty don't pull apart. They're one job. It feels so good I'm suspicious of it. Writing that down too.

Quenna, at Greyvane, asked whether I could do the harder thing: whether you can not do it. In front of people who wish you harm. I said I didn't know. True then: one reach is a story, not a record.

Now I've reached twice. I own a thing that never switches off. And there's a date on a board.
