Hall three had frightened him to the bone once before, on the day of the pin. The next afternoon it did it again.

It was an ordinary supervised hour. The wing sent somebody to watch two of his four hours each week, because the provision said that floor time bound to an evaluation had to be witnessed, and the somebody was nearly always the same quiet woman from the wing. She kept to the north rail with a board on her knee and a pencil, and in half a year Cael had never once seen her look surprised. Brom was his partner, as he usually was on Third-days. They were running a redirect sequence at half pace round the north bay on the new pins: Brom fed, Cael took the feed and turned it, Brom fed again from the new angle, round and round, a pattern they had worked so often that it had worn a faint pale track into the timber.

It was the sort of work that wanted every part of a person. He had chosen it in the first month for that reason, because the way to learn a sequence was to give it all of you. He had not thought about that choice since.

On the fourteenth turn the sequence took the last corner of him, and he did not feel it go.

That was what frightened him afterward, more than anything. There was no lurch. There was no spike behind the eyes and no warning of any kind. There was only the sequence, which was going beautifully, better than it had gone all week. Brom's feeds were arriving where he wanted them and his own turns were coming out clean and early, and the hold, for the first time in days, was costing him nothing. He noticed that, dimly, as a pleasant thing, the way you notice a room is warm.

Then Brom stopped.

He stopped in the middle of a feed with his guard still up and his weight still set and the Iron read still running in his forearms. His eyes were open and turned toward the place where Cael stood. For a moment, a long strange moment, they were not quite on him. They were searching a little to one side of him, the way a man's eyes search a room he has walked into in the dark.

Then they found him.

"You went," said Brom, very quietly.

Cael did not move.

At the north rail the woman from the wing was writing on her board. She had been writing on it, Cael saw, with a cold that went down through him into his boots, for the whole of the last minute. Her head was bent over it, and stayed bent; she turned a page and wrote on.

Two breaths, he thought. Three at most.

They went on to the bell at the posted half pace, and on the boards neither one spoke of it. Cael fed and turned and held his edges so hard that the ache rose behind his eyes like water behind a sluice. At the bell the woman from the wing signed both their sheets in her small neat hand, without comment, and went out with her board under her arm.

In the corridor Brom stopped dead in the middle of the flagstones, square across the way, as a post stands in a yard, so that Cael would have had to walk round him.

"How far."

"Thin," said Cael. "Not gone. Thin. She had her head down."

"Down today." Brom's voice stayed low. Shouting would have been easier to bear. "Nine days from now you're going to be on a floor for three hours. Gault, and the panel, and an Archmarshal, and whoever else they've brought with them. And somewhere in that gallery there'll be a person whose whole trade is noticing when a thing isn't where it should be. And you've just shown me that the one thing you can't steer goes thin when all of you is busy." He did not move out of the way. "What do you call a three-hour evaluation, then?"

Cael took all of it standing, because every word was true, and in two years Brom had never once said a hard thing that did not need saying.

"All of me, busy," he said.

"For three hours."

"Yes."

"Then it isn't a drill you've got wrong." Brom stepped aside at last, so that the corridor was open again. "It's the whole thing. You've had it at the foot of the page all month. It goes at the top."

It did, and he knew it before Brom had finished. Three nights ago he had written two lines at the foot of a page with a small cross beside them: thinking about somebody else felt cheap, and perhaps that was because he wasn't paying. The sequence had felt free for the same reason. Nothing in him rang when he stopped paying. Nothing ever would. He would have to be the bell himself.

That night the plan came apart and went back together, top to bottom.

The three columns stayed, because Karis's slate had been right. But above them, where the first thing goes, he wrote a line that was not a column, and ruled it off from everything under it.

Hold. First. Before growth, before control, before the five. Nine days of it on every floor I stand on, and then three hours of it in front of the panel. Everything else stands on this, and if this goes, everything on top of it falls.

Then, under the line, the thing he had understood in the corridor, set down as plainly as he could manage.

The twentieth is two jobs at once. The one they watch has to look easy. The one under it has to last the whole three hours, and nobody in the room will ever see it, and nobody will thank me for it, because nobody will know it was there.

It's a bout. My opponent's a stranger, and the stranger's me. And the crowd won't know there's a fight on.

Chapter 44 — No Tells

[Dry, precise narration; sharpen the institutional pressure through exact detail]

On the tenth of Reaping, the morning after the file was closed, the woman who kept the wing's instruments came into the wing's outer office with her oil can and her brass rag at the third bell, as she did on the posted day of every month, and checked the instruments.

Cael was at the counter for a floor sheet and watched her do it. She took the long measuring rods down from their rack one at a time and sighted along each against the window. She opened the case of the pressure gauge and wiped the dial and wound it, and tapped the glass with one fingernail, and listened. She set the little brass weights from the wing's balance in a row on a cloth and touched each one with a clean rag. Then she took a printed card from her apron, the wing's schedule of checks, which had been pinned on the wall by Gault's door since the first week of term and had gone yellow at the corners. She initialled the day's line in pencil, and went away to her next room.

Nobody had told her to do it today, and nobody had told her not to. It was the posted day.

That was how the days went, from the closing of the file on the ninth to the eve of the twelfth. Cael watched them the way he watched a bout from the tier, without blinking at the wrong moment.

Nothing moved. That was all, and every bit of it was hard. A building full of frightened people, waiting for eleven strangers and a man with no stated business, did not want to stand still. It wanted to sweep its passages and re-ink its ledgers and move its awkward things out of sight. Cael saw the want everywhere. He saw a Stone instructor stop in the second quadrangle with a broom she had picked up from somewhere, and look at it, and look at the flagstones, and then lean the broom carefully back against the wall where she had found it and walk away with her hands in her pockets. He saw two clerks from the bursar's office arguing in low voices at the foot of the lecture stair about whether the lamp-oil ledger ought to be copied fair before the twelfth. Then one of them said posted day, and the other said posted day, and they went back up the stair together without copying anything.

The final stayed on the nineteenth, and the evaluation stayed on the twentieth. Rooke's cohort worked its ordinary hours at its ordinary marks in the east hall, and the supervision sheets went across the quadrangle to the registrar the same afternoon they were signed, as they had gone every afternoon since the night of the notice. The fire-watch boy stood on his bucket at the covered walk's north arch each morning and chalked the night's hours on his slate in his flat-footed figures. Withrow walked once round the first quadrangle at the fifth bell with her spectacles in her hair, as she had walked it every day of the season, and stopped at the same place under the clock to speak to the same porter about the same leaking gutter. In the registrar's outer office the four grey boxes sat on their shelf with their lettering turned to the room, and nobody touched them.

Withrow had told five hundred people not to perform. Then the whole of Halcenvane went three days without performing, the ninth and the tenth and the eleventh, and it was, Cael thought, standing at the covered walk's rail on the evening of the eleventh, the hardest feat of athletics he had watched all season. Lira on her table of oak had held still for a minute with a leg on fire. This was a whole hill holding still for three days with nothing on fire at all, and it was harder, because there was no sand running and no crowd to see it.

The eve went into the Log by the low lamp.

Three days of a whole hill not doing anything. It's harder than doing something. I know, because not doing anything is what I've done on my own account for two years, and I've never once seen anybody else try it. Withrow's bet is that a visit can only see what's been changed for it. So she's changed nothing, and made five hundred frightened people change nothing with her. I didn't expect the first person I ever watched play my own game to be a chancellor, and play it better.

Bumps: one, in hall three, the one Brom caught. Otherwise none for three days, and I've paid for every one. I know now what free feels like. Free is the thing to be frightened of.

They come tomorrow. Final in eight days. The twentieth, nine.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Havel rode up the bluff road in the second carriage, facing backward, with the counsel's knees an inch from his own and the counsel talking.

She had talked since Ostrand bridge and, if he was honest, most of the way from the coast, four days of it. Her voice was low and pleasant and never rose and never stopped, and it went on about the inns, and the state of the road, and a case she had argued nine years before in which a schedule had turned out to have two different pages numbered eleven. She did not need answers. She needed somebody to aim at, and Havel, facing backward with his case on his knees, was the nearest thing in the carriage with ears. He had learned by the second day to nod at the end of her sentences and think about something else in the middle of them.

Beside the counsel, Assessor Ilsev sat with her own case on her own knees and her eyes shut, though she was not asleep. Havel had sat beside her for four days now, and through the whole of the Greyvane hearing before that, and he had never once seen her asleep. She shut her eyes in carriages the way other people shut a book they had finished with, so that nobody would ask her what she thought of it.

The carriage leaned into the first bend of the bluff road, and Havel looked out of the window at the river falling away below.

He did it properly. He had been trained to arrive at a place properly, and he did it now out of a habit so old it no longer felt like a decision. First the road behind them: the bridge with its toll board, the town, the ferry landing on the near bank with its lamp post and two men in road-grey coats standing under it. He noted the two men, his own service's coats, briefly and without staring, and looked away again, because a records officer who stares at a rotation from a carriage window is a records officer who will be asked by somebody, later, why. Then the road ahead: the bends, the wall, the gate. Then the slope of the hill itself, the roofs above the wall, the long range of grey stone along the top of the bluff with its tiers of seating, open to the sky, standing up against the morning like the side of a ship.

The Crown yard. The academy's papers had a plan of it, and he had studied the plan on the road.

He knew who would be up there.

He had known it since the coast. He had sat at the end of the delegation's table at Greyvane through every sitting, with his recorder's case open and his brass glass turning, and written down every word the boy said. That had included all of the schedule the boy had read aloud in a level voice that stopped at the end of every entry for as long as a pen needed. Before that there had been a cold bright morning in the Unranked District at Ardenmere, a pump step, a form with four questions on it, and a fifth question that had not been on any form. And a pear, held out in a twist of paper, that he had wanted and had not taken. He still did not know why he had not taken it. He had thought about it more often since than a man ought to think about a pear.

A boy like that, on a morning like this, would want to see the delegation come in. He would want to see it from somewhere legitimate, where nobody could say he had no business to be. He would want a clean line down the last of the road and across the courtyard. He would want to be high, and empty, and early.

The upper tier of the Crown yard, then. The east end of it, most likely, where the morning sun would be behind him.

Havel looked at the plan of it in his head. Then he decided not to look up there.

It was a small decision, and he made it the way he made most of his decisions now, quickly and without enjoying it. A man who looks straight at the place where he knows someone is standing has told that person something: that he knew, and that he thought about it on the road, and that the knowing mattered to him. Havel did not want to tell the boy any of that. He was not sure it was true. He was not sure it was his to tell. And there was a correct way to arrive at an inspection, which was to look at the building, and the door, and the officer waiting at the door, and the ground. He would do it the correct way.

The carriage came up the last bend, and leveled, and went in under the gate.

He had risen twice since the pump step, and he thought about that sometimes in the evenings. The first rise had come not long after Ardenmere. He had been taken off the district rota and given a recorder's case and a seat at the end of hearing tables, where the work was to write down exactly what was said, and nothing else, and to be thought careful. He had been thought careful. The second had come after Greyvane, and it was the one that had put him in this carriage. Records officer to a delegation was a grade that sat at the main table and not the end of it. It was a grade that handled the delegation's papers before the senior seat saw them.

Neither rise had come with an explanation, because promotions in the service did not. A sheet arrived with a new grade on it and a date, and you moved your desk.

Some things on the boy's file stood above his clearance, and he did not think about those in carriages. He had a notebook with a cardboard cover in his inside pocket, and in it, among dates that meant nothing, there were three short entries in pencil that he had written over two years and did not read in front of anyone. He did not take it out now, since there was nothing to add to it this morning. There might never be. A careful man kept a notebook like that for the reason he kept a spare button sewn inside his coat: not because he expected to need it, but because when you needed it, there would be no time to sew.

The carriage stopped.

The counsel was still talking as she gathered her gloves. Havel opened the door for her and got down first and held it, and she came down the step after him, talking. On the cobbles of the outer courtyard she stopped, and looked up at once at the roofline of the long building in front of her, the one with the stone hood over its door.

"That gutter," she said to the clerk who had come across from the first carriage, "has been mended three times, and badly, and the third mend is newer than the second. Write it down."

The clerk wrote it down, and Havel did not look at the gutter.

He looked at the courtyard. He took it in the way he had been taught, the corners first and the centre last, because the corners are where people stand who do not want to be in the centre. The north-west corner, with a water butt and a boy sitting on an upturned crate with a bucket at his feet. The north-east, where the covered walk came out under an arch, and a knot of perhaps twenty students were standing about with the elaborate unconcern of people who had found a reason to be crossing a courtyard at this hour. The south corners, empty, swept, with the morning sun lying across the cobbles. Then the door of the long building, under its stone hood, and the man waiting at it: a man in a dark coat with ink on one cuff and a pen behind his ear, standing very straight, with a younger clerk at his elbow. The registrar, Havel thought; he had read the name in the papers. Then the ground, the cobbles between the carriages and the door, which were clean and dry and had not been swept that morning, because the dust along their edges was a day old.

He did not look at the long grey wall of the Crown yard rising above the courtyard's east side. He did not look at the tiers along the top of it, or at the east end of the upper tier where the sun was. He knew where it was. He kept it at the very edge of the side of his eye, where a thing is not looked at but is still known, and he kept his face toward the door.

It was harder than it sounded. Every instinct a records officer owns runs the other way, toward looking, toward the high place and the far corner and the window with a shape behind it. He had learned at a desk by a window, with a manual open in front of him, that a correct officer and a careful one are not always the same man. A correct officer looks at everything he can see. A careful one decides which of the things he can see he is going to be seen seeing. For most of his life Havel had been correct, and been praised for it. For some time now he had been trying, with no instructor and no manual, to be careful as well, and he was still not sure that he was any good at it.

His right hand ached in the web between the thumb and the first finger, as it always did at the end of a long road, from years of pens. He flexed it once against the handle of the case and kept walking.

Behind him the second carriage creaked as Ilsev got down. He heard her feet on the step and then nothing, because she had stopped on the cobbles and was standing still, as she always did when she arrived anywhere, while everything round her moved. She did not need help with her case. Nobody offered any. In four days Havel had never once seen anybody offer, and he suspected that the last person to try had been very young.

Then the third carriage.

Havel did not turn round for it, because he did not need to. He heard the clerks from the first carriage go across the cobbles toward it at a quick walk. He saw, without looking straight at him, the ranking man of the escort move four paces to his left, unbidden. He heard the counsel, beside him, stop talking in the middle of a sentence about the gutter, for the first time since the bridge.

He had ridden behind that carriage for four days and eaten in the same inns, at a different table. He had stood in the same yards while the horses were changed. And he could not, if anyone had asked him on oath, have said one thing about the man inside it beyond his rank and his name, because the man had given him nothing to say. That was not a complaint. Havel had simply noticed it.

He walked toward the registrar's door with his case held close against his side, at an ordinary pace, looking at the door.

The registrar met him on the step. He was not what Havel had pictured from his signature on the enrollment record: he had a pen behind his ear and ink along the edge of one cuff, and he did not bow.

"Records officer," he said. "You'll want the enrollment basis first, I expect."

"Whatever the senior seat asks for first, Registrar."

"Of course." The registrar inclined his head. "Whenever she asks, it's on a shelf in my outer office. Four boxes, with an index on top. I'll have a clerk carry them to your table."

In a good many years of arriving at institutions he had met a great many registrars, and nearly all of them had told him first, at the door, how difficult the records were to find. He had never before been told at the door where a file was and how many boxes it filled, by a man who seemed to think that was the ordinary thing to say. It was the manner, he thought, of somebody who had built a thing for strangers and was quite content to let strangers have it.

"Thank you," said Havel, and meant it, and wrote nothing down.

Inside, under the stone hood, the hall was cool and dim and smelled of old paper and lamp oil, and his footsteps went ahead of him along the flags. He let himself think, once, about the high tier above the courtyard behind him, and the east end of it with the sun on it, and who was standing there. He did not turn round. There would be days on this bluff for looking. This was not one of them.

Before the carriages were even in sight, Cael set the stake.

He did it at the rail of the Crown yard's upper tier, at the east end, with the morning sun warm on the back of his neck and the whole of the bluff road's last bends laid out below him like a ribbon dropped on a hill. He had written it at the head of the plan the night before, ruled off from everything under it: Hold. First. So before he looked at anything, before he let himself begin to read, he took one small hard corner of his attention and gave it to the half-yard of air round his own body, and told it to stay there, as a man sets a stake in a field before he lets the horses out. The rest of him could go where it liked. That corner was not for reading.

Lira stood at the rail beside him with the safety instructor's stick hooked over it and her weight on the good leg. She had climbed every step of the tier on that stick, against orders, and had informed Cael on the way up that a stair a friend asks you to climb is not a stair you can avoid. Karis had asked. It was written at the foot of an empty page in Cael's notebook, under a name that had nothing else on it: Lira.

"I'm not watching them," Lira had said, at the top. "I'm watching you. If you go thin, I'll stand on your foot."

"That isn't in the plan."

"It's in mine," said Lira.

Karis herself was down in the records hall with Bracken. She had said long ago that she would sooner read what a delegation wrote than look at what it wore, and nothing on the bluff could have shifted her.

Below them the outer courtyard was filling with people who all happened to be crossing it, and Cael did not count them. He had stopped himself at forty, on purpose, and put the number away.

The carriages came round the last bend at the fourth bell: three of them, and four riders.

The first was a plain travelling coach, and it carried chests. Four of them came down from its roof, iron-banded, two riders to a chest, and went across the cobbles toward the stone hood of the records hall. Cael saw Bracken's young clerk step out from the door to meet them with a ledger open on his forearm. The clerk signed for every chest, one by one, before a single person from the delegation had been greeted, and Cael liked that very much. Across the quadrangle, he thought, the grey boxes would be sitting on their shelf in the registrar's outer office with their lettering turned to the room, waiting for the chests to come and find them.

The second carriage. A woman came down from it already talking, and her voice carried up to the tier in pieces, mended three times, and badly, while a clerk at her elbow wrote. The delegation's counsel, then: the woman whose findings went for where a paper came from before they asked what it said. Cael thought of librarians' brass seals on three hundred and eleven sheets, and something in his chest that had been clenched for a week let go by about a finger's width.

Then the man who had held the carriage door for her.

Cael knew him before he had properly looked. It was the way the man held his case: flat against his left side, close, with his hand spread across the lid, holding it shut. A young assessor had held a case just like that, crossing a square at Ardenmere toward a pump step, on a bright cold morning that felt a great deal longer ago than it was. The young assessor had stopped being young, and his coat fitted him better than it had. There was a newer mark at his collar than the one he had worn at Greyvane.

He walked across the courtyard toward the registrar's door, and he did a thing that Cael noticed only because he was looking for something else.

He did not raise his eyes.

Not at the clock over the arch. Not at the roofs. Not at the long grey wall of the Crown yard or any of the tiers along its top. He looked at the corners of the courtyard, one and then the next, the water butt, the arch, the swept empty south side, and then at the door and at Bracken in it, and then at the cobbles, and he kept his chin level the whole way across. Nobody does that in a strange place. Everybody arriving anywhere new looks up at least once, at the roofline, at the height of the walls, at the sky. Havel walked the whole width of the outer courtyard like a man walking under a ladder he has made up his mind not to notice.

"That's the pear one," said Lira. She had not been looking at the courtyard; she had been looking at Cael's face, and she must have seen the man arrive there.

"That's him."

"He's gone up."

"Twice."

"Is he looking at you?"

"No," said Cael. "That's how I know he knows where I am."

Lira thought about that, and did not ask him to explain it. He was glad, because he was not sure he could have. He only knew that the upper tier was the one place on the bluff from which a person could see the whole courtyard without being in it. A careful man who had once refused a pear would have worked that out on the road. And a man who works out where you will be, and then keeps his eyes off it, has decided something. He did not know what, and he wrote nothing down about it. Some things you do not put in a notebook until you know what column they go in.

The second carriage gave up one more passenger.

She was small, and upright, and wore a dark coat, and she came down onto the cobbles and then stood quite still for the space of several breaths while everything in the courtyard went on moving round her. It was the stillness of a reader who has come to a heading and stops on it before going on. She had a plain brown case in her hand, with a strap. One of the clerks half reached for it as she passed him and then, very wisely, thought better of it, and she carried it to the door herself.

Assessor Ilsev. She had read his Kindling across a desk in a district office with a wall so thin he had heard the next clerk sneeze. She had read a Greyvane hearing's exhibits to the last page and followed them where they went with a warden glaring at her across the table. Six of her findings were in his head, and he had still not settled whether she was the worst danger on that manifest or the best hope on it. Seeing her walk did not decide it.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

The third carriage was the oldest of the three.

Its varnish had gone the colour of weak tea. Somebody had painted out the device on its door so carefully, and so long ago, that the shape of the old device still showed faintly through the paint. Cael looked at that door and knew, before it opened, that the carriage had been chosen. Nobody arrives at the head of an eleven-name manifest in the shabbiest coach by accident. And he knew, in the same moment, that he would never be able to show anybody how he knew it.

The door opened.

And the count went wrong.

It did not come back empty. He knew empty; empty was a number too. It came back arguing with itself. In two years of counting rooms, his method had given him too little and too much and once, at Ardenmere, nonsense. It had never before given him three answers at once that would not agree.

One. The courtyard leaned. The two clerks from the first carriage were crossing toward the third before its door was fully open. The ranking rider of the escort moved four paces to his left without anyone telling him to. The counsel, at the records hall's door, stopped in the middle of a word about the gutter and stayed stopped. The whole courtyard leaned toward the third carriage. Cael had seen people do that round Withrow every day of the season, and he could have drawn it.

Two. The man who stepped down gave the leaning nothing to lean on.

He came down the step without touching the rail and moved aside from the door so that the clerk behind him could get down. Then he stood on the cobbles with his hands at his sides, and the whole careful shape that had gathered itself round his carriage was left holding the air, the clerks and the rider standing in a ring round a man who was not using the ring. He did not wait to be attended. Nor did he make a show of not waiting, the way a certain kind of great man carries his own gloves so that everyone will see him carry them. He was simply there.

Three. His collar spoke, and the rest of him kept silent.

He wore the plain grey that inspectors wore on the road. At his collar was a mark Cael had seen nowhere, ever, on anybody. He had read of it once, in the appendix of marks at the back of a regulation book in Halcenvane's library: a narrow bar on a plain ground, no colour, no device, alone at the foot of the last page. Every other mark the Compact handed out was made to be read from across a room. That was the purpose of a mark. A warden's coat shouted before the warden did. Coss had shouted with his whole body, every day, in every room, and it was why Cael had been able to read him inside a week. This man's collar named a height in the service that had stopped a magistrates' counsel in the middle of a word. Nothing else about him reached for it.

He looked at the records hall's door. Cael counted two.

He lifted his eyes to the tiers. Cael counted two again, and somewhere in the middle of the second count the man's glance crossed the east end of the upper tier, and crossed Cael. It neither stopped nor hurried. It went over him at precisely the speed it went over the empty bench to his left, and the empty bench to his right, and Lira's stick on the rail. Then it moved on to the roofline, and the man walked in under the stone hood, and the door took him.

Cael's hands were flat on the cold stone of the rail.

He read the man anyway, with everything he had. An empty answer only counts if the question was really asked. He went through every layer of the gaze, the way he had with each watcher in turn since the very first. There had been Coss on a road and Coss in a hall, a young assessor at a pump step, the open coats on the Greyvane road who had let themselves be counted, a copying clerk at a gallery rail whose eyes went everywhere except to Cael.

Rhythm. The step down from the carriage and the steps across the cobbles came at the same pace. Not tired, then. Not hurried. Nothing more.

Weight. Low, settled, declaring nothing. A man of that height in the service had surely carried a Path for most of his life, and Cael could not find it anywhere in the way he stood.

Breath. Too far to see.

Attention.

That was the one that stopped him. All season he had measured where other people's attention went, in yards and halls and on stairs. In all that time he had never once thought to turn the measure round and ask where one man's own attention went. He asked it now. The answer was everywhere, at one speed. The door had two. The tiers had two. The roofline, as the man turned, had two. An empty bench had exactly what Cael had.

It was not carelessness. Carelessness has a slackness to it, and there was nothing slack anywhere in that man. It was a reader running his finger along a page at one even speed from the first line to the last, so that nobody watching the finger could ever tell which line he cared about.

He had been doing a rough cousin of it himself for two years, sampling crowds he could not count. But he sampled to save effort. This man did it so as to give nothing away.

The last clerk went in under the stone hood, and the door shut. The riders led the horses off toward the stables, and a boy ran out for the baggage. In about the time it takes to tie a boot, the outer courtyard was only a courtyard again, with the sun lying across its swept south side.

"What?" said Lira, at his shoulder.

He did not answer at once.

"Everyone they've ever sent has had something showing," he said at last. "Every one. A want, or a fear, or an order they didn't like being given, or a trick. Even Seln. What Seln hides has edges to it, and I can feel along the edges." He took his hands off the stone. "Something always shows."

"And that one?"

"That one crossed a courtyard," said Cael.

Lira unhooked the stick from the rail, leaned on it, and gave him a sideways look.

"You stayed," she said.

He looked at her.

"The whole time. You were reading him the way you read everybody, all of you at once. I could see it in your face. And you stayed where you were." She tapped the stone with the end of the stick. "I was ready to tread on you. I never had to."

He had not known. He had set the stake before the carriages came, and minded it, and then a man in grey had come down a step and Cael had forgotten there was any stake at all. And it had held, because he had driven it in first, at the head of everything, before he tied anything else to it.

"I didn't know," he said.

"I did," said Lira. "That's why I came up."

He wrote one line that night. He had five others ready, and he struck every one of them out in his head before the pen reached the page, because each of them was a guess, and guesses had a column of their own at the back of the Log, and this was not it.

New opponent. No tells. Begin.

Then he sat a while longer by the low lamp. Below the bluff the river went on, and at the fourth hour the two grey coats at the ferry landing changed under their lamp, on the bell, as they had changed every night since the bridge. The delegation was inside. Somewhere in the long building under the stone hood, a small woman who read everything to the end was reading. The final was in seven days, the evaluation in eight. And the one man on the bluff he could not read had looked at him for exactly as long as he had looked at an empty bench, and gone indoors.

On the thirteenth of Reaping, before he lit the lamp, Cael did nothing at all, and he did it on purpose.

He lay on his back in the dark with the blanket to his chin and set the stake, and only when it was settled did he let the rest of him wake up and start thinking about the day.

The ache came up behind his eyes as he sat, the dull one, the rent. It was cheap in the mornings. By evening it would have corners.

He lit the lamp low and opened the notebook at the delegation's pages.

There were eleven names on the manifest and he had pages on nine of them. The library had given him three of the four escort riders out of a dozen years of attendance lists, the counsel out of her published findings, and the three clerks out of a registry yearbook that nobody had borrowed in a decade. Havel had a page with a question of Lira's at the foot of it. Ilsev had the thickest page and the least use, because six findings told him what she would do with a document and nothing at all about what she did with a morning. The fourth rider was too new to be anywhere. And the eleventh name had one line on its page, and under the line, in his own hand, a single word: Lira.

He read the eleven through once and closed the book. Then he opened the plan instead, at the page with two words ruled off across its head, written on the eve of the twelfth in a hand that had not been quite steady: Hold. First.

None of it was the first task any more. That had changed in a corridor two days ago, with Brom standing square across the flagstones like a post. Reading the delegation was the second task. The first was to stay as thick as an ordinary boy for every hour of every day they were on the bluff, and the first task did not care how interesting the second one got.

Lira came down to breakfast without the stick.

She came down the residence stair one step at a time, with her hand on the rail and her face arranged to suggest that this was simply how she had always preferred to come down stairs, and that anybody who thought otherwise was welcome to say so. Her four days were over. The safety instructor had said four days with nothing on it, and four days had ended at midnight, and Lira had always kept to the letter of an order she disliked.

Brom half rose from the bench. She looked at him, and he sat down again and became very interested in his porridge.

"Well?" said Karis.

"It holds me up." Lira lowered herself onto the bench beside Cael with the leading leg out straight, and set her bowl in front of her, and did not look at anybody. "It isn't happy about it. It holds me up."

"Six days," said Brom, to his spoon.

"Six days," said Lira. "Nobody talks about hips."

In six days she would walk out onto the oak for the Copper final, Copper Rank Two on her certificate and Iron-equivalent by every honest ledger on the bluff, on a leg the safety instructor had not cleared, against the one fighter in the bracket who knew it best.

Karis had the grey notebook open beside her bread, at a page Cael knew. Down its left side ran a column of small ruled boxes, one for every night between the semifinals and the final, and every box above this morning's line had a neat cross in it. It was the second round of Rooke's nineteen exercises, the ones Brom did by lamplight in the corner of the common room. All season he had done them four a week, but on the night of his semifinal Rooke had put him on one a night until the final, and Karis had ruled a fresh page to match. The boxes ran out to the eighteenth, the night before the final, and she had told nobody but Cael why she stopped there.

"You didn't miss one," she said to Brom.

"I never miss one."

"I know. I'm writing it down so that you'll know I know." She inked a cross into last night's box and blotted it with the side of her hand. "They signed for the chests, by the way. Yesterday. Bracken's clerk made every one of them sign before he'd let a box through the door. The counsel signed with a face like a cat in a bath."

"Good," said Lira.

Brom thought about it, and nodded slowly, and went back to his bowl.

"I'll walk with her," said Karis. "I don't know anything about feet."

"That," said Lira, "is the nicest thing anyone's said to me in four days."

Cael ate and listened and minded his edges. Across the hall a table of Mire second-years were telling each other in low voices what the Archmarshal had eaten at supper, which none of them could possibly know. At the next table a Blade fourth-year was explaining to a first-year, at length and with diagrams drawn in spilt water, how an inspection worked, and Cael listened to that for a while because the fourth-year was wrong in a very confident and orderly way. Then he stopped listening, because the stopping was also practice.

"You've got your morning face on," said Lira, without turning her head.

Cael ate. In seven days it would be his own turn on the oak, with an Archmarshal at the rail, and if the five came out no bigger than his baseline, the one true sentence anybody had ever written about him would stop being true.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

Through the wall of the guest floor, the counsel was talking to her clerk while she dressed.

Vastin had heard her through walls for four nights of inns, and he no longer heard the words. He heard the shape. It went on low and level, about the water in the jug and the state of a collar and something a magistrate had once said to her on a stair. Then it stopped in the middle, and there was a silence about as long as a page, and then it went on again from the exact syllable where it had broken off. She had been handed something to read. He had noticed the habit on the second day of the road and had not written it down, because he did not take notes on colleagues. He only noticed that he had noticed, and let it go.

He sat at a scrubbed table under the window with his coat on, because the guest floor was cold before the fires were lit, and his watch lay face-up beside his hand.

It was a plain brass watch, older than the clerk who had brought up his water. Every Seventh-day for longer than he cared to count, wherever he happened to be, he had set it against the best clock in the building and written the difference on a card in its lid, and so he knew that it gained in the cold, and by how much. A thing that measured anything had to be checked, now and then, against some other thing that measured. Otherwise it was only a thing with a number on its face.

On the table in front of the watch lay the wing's filings.

They had come across the evening before, under the assessment wing's own seal, in answer to a requisition the counsel had written on the road in the ordinary form. The wing had answered it in the ordinary time. Pink tape. A covering index on top, in a hand that was not the hand of the filings under it. Six filings, with an appendix behind each, covering one term of embedded coverage on an enrollee who held his place under a provision.

He had put them at the bottom of everything, on purpose. Everything else was read now. So he cut the tape at the knot, where it could be tied again exactly as it had been, and began.

Nine minutes, by the watch. He went down every line and did not lift his pencil once. At the end he squared the sheets and laid the index back on top. Then he sat with his hands flat on either side of the stack and looked out of the window at a wet roof, on which a gull was standing on one leg and disapproving of the morning.

Complete in its form. Correct in every appendix. One term of a capable officer's work.

He had made a great deal of such work himself, in his time. For years he had been the man at the edge of the room with a board on his knee, writing down what could be seen from the chair he had been given. He had been good at it. He had been told so, honestly, and the work had been honest too. It was out of those years, long after, that he had made a sentence for himself. He had said it aloud perhaps half a dozen times since, always to somebody young, and had never written it anywhere.

Observer product is testimony about the observer.

He did not mean it unkindly. He meant it as a sum. Any filing carried three things inside it, and only one of them was the thing it said it was about. It carried what a person had noticed. It also carried the chair that person had been put in, and the list of what they had been told to look for, and nobody in the whole history of the service had ever found a way to wash those two out of the ink afterward. You could not ask a filing to see round its own chair. You could lean on it a little. You could not lay a floor across it and stand.

These six told him, plainly and well, where a good officer had been asked to sit for a term, and what he had been asked to watch for from there. That was a true thing to know. It was a thing about the chair.

He set it in its place, a long way under the record and a little way under the exhibits, and turned the watch face-down.

There was a knock, and the counsel put her head round the door with her collar still undone.

"Archmarshal. Will you sit with us today?"

"Not today."

"The provision's paper is up this morning. The registrar's boxes." Her eyes went to the tied stack by his hand and came away again without a question. "I'd value the company. I'm told their index is better than ours, and I'd like a witness when I admit it."

"The first three days are yours," said Vastin. "If I sit at your table, your clerks will write down what I look at instead of what you ask. I'll come on the fifteenth."

She considered that, and him, with her head a little on one side.

"That's a kindness," she said, "dressed up as a procedure."

"Most procedures are," said Vastin. "It's what they're for."

She laughed once, a short surprised sound, and went away down the passage talking. Through the wall he heard her take up her sentence to the clerk at the exact word where she had left it.

The record he had been through four times on the road, in the oldest of the three carriages.

He had taken that one because nobody else had asked for it. It rode hard, and its door had a device painted out so long ago that the paint had worn thin over it, and nobody wanted to be seen getting down from it. That suited him. A carriage nobody wanted was a carriage nobody came to talk in. For four days the road's grit had ticked against the half-closed shutter. The papers had ridden on the bench opposite him, and somewhere ahead the counsel's voice had gone on and on, faint, like a stream on the other side of a wall.

At the coast he had tied the papers into three bundles, each in a different tape, so that his hand would always come to them in the same order without his having to think. Grey tape round the record itself. Red round everything tendered in it. Plain string round what other officers had written about the boy over two years.

The order was the panel's. It was the order the panel had been given the matter in, and so it cost the most to read, and he had paid that price on every file for most of his life.

He read the grey bundle first and all of it, from the top: the magistrate's opening words, which the clerk had asked to have spoken twice because he had dropped his pen; the roll of the room; every dull procedural quarrel, including a long one about whether an academy's day-book was a paper of the academy or of the man who kept it. Then the red bundle, in the order the papers had been handed up, which was never the order anyone would have chosen afterward. Fourteen demonstration sittings from a single semester, sheet on sheet. A framework of movement that the record called Wind-adjacent, measured on a stone floor. A read along the skin, logged trial by trial. And at the very back, late and thin, one sheet about a spark. Last, the string bundle. He had untied that one once.

The red bundle he had read the most slowly of the three. One semester of a boy's sittings, fourteen of them, signed in turn by two officers of the academy, and the numbers in them agreed with one another. They agreed from sitting to sitting and from week to week, a good deal more closely than numbers usually agree when the person producing them is fifteen and growing out of his boots between one sitting and the next. He had made no mark about that, because agreement was not a question. It was simply a thing that was so. But he had read those sheets twice where he read most things once, and he had noticed himself doing it.

People liked to believe that order did not matter. It mattered more than almost anything. A digest was always laid out for its own ending, so that the reader arrived at the ending feeling he had walked there himself. And once a man knows where a road comes out, every bend of it looks like a turn toward that place. He had watched able men read that way all his working life. He had once done it himself. That was the reason for the tape.

His marks were in the margins of all four passes, one colour of pencil to each, and every mark was a question.

It was the only part of his method that had ever embarrassed him a little. In the registry's lower vault there was a long drawer of his old working copies, kept because a rule somewhere said they must be. On a wet afternoon once he had reckoned, idly, that the drawer held about two thousand of his margins. He did not believe a clerk could go through it from end to end and come away with six conclusions.

Three of the margins in this record carried the rest.

The first stood beside the respondent's opening. A boy of fifteen, with nobody beside him at the table, had begun by agreeing with the challenge. He had handed it, flatly and before anyone had pressed him, the one thing the whole room had come there to watch him fight over, and then he had calmly built his entire argument on the far side of the gift.

Why concede the category?

The second stood beside the stretch where the boy had counted the schedule's places out loud for the panel, five of them and then a sixth bound in at the back, and had treated the count as a wall. He had understood that a list which says these and no others shuts out its own author as firmly as anybody else. Men with long registry careers forgot that every year.

Who taught him the schedule's structure?

And the third stood at the foot of the record's first sheet, beside two dates the Compact's own clerk had entered there: the day the challenge was filed, and the day the first sitting was called. He had drawn two lines under it.

Verify: three weeks' preparation — from what baseline?

He never underlined to make a thing louder. Two lines meant a note to the man who would read this copy next, who was always himself. It said: everything else will rest its weight here, so watch yourself, because the cheap answer will look very good.

Three weeks was in the record, and no one had argued with it. Both dates were in the Compact's own hand.

So there were two ways to read it. Either the three weeks were wrong in the record, which happened, quietly and for years. Or something in the two years before them had made a boy who could do that much with three weeks. And nowhere in the file, in two years of district filings or in any page of the warden's long reports, did a single sentence say what. There was a great deal about what the boy had done. There was nothing about what had made him able to do it.

There was the gap. He had come on it in the first pass, somewhere on the coast road with a gull's cry outside the shutter. The next three passes had not closed it by a hair. It was the most interesting gap that had crossed his table in a long while. He meant that in the plainest way a craftsman can mean it, the way a joiner is interested in a joint that ought to have failed and has not.

He had no theory about it. He took some care not to grow one.

He had been taught that care at twenty-three, at a scarred table in a cellar office that smelled of lamp soot and wet wool coats. The man across the table had spoken to him perhaps twenty times in two years. Once, though, he had leaned his elbows on the scars and said a sentence that had outlasted everything else about him: his face, his voice, and very nearly his name.

An evaluation that begins from its conclusion is a report about the evaluator.

Vastin had heard it and copied it into the back of a book and gone on not understanding it for four years. He understood it in a bad month, sitting on the end of a narrow bed in a posting-house with his boots still on. A finding of his had come apart that afternoon at its first review, and he had sat there and traced it back. He had built it step by step from a suspicion he had liked holding, and every step had looked to him like evidence, because he had been walking toward the place where it came out the whole time and had never once turned round to look. The finding had not lived. His career had come within a sheet of paper of going down with it.

He had read files in the panel's order ever since, and grown no theories he could help.

His left hand had begun to complain on cold mornings, a stiffness across the knuckles that eased by the second bell. It was complaining now. For the last two winters it had wanted the pen held a little further back, and he had let it have its way and said nothing. A man who argues with his own hand writes worse, and he still had a great deal to write.

Below the window, across the wet quadrangle, a boy was standing on an upturned bucket under an arch. He was writing on a slate that hung on the wall there, a figure at a time, with his tongue in the corner of his mouth. Then he got down and looked at what he had written from the cobbles, and got up again, and changed one figure. Vastin watched him do it twice. He had no idea what the slate was for. Whatever it was, the boy had decided it ought to be right, though there was nobody anywhere in the quadrangle to check it.

He tied the wing's filings in their pink tape again, knot over knot, as they had come, and set them by the door for the clerk.

The notice that had sent him here was a true notice. It named an academy that had done an unusual thing lawfully, and an inspection of the ordinary kind, and nothing else. He had filed no question. He knew perfectly well that not one person on this hill would believe it. Years ago he had given up trying to close the space between his work and the work people imagined for him. It was a useful space. It showed you what each of them feared he had come for. But what it showed was theirs, not his, and he left it to them.

He would walk the building. He would watch its rooms being used. Rooms told you what a house had decided to be, if you let them talk long enough.

This house had answered the notice by changing nothing, and it had not troubled to hide that it was doing so. He had seen it in the courtyard yesterday. There was a gutter mended badly three times and left that way. The cobbles had not been swept for visitors. And the registrar had told the first man through his door where the file stood and how many boxes it filled, instead of how hard it would be to find. A house that changed nothing for an inspector was either very sure of itself or very well advised. Either was worth knowing. Neither was a finding.

A bell began somewhere below, the first of the day. He laid the grey bundle on top of the others, the right way up, and went down.

An inspection, it turned out, was mostly doors.

He had read the schedule a dozen times, and nothing in it had warned him how small the whole business would look from the floor. The hill did not stop for eleven people. It made room for them, and everyone stepped round them, and by noon nobody quite saw them any more.

But three doors that had stood open all season were shut now, from the second bell until the fourth. One was the records hall's back room, where Bracken had built the file. One was the long upper room over the lecture range, where the faculty argued on Fifth-days. The third was the wing's document store behind Gault's office. Cael had never before seen it closed. He had always known it by the instrument woman's oil can, standing on its sill.

And the covered walk filled with boxes.

They were black, with brass hasps, and they went across in the morning and came back at the fourth bell. A young clerk carried them at a fast walk in front of his chest, breathing through his mouth. A second clerk walked beside him with a list. The third came along behind, at his own pace, and never carried anything.

He was the eldest of the three, a grey man with a careful face, and his left knee was bad. Cael saw it on the walk's two shallow steps, which the man took sideways, one at a time, the way somebody does who has worked out to the farthing what a step will charge him. He wrote with his left hand as well, on a board pressed flat against his coat. He was the one who said which box went. The young man only carried what he was told.

So whatever crossed the walk at the second bell was what the sittings would read by the third. Whatever came back at the fourth was finished with.

Cael did not have to do anything to learn it. He only had to stand at the walk's rail on his way to the morning lecture, as he had stood there every morning of the term, and see what was in the young clerk's arms as the young clerk went hurrying past. At the second bell it was two boxes that wore the registrar's index labels. At the fourth those two came back, and one went over the other way, labelled in the wing's hand.

They're on the provision's paper today, he wrote at noon, on the clerks' page. The wing is tomorrow. The old man's knee tells you half a day early. Nobody has to say a word.

The counsel he had in four minutes, on the same walk, before the first box had come back.

He took that to carrel eleven at noon, where Karis was eating an apple over a sheet of the archive's lending rules. She was being very good about it, in a way that made her bite apples hard.

"Her talking and her reading keep to different rooms in her head," he said. "She can argue with you and read your file at the same time, and she won't lose her place in either."

He told her the labels. She shut her eyes and said the index numbers back to him in order, and what each box held, and what in each of them a good counsel would go for first. She was right about all of it. He could see her being right.
