"The standardization directive didn't touch practitioner classification here and there," said the delegation's counsel. "It took the whole of it. It moved in, end to end, on purpose, and built a new house on the ground where the old one stood. When a later law takes over a whole field like that, an old clause left standing in the middle of the field isn't alive just because nobody remembered to pull it up. It's a stump. It has the shape of a law and none of the life. And an enrollment on a stump is an enrollment on nothing."

It was a very good argument. It was better than very good. Cael had spent two years reading registry law because he had to, and he felt this one come down on the table with real weight. He felt it reach the academy's side. Bracken's pen stopped. Withrow's counsel drew a long breath and put her hand on her leather case. Karis had stopped writing altogether, and two chairs along from Cael, the inky-knuckled clerk sat up very straight.

Withrow laid one hand flat on the table, and her counsel took her hand off the case.

"Let me take that one, counsel, if you'll allow it," said Withrow. "I've argued it myself. For twenty years at the registry I argued it whenever a case let me, because it's a fine argument, and it usually wins. So I know the exact place where it stops working, and I'd like to put my finger on it for the record."

She did not raise her voice. The hall was quiet enough without that.

"It works when the later law is silent about what it's sweeping away. Then a reader has to guess what the drafters meant to clear, and he may fairly guess they meant to clear everything. It does not work when the drafters wrote down what they meant to clear. If they've given you a list, the list is their answer, and you don't get to add to it after they've put their pens down." Bracken was already lifting the lid of the third box, and he found the green tab without looking. "The directive has such a list. Article forty-one. Eleven clauses, every one named, every one pinned to its book and its place. The men who wrote it had the founding schedule open in front of them and went down it clause by clause, choosing. You won't find ours among the eleven."

"An omission—" said the delegation's counsel.

"Is a possibility," said Withrow. "Which is why the file answers it. Document sixty-two, please."

The young clerk on the chair beside Cael had it out of the box and on the table in front of the chancellor almost before she had finished the number. Across the table the Archmarshal's pen lifted, and marked, and was laid down.

Three, thought Cael. A clerk who can find a sheet in a breath.

"This is the directive's own transitional article," said Withrow. "It tells every academy how to convert existing assay enrollments into the new terms. I'd like it read aloud into the record, the whole of it. It's short, and when you've heard it, you'll have heard the answer."

Havel read it, in his flat recording voice, every word weighed the same.

Cael knew it before the second sentence. He had seen it once before, at Greyvane, on the last page of Bracken's fifteenth letter, copied out with no comment and a line drawn under two of its sentences, in Prynn's archive. Karis had read straight past it, because she was hunting a repeal and not a conversion, and had been cross with herself about it for a day. Now it came out of Havel's mouth into the Compact's own record, and somewhere in Cael's head a thing he had been carrying loose for a year dropped into its slot with a small cold click.

Nobody sits down to explain how to change a thing that has already died. The drafters had known there were assay enrollments; they had known there were practitioners standing on that clause in the very year they sat down to write, because they had sat down and written out what was to be done with them. They had not killed the practice. They had cut a door in it and hung a sign telling everybody to go out that way, and then they had gone home and let the clause be.

"They discouraged it," said Withrow. "They gave it new words. They built a way out of it. And they left it standing. Every one of those was a decision, made by people holding pens. The decision you need, counsel, is the one they didn't make. They had their list in front of them, and they stopped at eleven." She took her hand off the table. "Nobody drafts a conversion route for a dead letter."

At the end of the academy's side, Karis's pen had begun to move again. From behind her shoulder Cael could see her page. Her handwriting was the most level thing he knew. At the transitional article it had gone off at a slant, as if the page had tilted under it, and it had not come back.

The counsel came at it again three times over the next twenty minutes, from three new sides, and each time she found the door shut.

Cael watched every attempt with the gaze opened as far as he dared to open it. After three days of the Archmarshal giving him nothing, she gave him everything, and it was like drinking water. Under pressure her rhythm did not break; it tightened, like a rope taking a load. And before every new attack, every time, without fail, her weight came forward onto her forearms on the table a half-beat before she spoke. She did it before the attempt through the directive's preamble, and before the one through custom, and again before the one through the plain meaning of the word existing, which Withrow's counsel answered in two sentences from her notes. By the third he could have leaned forward and whispered to the back of Bracken's head what was coming next, a breath before she knew it herself.

He kept still. Nobody had asked him, and the chair he had been given was against a wall for a reason.

The last attack broke. The counsel sat back and said, "Nothing further on repeal, Chancellor," in the tone she had used to praise the index, and Withrow inclined her head. Then came a long flat stretch of procedure about the comparing clerk's attestation. Did a clerk's signature stand without a second signature beside it? Did the registrar's seal cover the clerk, or only the registrar? Bracken had a sheet in a box for every one of these questions. It was slow, and it was necessary, and there was nothing in it anybody could watch.

And it was in the slack of that stretch, between one sheet and the next, that the hold went thin.

He did not feel it go. That was the whole trouble with it, and he knew it, and it still caught him. One moment he was listening to a clerk explain a seal. The next, with no seam between them, the clerk was saying something else, and there was a short piece of the sitting he could not account for, as if somebody had turned a page in his head while he was not looking. He took the corner back at once. Nobody had looked his way. The inky-knuckled clerk, two chairs along, was writing.

A little later, during a question about the date on the comparing clerk's sheet, it happened again. It was shorter this time, two breaths, perhaps three, and again he only caught it from the far side, after it was over.

A floor had never done this to him. On a floor his attention was either all in the drill, or held back from it by main force, and he had learned in a corridor how to hold it back. A sitting was different. A sitting took his attention in long slow pulls and then let it go, and in the slack between the pulls there was nothing to brace against, and that was where he went, in the gaps.

He sat very straight on the hard chair and set the stake again. He wrote nothing, because there was nowhere he could write that would not be seen.

At the end of the attestation the delegation's counsel looked up at the clock over the door.

"Chancellor, with your leave," she said. "A recess."

Chapter 49 — Live on an Active File

[Taut, spatially clear narration; keep danger readable and thought moving under pressure]

Recesses were where findings went wrong, in Ilsev's experience, so she did not take them.

People talked in recesses. They stood at windows with cups and told each other what the morning had meant, and by the time the sitting began again, half of them had agreed on a meaning that nobody had read anywhere. She had seen it happen in a hundred halls, and so when the counsel rose and went out talking, with two of the clerks trailing after her, and the academy's people drifted to the far windows to stretch, Ilsev stayed in her chair and opened the file she had asked for.

She had asked for it at the first bell, because the afternoon would come round to what the clause required term by term, and that touched the monitoring of the enrollee. Havel brought it at the recess and laid it at her elbow, square to the edge, and went back to the foot. She liked that about him. He never told you he had done what you asked.

The routing file was a long narrow ledger bound in grey, every request and transfer that had ever touched the subject's file entered one to a line, in a dozen hands over two years. She went down it from the top. A district office and a first filing. A records request in an autumn, with the designation in its priority field, two grades above anything its signatory could have entered. Greyvane: her own query, the return, her referral. A transfer to this house. And at the very end, the requisition for the wing's filings, and their return to the wing the evening before.

Behind the ledger, in a pocket of the back board, was the file's correspondence. Most of it was ordinary paper. At the very back, under a brass clip, lay a single folded sheet with the registry's stamp on it. Pinned to it was a narrow docket in Havel's hand: Correspondence in. Delegation's courier, up. Eighth bell. It had come up the bluff the evening before.

He had had it since the eighth bell last night, then, and had let her come to it in its place. She approved of that, and did not ask herself why it pleased her quite so much.

She knew what it was. She unfolded it anyway, because knowing what a thing is had never once been the same, in her life, as having read it.

Return, from the chain of review, to the senior evaluation seat, on referral of the matter at Greyvane. Designation: Suppression-Advisory Watch, Priority Level 4.

Determination: no originating authority of record. Designation predates file creation. No action available at this clearance.

She turned the sheet face down on the table and squared it to the edge with two fingers. Then she turned it face up again, which was a thing she had never in her life done to a document before, and did not do again.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

She had met the first two sentences before.

At Greyvane, on the last day of a week, after the fifth bell, they had come to her on a sheet laid square on the corner of a long table, in answer to the plainest question her form allowed: who had entered this mark, and on whose authority? She had read the answer twice. Then she had written a referral, pinned the return to it, marked it an irregularity of administration, and sent it up on the first courier of the next week, to the office above the office that had answered.

Twice in her career a mark she could not place had turned out to be some district's old shorthand, and both times a polite letter had come back from above, explaining it in six lines. So she had pictured that office, a little, while she wrote. A room with better lamps. Older men, with longer memories, who would write back a paragraph. She would read it and think of course, and forget the whole thing by the end of the week.

That had been eleven months ago.

And here were the better lamps. They had read her referral and the return pinned to it, and they had sent back the same two sentences, word for word. Then they had added a third, the way a man adds a latch to a door he has already shut.

She took the three sentences one at a time, as she would have taken three witnesses.

The first witness said that nobody had done it. A mark in the registry was not rain; it did not fall on a file out of the sky. Somebody entered it, and the whole reason the registry existed was so that an entry could be traced to a hand. Every finding she had ever put her name to stood on that.

The second witness said the mark was older than the file it was written in, and that was the one she could not get round.

Ink goes onto a sheet. The sheet does not grow up round the ink, so either the file had been made over at some time, and the mark carried across from an older file, in which case the older file was the true record, and her question had been sent to the wrong door twice. Or else the second witness meant precisely what it said. There had been a value in that field before there was any field to hold it.

She took her working sheet from her case and wrote on it, small:

Misrouted, or no answer at all. Both go up. Neither is mine to settle.

There was a next thought. She could feel its edge, just past the end of the line. She did not take it. She knew she was not taking it, and she was quite comfortable with that.

She had known a man once, early in her service, who had been right about a thing a full year before he could prove it, and had said so in writing, and had spent the rest of his career being right about it in a much smaller office. She had learned more from him than from anyone, and had never once been tempted to be him. A mark in a registry with no author anyone could name was a thing. Things like that were slips, or they were somebody's practice. She had not one line of paper that told her which, and a guess was not a finding just because the guesser was senior.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The third witness said: and you may not ask.

No action available at this clearance.

She had left that one till the end on purpose. Whatever she did next would turn on it, and she wanted the other two already weighed before she came to it.

It was a well-made sentence. She could admire it as work, even while it was being done to her. It was courteous and final, and it cost nothing to accept, and it had plainly been made to be accepted. Most people who received it would nod and lay it in the file, and by every rule she knew they would be right to.

She read it a second time for its grammar, which was a habit nobody had ever been able to cure her of. It did not say that no action existed. It said that none was available, and then it said to whom: to whoever held the clearance it had been sent to. Somewhere, then, the sentence admitted, there was a clearance at which some action was available. It simply was not hers. She did not let herself go on to wonder whose it was. She only noted, in the margin of her working sheet, available: at this clearance, and underlined the last three words once, because they were what the sentence actually said.

It left her the same choice it left everybody. She could take it as her answer, note it in the file, and go on with the afternoon. Or she could send it up again.

She reached into her case for a referral form.

The hall had nearly emptied round her. Somewhere behind her a clerk was moving chairs that did not need moving. One of the registrar's young men came along the table with a tray, and set a cup of tea at her elbow, and went away. She did not look at it.

She filled the form in its own order, line by line, because the order was there to protect whoever would read it. First the date and reference of her referral from Greyvane. Then the date and reference of the sheet in front of her. Then the return's working words, written out in full, every one, with nothing put into her own words. A question that has been put into somebody's own words can be answered by answering their words instead of the question, and she had watched whole matters die of that. Then, in the box at the foot headed grounds for escalation, one sentence. She wrote it without a pause, because she had known it since she reached the third line of the return.

A determination that no originating authority exists is not a determination as to the designation's validity, and the designation remains live on an active file.

She read it once. It said what needed saying, and it did not reach one word past the paper on the table.

She marked the form for the next level up from the office that had sent the return, and she signed it, and dated it, and checked the date against the return and against her own Greyvane reference, since a referral with a wrong date could be sent back for nothing but its date. Then she rose, carried it down to the foot of the table and laid it in the shallow wooden tray, where the records officer would find it, and came back to her chair.

It had taken eleven minutes by the clock over the door, which she had glanced at from long habit when she took out the form.

The tea at her elbow was cold. She drank all of it, in four swallows, and set the cup back in its saucer without a sound.

Then she put the matter down, on purpose. A form was a place to leave a weight. That was what forms were for, whatever the people who printed them believed, and a woman who could not leave a filed thing where she had filed it would sooner or later file badly, just to be rid of it.

Across the hall, against the far wall, the enrollee sat on his hard chair among the registrar's clerks, with a floor sheet on his knee and his eyes on nothing in particular. The designation she had just sent up for the third time sat on that boy's file, and had sat there since before the file was made. She did not look at him for longer than it took to see where he was. He was not her question, any more than he had been in hall three. The paper was her question.

Cael had spent the recess on that hard chair, because a clerk would have, and because getting up to walk about was the kind of small change he had promised himself at dawn not to make. Of the whole delegation only two had kept their places: the Archmarshal, with his folder shut and his pen across it, and Ilsev, who had read something from a file and then written on a form for about eleven minutes, by Cael's count of his own breaths, and laid it in the records officer's tray, and drunk a cup of tea in four swallows. He read the new one as he entered it. He read everything he entered. A records officer who logs a sheet without reading it is a tray with legs, and if the service was going to use him as a tray, he would at least be a tray that knew what it was carrying.

At Greyvane, when the first return came, he had watched her read the designation a third time after she had already referred it, which was nearly the only sign he had ever seen her give that a thing had reached her.

Today she had not read it a third time. She had read it once, and filed again inside the recess, and drunk her tea cold. And Havel, at the foot of the table with his head bent over the ledger, found that it moved him more than the third reading had. The third reading had been a person puzzled. Nobody was in the room. Then he broke his own rule. The rule was that the notebook held only what had happened, and nothing of what he made of it. Once, he thought, sitting there with the case on his knees. Once would not ruin it.

Two years. Two of us now. Nothing has ever come back with a name on it.

He looked at the line. It was not like the lines above it. A stranger who found the notebook would know from it, and from nothing else in it, that it had been written by a man.

He closed it and put it back in his inside pocket. At the second recess, again, Cael did not leave his chair. He sat as a clerk sits through a long day, stiff and bored and minding his paper, kept the corner that held his edges where he had set it, and watched the hall empty round him.

4. Havel logging the tray.

5. Gault: write it down.

Nothing for any argument. Nothing for the finding.

He looked at the five for a while, and then at the empty line under them, and made himself write what they added up to.

Nine hours deciding whether I'm here lawfully, and he marked five things, and every one of them was the house's paperwork. Whether its copies are checked honestly. Whether its index works. Whether its clerks can find things. Whether its records officer logs what he's handed. Whether its wing writes down what it does. It's the posts all over again. It's the table in the yard. A different door into the same room every day since he came.

He doesn't care yet whether the clause is good. He wants to know whether this house can be trusted to measure.

He is calibrating the instrument. I am the reading.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

It was while he was looking at that last line that he went.

The sitting had come to its last flat stretch. A clerk at each end of the table was reading the day's exhibit list into the record, turn and turn about, numbers and titles, a hundred and some of them, in voices with nothing in them, while everybody else waited for it to be over. Two of Bracken's clerks had been sent off with boxes at the second recess and had not come back, so the chairs on either side of Cael stood empty. He was looking down at his own pencil on the back of the floor sheet.

Then, with no seam at all, he was looking at the same pencil, and the clerk at the far end was reading out a number nowhere near the one he had last heard. A good many numbers had gone by while he was elsewhere. He could not have said how many. He had felt nothing at all.

And on the empty chair at his side lay a folder.

It had not been there before. The inky-knuckled clerk, two chairs along, had put it down while Cael was gone. He had not put it on the empty chair beside his own, which was nearer his hand. He had reached past that chair and across Cael's knees, across the whole of a boy, to lay his folder on the seat beyond, the way a man reaches across an empty bench.

Nobody was looking. Nobody had seen anything. The clerk was turning a page. Cael sat with his heart going hard, and a pressure rising behind his eyes like water rising in a lock, and one plain thought came to him a word at a time. He put it down where nobody was.

Then something touched his ankle.

It was Karis's foot. She had not turned round. Her pen had not stopped. She had simply slid her foot back under her own chair as far as it would go, until the side of her shoe found the knob of his ankle bone, and rested there. It was perhaps three-quarters of an inch of contact. It lasted about the length of a breath.

He was back inside his own edges before the breath was over. No method he had ever put in the ledger had ever done it half as fast.

He sat very still and let the pressure behind his eyes come up and up until it reached its own top and stopped there, and he did not look down at Karis, and Karis did not look round at him. Her foot stayed where it was for one breath more. Then it was gone, back under her own chair, and the pen kept moving.

He set the stake again and held it, hard, through the rest of the list. Some while later the inky-knuckled clerk took back his folder without the least surprise, and went on writing. The sitting closed at the seventh bell. People stood and stretched and talked. Within a minute the delegation's counsel had found Withrow's counsel and begun, very happily, to argue with her about the age of a binding.

Cael sat on in his chair, with the floor sheet on his knee, and wrote two more lines at the foot of the margin in the worst hand he had written all term.

Nine hours. Two thin, and one bad. The bad one in a gap, with my eyes on my own paper. Brom found it for me on a floor, and I've been guarding against it in the wrong kind of room. On the twentieth there are three hours, and between every trial the panel stops to confer. That's where I'll go thin.

No answer for it yet. Karis's foot isn't an answer. It's a friend. That's worth more than an answer, and it works less often.

When he looked up, Karis had turned round at last and was looking at him over the back of her chair. She did not say anything. She did not need to.

Lira and Brom were on the records hall's steps when he came out, sitting side by side on the cold stone. Lira had her bad leg straight out along the step and her hands round her knee. Brom had his elbows on his thighs and was watching the door the way he watched a fighter's back foot.

"Well?" said Lira.

"Sound law," said Cael. "Ilsev stood up and said it into the record. Whatever else the delegation reports, the basis is sound law."

Lira let out a breath that she seemed to have been holding since noon. Brom did not move at all. Then he put out one big hand and set it flat on the stone beside him.

"Karis?" he said.

"Inside. She stopped writing. I've never seen her stop writing."

"Good," said Brom. "She's earned stopping."

Lira was looking at Cael's face, not at the door.

"And you?" she said. "Nine hours in a chair. How many times?"

He told her. Two thin, one bad. The folder.

Lira did not say anything. Then she reached out and caught the toe of his boot with her own good foot and held it there.

"I'd have stood on you," she said. "If I'd been in there."

"Karis did it with her foot. Under the chair."

"Did she." Lira looked pleased, and then, very briefly, a little jealous, and then pleased again. "Then she's learning."

"And the Archmarshal?" said Brom.

Cael sat down on the step below them, because his legs had decided for him, and told them about the pen: five marks in nine hours, every one for the house's paperwork, and nothing for the argument or the finding.

Lira was quiet, with her hands round her knee.

"The beam," she said.

"The beam."

"He's still proving it." She looked out across the dark quadrangle toward the guest floor's windows. "All this time, and he hasn't put a single ingot on it yet."

"Five days," said Brom, "and then he will." He said it without any weight at all, the way he said the time of supper, and Cael was grateful to him for that more than he could have said.

"Then we've got five days," said Lira, "to make sure the thing he weighs is worth the trouble." She hooked her good foot under Cael's boot again and gave it a small shove. "Which starts with you eating."

The records hall's door opened behind them. Bracken stood in it with his sleeves pushed up and a pen behind each ear, which Cael had never seen before.

"Enrollee," said Bracken. "If your hands are free. Half the old founding volumes are out of their boxes and lying about my back room like a lending library, and I won't sleep until they're home. Miss Karis is already at it." He looked at the two on the step. "Not you. Your leg, and your knuckles. Go and eat."

Lira opened her mouth to argue, and Brom stood up and took her elbow, very gently, and she closed it again.

Cael went in.

Chapter 50 — A Working Method

[Taut, spatially clear narration; keep danger readable and thought moving under pressure]

Bracken was in the back room when Cael got there, which he had not expected, with his coat off and his waistcoat unbuttoned and a founding-era volume open across his forearm like a waiter's napkin.

Karis was at the long press against the far wall. She had her sleeves pushed above her elbows and ink to the second joint of every finger, and she was sliding volumes into their places one at a time, reading each pencilled shelf-mark on the inside board before she let go of it. She did not look round when the door opened, and she did not have a pen in her hand, and Cael realised that he could not remember the last time he had seen her without one in the whole of the term.

"Enrollee," said Bracken. "Good. Take the low shelves. I can't bend the way I could, and Miss Karis won't let me near the high ones in case I put something back in the wrong century."

So Cael took the low shelves, and for a while the three of them worked without talking, in the smell of old paper and lamp oil and the beeswax Bracken rubbed into his box corners. It was the kind of quiet Cael had grown used to in carrels and archives over the past year, where nobody needed to say anything because everybody was doing what the others would have done.

Bracken broke it, which surprised him.

"I'll tell you a thing I didn't know until today," said the registrar. He was holding a volume up to the lamp to read its board. "Twelve years I've had this office, and I've always believed the best day a file can have is the day you close it. You tie the last box. You write the count on the lid. It's done, and it's right, and you go home." He slid the volume into its place and squared it with one finger. "It isn't. The best day a file can have is the day somebody who wishes it ill opens every box, with a good mind and a whole morning, and can't find anything wrong."

"She said your index was good," said Cael.

"She did." Bracken did not smile, quite. "I've had my work praised by people who liked me. It's pleasant. I'd never before had it praised by somebody who'd come all the way up the river hoping to dislike it." He reached for the next volume. "It's a different thing altogether. I find I'm too old to know what to do with it."

He worked a while longer, and then he took the last empty box under his arm, looked once along the press with the air of a man counting soldiers, and went to the door.

"Lock up behind you, Miss Karis. The key's on the nail. Not later than the eighth bell, please, or the porter will think we've been robbed and wake the whole range."

They heard his steps go away down the records hall, slow and even, and the outer door close.

Karis slid a volume home and did not let go of it at once.

"Did you see my writing?" she said, without turning round.

"From the wall. At the transitional article."

"I thought you might have." She took her hand off the spine. "I could feel it go. Like a table tipping. I tried to straighten it and it wouldn't straighten, so I left it." She turned round at last. "It isn't a finding. I want you to know that before I say anything. Nothing I'm about to say would stand up in that hall."

"All right," said Cael.

On the long table lay the one book that was not a founding volume. It was the directive, all forty-one pages of it, the copy Bracken's clerk had made and a librarian had sealed, and down its fore-edge stood a row of small green paper tabs.

Karis opened it without sitting down.

"You know the green ones," she said. "Bracken put them in. One for each place in the whole directive where it takes an old word out of the law and puts a new word in." She ran her finger down the four of them, just above the paper. "And this one," she turned to a page with a white slip pinned to it and a thread of red through the slip, "is the transitional article. Havel read it out this morning. It's what won."

She laid one forefinger on the last green tab and the other on the white slip, and held them there, as people hold two fingers on a map to measure a road.

"Count the articles between," she said.

He leaned over and counted, and it did not take long.

"Four."

"Four." Every word came out level and even, as though somebody else had written them and she was only the one reading them out. "One directive. One drafting. As near as anybody could ever say, one table of men with the same ink. On this side of my finger is the article that tells every academy how to take enrollment by demonstration and change it into something else. It doesn't end the practice; it walks everybody out of it. And on that side of my finger is the last of the articles that take old words away."

Cael said nothing, because he had seen where she was going as soon as she touched the tabs, and he wanted to hear her go there in her own way and at her own pace, without any help from him.

"You've got it in your old notebook," said Karis. "In a box you drew round it when you were younger and didn't know what it meant. I've got it twice in mine. We read all three copies aloud to each other at Greyvane, in Prynn's archive, at the reading shelf, a few days before the whole of that archive went under the Compact's seal. Do you remember the later hand? The black ink that didn't cross its sevens?"

"Per standardization directive," said Cael. "It didn't say which."

"It didn't say which, because nobody writing it ever thought there would be a question of which. There's only one." She tapped the green tab, very lightly, with the nail of her finger. "It's this one. So the article that told that clerk to change the word is one of these four. It's here, in this book, on this table, four articles from the article we won on this morning."

She lifted her fingers off the page and gripped the table's edge with both hands.

"Shattered was written in at that table, by somebody holding a pen, over an older word. And the older word meant unbound. Four articles along, somebody took the old system's only way of judging a person by what that person could actually show, instead of by which box they would go into, and turned it into a road out of itself, and put a sign up telling everybody to use the road." Her hands had tightened on the wood. "And the old way works. That's what I keep coming back to. It isn't a museum piece. It's working tonight, in this house, on the record, with seals on it. I sat at that table from the second bell to the seventh and watched it bear weight."

Shattered was the word in brackets on Cael's own registry sheet, beside his number, in the Denvash station's hand. He waited until he was sure she had finished.

"And you're not saying they're connected."

"I'm not saying anything about them at all." It came out quick and firm, like a hand coming down on a lid, and there was nothing frightened in it. "I haven't got a single sheet that joins them. I've no drafter's name for either article. There's no minute and no memorandum. There isn't one letter from a man at that table to another man at it. I've got two articles in one book with four articles between them, and that's all I've got." She looked down at the green tabs. "I know what that looks like. It looks like a pattern. And a pattern with no paper under it was the warden's whole method. I watched him build a case for two years out of things that looked alike, and I watched you beat him by reading what was actually written. I won't do it his way the same week we won by doing it ours. Two articles in one directive, four apart, is nothing to stand on. It's a coincidence with good posture."

"Then what have you got?" said Cael.

Karis did not answer at once. She reached into the satchel that hung on the back of a chair, and took out the grey notebook, and opened it, and turned it round on the table to face him.

It was a fresh page, and at the top of it, in her small upright hand, which had come back level, there was one line. Under the line the whole page was empty, to the foot.

Why retire a working method?

"I wrote it this afternoon," she said, "while the clerks were reading the list. It goes on a page by itself, with nothing under it. That way, whenever I open the book, I'll see it's still waiting, and I won't be tempted to fill the page with things I'd like to be true."

He read the line three times over and said nothing.

"That's all of it," said Karis. "I'm not asking who did it. I'm not asking about the word. I'm not asking any of the things I'd give a year of my life to know. I'm asking one thing. There was a way of looking at somebody the boxes couldn't hold. It worked, and it made records, and we've spent today reading them. Somebody turned it into a door and walked everybody out through the door, and nobody, anywhere in forty-one pages, wrote down a reason." She closed the notebook. "I don't know the answer. I don't know where I'd begin to look. The archive that held the other half of it is under the Compact's seal at Greyvane, and nobody alive can tell me whose hand held the black ink. I've got one line on one page."

"Do you think it's something?" he said. "Or nothing?"

Karis put the notebook back in the satchel and buckled it before she answered.

"I think I proved something today," she said. "A real thing, with seals on it, that will go on being true whether I'm here or not. I'm going to go to bed holding that. A thing I can prove is worth more to me tonight than a thing I'd only like." She looked at the press. "Three left. Then I'm going to eat something, and sleep until the final."

They put the last three volumes into the run between them, each into its pencilled place. Karis took the key from its nail and locked the door behind them and tried the handle twice, and then hung the key on her own wrist by its string, to give back to Bracken in the morning.

At the end of the records hall she stopped and turned to him. She seemed about to say something more, and then to decide against it. She only put her inky hand flat on his sleeve, the way she had laid it on the closed directive, and took it away.

"Thank you for the wall," she said. "You held it."

"Not all of it."

"Enough of it." She started off across the dark toward the residence. Over her shoulder she said, "And my foot is going to be famous," and he laughed, for the first time that day, out loud in the empty quadrangle.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

He did not go straight up.

He stood for a while in the dark under the covered walk's north arch, where the fire-watch boy kept his slate. The boy was there already, on his upturned bucket, with the slate wiped clean and a stub of chalk in his fist. He was writing the night's first hour in large, careful, flat-footed figures. When he had written it he got down and stood back on the cobbles to look at it, and then he climbed up again and rubbed out one figure with the side of his hand and wrote it again, a little straighter.

Nobody had asked him to straighten it. Nobody would check it until noon, when the bursar's clerk came to copy it down for his quarrel with the chandler. The boy did it anyway, because it was his slate and he wanted it right.

Cael watched him do it and felt something he could not have put a name to; it was not quite comfort, but it was near it.

"Evening," said the boy, seeing him.

"Evening. That's a good four."

The boy looked at his four with suspicion, and then with pride, and nodded.

Above the quadrangle, on the guest floor of the administration range, a single window was lit. Cael looked at it for exactly as long as he looked at the clock over the arch and at the dark roof of the records hall, and then he went in.

Brom was still up when Cael came into the common room, on the floor in the corner by the one lamp, with his right wrap off and the round-two exercise for the night half done. He was doing it slowly, as Rooke had told him to, with his eyes on his own hands and his breath counted out loud under it. Karis's grey notebook lay open on the settle beside him at the page of boxes, with tonight's box still empty, waiting.

He finished the movement before he looked up. He always finished the movement.

"Sound?" said Brom.

"Sound. Ilsev stood up and said it."

Brom thought about that. Then he reached out and knocked twice with his knuckles on the floorboard beside him, softly.

"Huh," he said, which from Brom was a celebration.

"Lira told you the rest."

"Lira told me two thin and one bad, and a folder, and Karis's foot." Brom went back to his hands. "I'm not going to say anything about it tonight. Four days. I've got four days to think about nothing but the other end of a forty-foot board. On the twentieth I'll think about nothing but you." He finished the next count. "Did the Archmarshal say anything?"

"Not a word all day. He wrote five times."

"About you?"

"About the paper. How it was checked. Whether anybody could find anything in it."

Brom considered that through two more counts.

"Then he's not looking at you yet," he said.

"He's looking at what looks at me. Tiers and ranks and ladders, all of it. Whether any of it measures true."

"That's the same thing," said Brom, "only later," and he picked up the pencil from the settle and inked a neat cross into tonight's box in Karis's notebook, very carefully, as if it were somebody else's property, which it was. Then he put his wrap back on, finger by finger, and went up.

The lamp was low and the hour was late when Cael sat down at the window, and the long day's pressure still sat behind his eyes like a hand. He did not write it the way he usually wrote, but took a clean page, as Karis had, and set her line at the head of it by itself. Then he wrote under it in numbered parts, because the day had been too big to go down in one piece.

Why retire a working method? (Karis's words. Hers to keep. Copied here so I don't lose sight of it.)

1. What held. Sound law, said standing up, into their own record, by the one person on their side of the table who reads to the end. A year of work. Two academies. Four grey boxes and three hundred and eleven sealed sheets. Bracken's index. Withrow's twenty years. And Karis, who spent eleven weeks of our last term at Greyvane trying to prove that nothing had happened to a clause, and proved it, and then let Bracken take every trace of her hand out of the file so that the file could stand without her. That's what today was for.

2. What doesn't fit. The clause I'm enrolled on and the article that changed the old word sit four apart in one directive. One drafting, as far as anybody will ever be able to say. That isn't what today was for. It's what today did to me.

3. What I'm not going to do. Argue from it. A warden spent two years building cases against me out of things that looked alike. A closed list and a plain reading finished him. I'm not going to start doing it his way in the very week the list held.

He stopped there with the pen lifted. Down the bluff, the dark river kept on going. At the hour, down at the ferry landing, the two grey coats changed under their lamp on the bell, as they had changed every four hours since the bridge.

Then he wrote the fourth part, which was his own. It had been coming toward him all term, a step at a time, from somewhere a long way off, and tonight it had arrived.

4. What I think the question is. A system that's muddled about somebody asks things. Naveth asked me things. Quenna asked me one I still owe her the answer to. Gault asks his four a session and puts every answer in his clerk's book. Muddled is honest. Muddled leaves a gap you can talk into.

The system over all of them doesn't ask me anything. It renames. It converts one thing into another and posts a sign. It discourages. It shuts doors behind itself. It does every bit of it in the same flat voice paper always has, a few articles apart, and nowhere does it give a reason.

I don't have to know who. The thing I can't leave alone is the reason it was put together like this. That could take me years.

He read it through once. Under all of it he added two short lines that had nothing to do with any system at all.

Tomorrow, ordinary again.

Four days to the final. Five to the twentieth.

Chapter 51 — Two Clocks

[Restrained, intimate narration; give loyalty and doubt room to register]

The hip woke before she did.

Lira lay on her back in the dark and listened to it, the way the foundry master had taught her to listen to a furnace before he let anyone near the door. It was not loud. It had stopped being loud on the fourth day.

Now it was a long, low, settled ache from the crest of the bone down into the meat of the thigh, the kind of ache that has moved in and hung up its coat.

Ten days. The oil on Fiske's boards had been ten days ago, and the click with it.

She sat up in two stages, because one stage was no longer on offer, and put her good foot on the floor first.

The bad leg swung round after it, and took her. The first half arrived the ordinary way. The second half came a breath later, and she felt the hip consider the question before it said yes.

Two stages, then: that was today's answer, and no amount of waiting for the fourth bell would change it.

She stood with one hand on the bedpost and did the sums. She had always done sums. At the foundry nobody had paid you to guess what a ladle weighed.

Standing, the leg was fine, and walking it was fine if she did not hurry; landing was the trouble.

Every burst ended in a landing, and every landing came home through that hip, and a hip that took weight in two stages would take a landing in two stages, too, with a gap between them that a good fighter could put a fist through.

Three bursts, she thought, three she could pay for. The fourth would be paid out of tomorrow, as it always was, and today tomorrow had nothing in it to pay with.

Brom knew that. Brom had known it for two years, since a wet afternoon at Ardenmere when she had told him so herself, out loud, sitting on the bench with her wrap half off.

You did not keep that kind of thing from somebody who sparred you four times a week. He would have worked it out anyway.

She dressed in the grey before the window, slowly, and did not look at the bed.

Fenmark came back to her while she was doing up the second boot, as it had come back most mornings this week. The station hall with its long bench, and the cold coming up through the flagstones.

The Arbiter had spent ninety breaths or so on her. Then a clerk who had not looked at her at all had written Copper on a sheet, and Rank One, and blotted it, and that had been her.

That was all it took to decide what a person was for the rest of her life. She had been fourteen and had not cried until she was outside.

Today a great many people were going to look at her for a good deal longer than a minute and a half. One of them was the best looker the Compact owned, and he was not here for her.

She found she did not mind. She would give him a very good fight, and if he was any good at his job, he would see what was in front of him whether he had come for it or not.

She took the stair a step at a time, with the rail doing half the work.

The other three were at the long table in the common room. Nobody said good morning, which she was grateful for.

Brom was eating porridge in the steady, joyless way he ate before a bout. He did not look at her leg. She saw him not look at it. Somebody had told him not to, and she knew who.

Karis had the marbled book open beside her bowl. When Lira sat down, Karis reached under her chair and brought up the two practice batons, still tied together in the middle with Lira's own hip bandage, in the ugly knot Lira had pulled tight nine days ago.

"Receipt," said Karis, and drew a line through her entry in the marbled book. "Returned in the condition received. I've been sleeping with them under my chair like a dog."

"Thank you," said Lira.

She worked at the knot. It had set hard, and it took her a while, and nobody helped her, because they knew better. When it came loose she wound the bandage round her own hand, and held one baton out across the table to Brom, grip first.

He took it. He turned it over once in his big hand, looking at the dark place on the grip where his fingers had worn the wood for two years. It went down next to his bowl.

"Nine days," he said.

"Nine days," said Lira.

Neither said more. There was no more to say.

For nine days they had not sparred, or talked about the bout, or watched each other cross a room. It had not been politeness. Without the silence, each of them would have spent nine days building a fight out of the other one's wound.

She knew his number. Everybody who had ever watched him knew his number. Somewhere past four minutes of hard contact, Brom's iron began to cost him more than it gave, and everything else he did got slower to pay for it.

And he knew hers. If either of them had spent the last nine days thinking about the other's number, they would have walked out today to fight a ledger instead of a person.

So she had not thought about it. She had thought about her feet.

Cael sat across from her and ate nothing, and held himself very still in the particular way he had been holding himself since the stair.

She could see the corner of him that was busy, even if nobody else at the table could. She did not say anything about it. The corner was his to keep, and he was keeping it.

"Eat something," she told him instead.

"I'm not fighting."

"You're watching. It's worse." She pushed the bread at him. "Eat it, or I'll feel you not eating it from the boards."

He ate it.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

By the second bell the back rows of every tier were packed and the front rows stood empty, which was the wrong way round.

Crossing the quadrangle, Cael worked out why. Regulars sat low as a rule, down by the rail, where the calls carried and the feet were close.

Today the second-years had done a different sum. They had come an hour early with bread in their coat pockets and climbed to the back, because a full yard would shut the late half of the bluff out in the covered walk, and the back rows were the ones nobody could take from you.

He climbed to his own place anyway. East tier, a third of the way up, on the same worn stone he had sat on for every session since the brackets were painted.

He had turned the question over before he slept, whether to sit somewhere else, and kept coming back to the same answer. A new seat would say that today was not like other days, and the whole hill knew that already without his seat saying it too.

It was ledger day twenty-one, and he had been holding since before he opened his eyes. The hold was where he had put it before dawn.

It weighed a little more this morning than yesterday. Every morning it did, and every evening a little more again.

Down at the north end, Bracken came out across the empty boards with two folded sheets held against his waistcoat. He walked to the panel's table and laid them under the edge of the sand-glass's stand, one on top of the other, squared them with a finger, and walked away again without looking up at anybody.

Half the yard did not notice. The other half thought he was a clerk.

A few minutes later Karis climbed up and sat on Cael's right. A sheet of her own, folded small, lay shut on her knee.

"Copies," Karis said. "The sealed originals sit under the glass down there. He certified both their season records at the first bell this morning, and sealed them, and filed them, and then he walked them down here himself."

"This morning. Before."

"Before. That's the whole point of it." She ran her thumb along the fold. "However it goes, there's a sheet already sealed that says what each of them did, from the first session to this morning. Nobody who made it knew how today ends."

She tapped the fold. "Bracken says a record made after the result has been coached."

Cael did not answer. A man who ran a registry had spent his first hour of the day building something that would stay true whichever of his friends walked off the boards with the crown. There was no sentence Cael could have made about that just then which would not have come out wrong.

The yard went on filling round them, down from the top like water rising backward. At the table the adjudicating instructor set out the chalk and the glass. The two safety seats took their places behind her with their hands clasped.

In the north entrance Rooke had planted himself with his arms folded, as he had for every bout of Brom's this season. He would not sit down; he never did.

Two rows down and some way along, among the Blade cohort, Ephram sat forward with his elbows on his knees and a space kept clear on the stone beside him. For whom, Cael had no idea.

Ephram looked round once, up the tier, and nodded to him, which was new. Then he faced the boards again.

With the fourth bell came Fiske, in plain clothes, to take a front-row seat on the north tier. Lira had told her to sit north, because from the east you could not see the far chalk properly, and Fiske had taken the advice as seriously as she took everything.

Two years the Copper Crown had sat on her shelf. Within the hour somebody else would be holding it in front of the whole bluff. She sat down in the front row with her hands loose in her lap and the face of a woman who had made her peace with that a long time ago, perhaps on the very afternoon she won it.

The delegation came a little after her.

Nobody had told the yard to keep the north tier's second row clear. It had kept it clear all the same.

First the counsel, talking over her shoulder, and then the two clerks, and then Ilsev, making a desk of the case across her knees. Last came the Archmarshal in his plain road grey, who took the middle of the row and sat.

Cael had not expected that. On the fourteenth the man had stood at the gallery rail in hall three for fifty minutes and shown no sign of wanting a chair. Now he sat at his ease, with a little notebook shut on one knee and his pen lying across the cover.

The end seat went to Havel, whose hands were empty. There was no recording case at his side, and no glass, and no sheaf of anything.

Cael held that for a count of four. An officer who brought nothing to hold was not working. And an officer who was not working, on an afternoon when he might have been anywhere at all, had climbed this particular stair.

With that, he put the whole north tier out of his mind on purpose, and kept it out. Two people he loved were about to try very hard to beat each other. He owed them his eyes.

He let the read up, too. That was a choice, and he made it with his eyes open.

For nine days he had kept the read at its thinnest layer, to spare the hold. This afternoon, though, no one on the bluff would spare him a look. Every eye in the yard, the Archmarshal's among them, would be on the oak.

So he kept the hold where it was, and took his hand off the read, and let it rise and see.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The card said that officers of the delegation would not converse with any party under review outside a sitting, and would not acknowledge such a party beyond ordinary courtesy. Havel had read it four times on the road.

It said nothing at all about sitting on a stone bench in the sun on an afternoon when no sitting was called.

He had checked. He had asked the counsel at breakfast, in the form a records officer uses when he would like to be told no, whether the officers' attendance at a public event on the institution's calendar was a matter for the schedule.

"It's a fight," the counsel had said, buttering her bread. "Go if you like. I'm going. Half the hill will be there, and I've never seen a Wind practitioner fight anything but paper."

So it was not his duty to be here. Nobody would write down that he had come.

He had left the recording case in the working room and the brass glass in its pocket, and his notebook was in his inside coat where it always was, and it was going to stay there. His hands had nothing to hold.

He found that he wanted to sit here with his hands empty, like anybody else who had climbed a stair to watch two young people fight.

He could not have said why, and he did not try very hard.

The tier was warm stone. The yard below it was very loud, and the noise had a shape to it, a long rising swell with no words in it, like water coming in under a door.

Below him, in the front row, sat a big quiet woman with her hands folded. He knew her from the bracket sheet. She was the champion who would stop being champion before the afternoon was out, and she looked calmer than anybody else he could see.

Three seats to his left the senior evaluation seat kept her case flat across her knees. She was reading the yard, and he knew that look. She read a crowd the way she read a sheet, from the top left corner, in order.

Beyond her the Archmarshal sat with his notebook shut on one knee and his pen across it, as still as a man asleep with his eyes open.

The east tier he left alone, by rule. There was a boy somewhere over there whose file he had carried up a road, and he would not be seen looking for him.

He looked at the north door instead, where the girl would come out.

He knew her only from paper, and from corridors. On paper she was Wind, Copper, Rank Two, on a certificate three years old that nobody had looked at since.

In the corridors this week she had been a girl walking very carefully on a bad leg and refusing, with her whole body, to be seen doing it. He had stepped aside for her once in the covered walk. She had thanked him with her eyes on the far end of the walk.

Now she was the top line of the Copper column, and the whole bluff had come to see her fight.

There was a thing he had not done that morning at Ardenmere. Somebody had held out a pear to him, in a twist of paper, and he had wanted it and had not taken it.

He had thought about that pear more often since than any grown man should think about fruit. Sitting on the warm stone with nothing in his hands, he understood that this was a little like the pear. It was a thing he would like to have, and could not quite reach, and would not try to explain to anybody.

He had asked himself on the stair, quite plainly, why he had come, and had got no better answer than that he wanted to. It was not a reason a records officer was trained to accept. He had accepted it anyway, and climbed the rest of the stair, and found the end seat free.

Along the row the Archmarshal shifted once, to settle the notebook more squarely on his knee, and was still again. Havel had sat at the same tables as that man since the road and had not heard him say thirty words that were not about a sheet of paper.

What the notebook was for, he couldn't say. He did not want to know, particularly. A man who had spent his whole working life at the end of tables, writing down exactly what other people said, learned early that there were notebooks it was wiser not to wonder about. He had kept to that lesson through every posting he had ever had, and he kept to it now.

Down on the boards a porter was sweeping the last of the dust from round the chalk marks with a long soft broom, slowly. Havel watched him do it and found he was enjoying it, which surprised him. He could not remember the last time he had sat anywhere without a sheet of paper on his knee and a pen expecting things of him. His right hand, which ached in the web of the thumb by the end of every long sitting, lay open and quiet on his thigh, and for once nothing in it hurt.

He would watch, and that was all. He would go back down the stair afterward and be a records officer again, and nothing would be written anywhere to say he had climbed it.

A bell rang somewhere behind the range. Down at the table the adjudicating instructor faced the yard.

Havel folded his empty hands on his knee, and waited, like everyone else.

Inside the north door it was cold and dark, with the yard's noise coming through the planks like weather.

Lira stood in the short passage with her back to the wall and her eyes shut, and let the hip tell her about the stone under her boots. All down the covered walk it had been telling her the same thing, two stages and two stages.

It did not complain. It only reported, flatly, like a clerk reading out a sum.

On the other side of the yard, behind the south door, Brom would be standing just like this. He would be opening and closing his hands. She did not need to see it. She had watched him do it before every bout for two years.

The safety seat at the door looked at her, and then at the leg, and then politely at the ceiling.

"Whenever you're ready," he said.

She thought about the station hall at Fenmark, and the clerk's pen. She thought about Fiske on the oil ten days ago, and the honest thing Fiske had said afterward across the boards.

She thought about Brom's number and put it away again, unplanned, where it belonged. She was not going to fight his four minutes. She was going to fight him.

Then she opened her eyes and walked out into the light.

The sound hit her like the heat at an opened furnace door: a solid, whole thing, everywhere at once. She did not hurry through it. Her pace to the chalk was her own, and slow today, and the yard saw it, and part of the noise turned.

Leading foot first, she took the chalk. The weight came down onto it in two halves, as it had in her room, with a small considering gap between them.

She saw Brom see it.

He was standing at the south chalk with his wraps on and his hands at his sides, and his hands were opening and closing.

His eyes dropped to her hip for precisely as long as knowing took, and came back up to her face. He did not look sorry. Had he looked sorry, she'd have hit him.

He looked like Brom, who had sat on the loser's side of a bench beside her more times than either of them could count, and who was going to try his hardest to put her there today.

Good, she thought.

She crouched and laid her palm flat on the oak, and held it there a moment longer than she needed to, and stood up.

Cael already had Lira. He had seen it on the walk: the leading boot set down first, and the weight coming onto it in a half and then another half, with a little pause in the middle like a word somebody has to think about.

All season she had come to her chalk in one piece. Today she came in two.

So he looked at Brom.

Brom's shoulders were easy and his feet were where they always were; the tell was lower down.

His fists were closing and opening, slowly, at his hips, over and over, the way a man works his hands on a frosty morning. It was not a frosty morning.

Cael had seen it three times this season, and by the second month he had understood it. It was not fear. Brom's hands had been told about the plan before the rest of him had finished agreeing to it, and the plan was a long afternoon of being struck, and they were getting ready.

Long, Cael thought. He means to make it long.

And then, a heartbeat after, the sum came in under it and turned his stomach over. No. She does. She has to. And he knows she has to.

That was the bout entire. He had seen it in week three of the season, doing the bracket arithmetic on the back of a page, when it became clear that these two would meet at the end unless somebody very good got in the way.

Fiske had nearly been that somebody. Nobody else had come close.

There were two clocks on the oak, and they did not run the same way.

The first was Brom's: four minutes, near enough, of hard contact inside a single exchange. The turn of the glass between exchanges gave some of it back, and never all. Brom had told him so one cold Greyvane winter, and Cael had written it down then and there, and every bout since had kept to it.

Four minutes didn't break the iron, nothing so kind; it simply got dear. Keeping the skin hard began to take more out of him with every blow, and everything else he did had to stand in line behind it and wait to be paid for.

The second was Lira's, and nothing gave any of it back: three bursts, on that leg, today.

There was a fourth in her, there always was, and she had told Brom about it herself years ago on a wet bench at Ardenmere: the fourth was bought on credit, paid back out of the next day's legs. Today the hip had no tomorrow to borrow from.

She knew his number, and he knew hers. And for nine days each of them had refused to build one single thought on the other's.

Standing at the table, the adjudicating instructor read the terms across the yard. The Copper column, its season's final, witnessed. Four exchanges, each on the table's glass, each to the cleaner touch or called even. The bout goes to whoever holds more touches after the fourth, unless a fighter can't go on, or yields, or the panel ends it first.

She turned the glass over, and the sand began to run.

For most of two minutes Lira asked Brom one question, in three different voices.

The question was the seam, whose address was common knowledge; nine of them had gone looking for it this season.

When Brom took a blow on hardened skin, he took it superbly, and then there was a pause, short as a hiccup, while the taking finished and before the answer began. For that sliver of time there was nobody home behind the iron.

Lira had been walking in through that pause for two years. She knew its every inch.

The first time, she asked plainly. She came in low off the chalk with a straight line at his lead thigh, not fast, meant to be taken, and as his skin went hard to take it she was already slipping round toward his open side, to be there when the pause opened.

The pause did not open. His answer met her coming round.

It was not speed. From the tier Cael saw it, and saw that most of the yard didn't.

Brom had not got quicker. The two things no longer came in turn. The hardening and the answer came out of him together now, overlapping, the way a good clerk blots one line with his left hand while his right is already writing the next.

Somebody had rebuilt him round a different frame. Rooke, with a term of patience and a sheet of nineteen dull exercises.

Lira skipped back out of it, light, unhurt, with her eyebrows up.

She asked again. This time she came at an angle, and halfway in she shifted her weight from one foot to the other, so that the blow would land a fraction late and stretch the pause out longer.

It was lovely work, and good fighters had lost to it. Brom took the late blow and answered it on time.

The third time, Cael made a sound out loud, and only knew he had when Karis looked at him.

Lira gave Brom everything. She threw a line so deep and so whole that there was no way to take it in part; he had to set his whole forearm and swallow all of it.

That was the point. If there was any pause left in him at all, a full swallow was where it would be widest, and she meant to be standing in it.

Brom swallowed the whole of it. The answer came out of the same motion: a hardened forearm, chopping down across her raised guard, with a crack that went round the yard like a door slammed in an empty house.

Lira slid back four paces on the oak and stopped.

The adjudicating instructor's hand went up. "Even," she called. "Taken on the guard."

The yard made an uncertain noise. Half of it did not know what it had just watched.

A blow on a set guard was not clean; that had been the ladder's rule all season, and nobody had scored. But everyone on the tiers who knew anything had just watched the most famous gap in the Copper column close, quietly, in front of them.

Cael looked past the heaving chest and the loose hands, at her face.

She was grinning at Brom, wide and delighted and quite unguarded. In three years Cael had seen that grin perhaps six times.

It never meant she was winning. It meant somebody had surprised her.

Lira did not care for much in the way of luxuries, but she had one, and she had never tried to give it up. She loved finding out that a person was more than she had thought. It pleased her more than any bout she had ever won.

Brom, at the far chalk, worked one shoulder round in its socket. No grin came back; it never did. Once, his fists closed and opened.

His clock had started. It would start again with every exchange, a little shorter each time.

The second exchange went to Brom, through the very thing that would lose him the bout.

Cael worked it out halfway through, and wrote it up that night in a page and a half.

Rooke had never closed the seam, because nobody could. It was not a fault in Brom; it was the way Iron Skin worked, the way a hinge works.

Rooke's real lesson had been smaller and stranger: stop swallowing whole. He took most of each blow on the iron, and simply let the last part of it through, unhardened, into his own body. Whatever he saved by not finishing, he spent on the answer.

It was a trade, and Cael could see both sides of the ledger at once. Contact had paid for the death of Brom's oldest flaw. Every blow now cost him a fifth of itself in bruises. And contact was what his clock was made of.

Her first burst went early in the glass. The second went a long minute after.

Cael felt them both. He had carried her Wind for three years in his own legs, and he knew the bill for a burst as well as he knew his own name.

No breath at the front, for the whole length of the move. At the back, the landing beat: half a breath of standing on the spot, unable to turn, when your body is only something that has arrived. And afterward, the hot line drawn down the leading side from the hip bone to the inside of the knee.

She used the first to escape. Brom had walked her toward the table end, step by patient step, never hurrying and never letting her past his lead shoulder, until the chalk lines ran out behind her and there was nowhere left to stand. Then she went sideways out of the corner on the Wind and landed in open oak.

She used the second to go in. She showed him a line high, let him start to set for it, and was simply not there any more.

She was under his arm and inside his reach before the iron had finished arriving, and her flat palm cracked across his ribs, a clean, ringing slap that the whole north end heard.

The table's hand stayed down. Brom had taken the slap on the struck side, unfinished, the way Rooke had taught him, and kept moving. And Lira was in her landing beat. She had no air and no way to turn, and for half a breath she was only standing there.

He took the half-breath. He swept her lead foot and pressed down through her shoulder in one motion, low and complete, and laid her on her back on the oak. His forearm settled across her collarbone, not unkindly, because Brom was never unkind on a floor.

The adjudicating instructor called it at once. Both safety seats were out on the oak and kneeling by her before the call was finished, and back at the table by the time she sat up.

"Wind, touch to the ribs," the table read out. "Iron Skin, touch to the floor. To Iron Skin, the cleaner."

Brom stepped back to his chalk, and Lira got up by herself. It took her a moment longer than it should have, and the whole yard saw that it did.

Karis had gone very upright on the stone beside him.

"Two gone," she said. Her voice had gone small. Cael knew that voice. Karis used it when fear had arrived and she had chosen to have a job instead.

"Two gone," Cael said.

"How much does she have?"

Karis said nothing. Her fingers had closed on the folded sheet in her lap.

Chapter 52 — The Exhibit

[Restrained, intimate narration; give loyalty and doubt room to register]

Ilsev did not know how to watch a fight, so she read the yard instead.

She had decided that on the stair coming up, and it had served her well enough for two exchanges.

A yard was a document like any other. It had a heading and a body and a hand at the foot that signed it, and if you read it in order, and did not skip ahead to the parts that excited you, it would tell you a great deal about itself.

The heading was the table: three faculty, one standing and two behind her with their hands clasped, and the glass between them on its little stand, and under the edge of the stand two folded sheets with seals on them. She had watched the registrar carry them out across the empty boards and lay them there, square to the edge, before the yard had filled. He had walked away again.

Nobody had told her what they were. She did not need telling. A man does not put a sealed paper under a sand-glass before a contest unless he wishes it to be seen that the paper came first.

She approved of that more than she could have said aloud.

The body was the crowd. More than a thousand people, she judged, on stone tiers open to the sky, and for most of the first two exchanges they had made one long continuous sound with no words in it.

Its pitch had shifted all along: up for the girl's entrance, down when her foot met the chalk, uncertain all at once at the first even, and flat and loud together when the girl went onto her back.

Ilsev could not have said what any of it meant on the boards, but she could hear that the sound was a record of something, kept by a thousand clerks at once, none of whom knew they were keeping it.

The signature at the foot belonged to the woman in front of her.

Almost directly below Ilsev's knees, in the north tier's front row, the champion had sat through both exchanges without moving.

Her hands lay folded on her thigh, and her broad back was perfectly still, and only once, when the girl went down, had her head turned a quarter-inch and come back. Of all the signatures Ilsev had read in her working life, few had been steadier.

Beside Ilsev, on her right, the Archmarshal sat with his notebook closed on his knee and his pen lying across the cover, where he had laid it when he sat down.

He watched the boards the way he watched a sitting, at an even pace, giving each part its share, and Ilsev did not try to read him. She had stopped trying on the second day of the road. A colleague's face was not her question.

Nor was the boy on the east tier, a third of the way up, beside the Ember girl with the ink on her fingers. Ilsev knew where he was sitting. She had known it since she sat down, as she knew where the doors were. She did not look at him.

Her own question was a long way off by now. Four days ago she had filled a form in eleven minutes and laid it in a tray, and since then it had gone down the bluff in a courier's satchel and up the river, one level higher than the last, to a room she would never see.

She had put it down when she filed it. She did not pick it up again here, on a warm stone bench, with a contest going on below her that had nothing to do with it. A woman who carried her filed matters about with her into every room soon stopped being able to see the room.

So she looked at the room.

In all her years of hearings she had read the word Wind on more forms than she could count, and had never once watched it.

On paper it was a Path like any other, a line in a register, a tier and a rank and a date. Down there on the oak it was a slight young woman with a bad leg who could, when she chose, simply not be where you had been looking.

Ilsev had seen it happen twice now, and both times her eye had gone to the empty place a moment after the girl had left it, like a reader whose finger has slipped a line. She did not much enjoy the feeling. She suspected it was the whole point.

It occurred to her that a registry clerk, three years ago, had written this girl down in about the time it took to read a short page, and that nobody had read the page again since.

She marked the thought and went no further with it. It was not a finding. It was an observation about a form, and forms were her trade, and the form was not in front of her.

The table turned the glass.

At first she thought nothing was happening, because the girl did not go in.

She stood at the edge of the big young man's reach and waited, and when he came to her she simply stepped back, on her own feet, and let him come again. The crowd did not like it. Ilsev heard it not liking it: a restless low murmur, like a hall at a long reading.

Then the young man reached her guard and hit it, hard, and she took it on her forearms and went back another step, and the murmur stopped.

Backward the girl went, the whole circuit of the floor, and then the whole circuit a second time. Every so often the young man caught up with her and struck, and every time she let him, on her arms and her shoulders, and gave ground, and he followed. She was not running, as even Ilsev could see. She was walking him.

Somewhere past the third minute the sound of the yard changed again. It did not get louder. It got slower, and lower, and more careful, the way a reading room sounds when a whole table has found the same line in the same moment.

In front of her the champion's folded hands had come apart.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

The first step told Cael everything, because it went backward.

Lira did not step backward. Three years of watching, and never once by choice. Backward was where you went when you had been beaten to a place, and she was never beaten to places. She went sideways, or through, or round, or she was simply already elsewhere.

Every page he had on her said so, nine pages of it, in a hundred different ways. The Wind did not make her fast. It made her early. She lived in the sliver of time other fighters spent deciding, and she spent it in tiny coins, and every coin bought her a square of floor that her opponent had not finished thinking about.

Now she stepped back off her chalk on her own two feet, and waited.

Brom came, and she gave him ground. When he reached her she put up her guard and let him hit it, and the crack of iron on forearm went round the yard, and she gave him more ground.

There was no burst and no Wind, nothing that cost her a held breath, only feet, and arms, and the long slow curve of the oak's rim behind her.

She walked him round the whole floor like that. Then she began again.

Cael's own forearms ached, watching. He knew what Brom's iron felt like arriving on a guard; he had a month of bruises from the wash-house to prove it.

Lira had none of the things that make that bearable, because she had never once trained to be struck, and her whole body had been built round a single idea, which was that being hit meant something had already gone wrong. Each blow she caught travelled up her forearms and lodged in her shoulders. And every backward step came down on the leading leg, on a hip ten days old.

"She's spending him," said Karis, very low. "Isn't she. She's paying for his clock with her own arms."

"Yes."

"For how long?"

"Longer than he can. That's the whole bet."

The glass was half run before the yard caught on. Cael heard the moment it did, because the noise did not rise. It sank, and thickened, and turned careful, like a crowd watching somebody carry too many plates.

Then Brom slowed.

Cael had been waiting for it since the first backward step, with his own count running silently under everything else. After every committed strike Brom re-squared his feet before the next. All season that had taken him four counts. Now, with the glass more than half gone, it took him five.

The fifth count was what Lira had walked round the oak twice to buy.

She went into it on her third burst. She was behind his lead leg before the re-squaring had finished, and her heel went into the back of his knee, and the knee bent the way knees must, and Brom sat down on the boards with a thump that Cael felt through the stone.

"Iron Skin, down," called the table. "To Wind, the cleaner."

The tiers came up off their seats all together. Karis was up with them, both fists clenched, saying "Three, that's three," to nobody.

By Cael's private count the exchange had run four minutes and eleven seconds. He stayed sitting and watched Lira walk back to her chalk.

She had stopped pretending. The leading leg took her weight in two halves, and then in three.

On the way she laid the flat of her hand on her own thigh, briefly. He had never once seen her do that on a floor. It meant there was nothing left over for hiding, and she had decided that hiding had stopped being worth its price.

Brom had seen it.

He was up and back at his own chalk, rubbing the back of his knee. Cael watched it come over him: the eyes going to her thigh, half a breath of standing quite still, and then something in the shoulders settling.

He'll go for it, Cael thought.

The next thought came straight behind it, and he could not have stopped it if he had tried. He should.
