Paper says: five up, one level, every trial inside tolerance. Renewed. All of it true. It's the first true paper about me I've ever carried out of a room without first having to fight somebody for it, and I'm not used to that yet.

Q.'s question, from Greyvane: could I keep it in, with people watching who'd be glad to see me hurt.

Answer, on the twentieth of Reaping: yes.

Thirty-five days since the stair. It wakes when I do. Three hours under the Compact's four best chairs, and it stayed in. Cost: one interval and one headache. The Pressure stayed in my arm. Gault wrote "no change" about the plate and then stood up for me over it, which I didn't earn and can't put right.

I've been keeping things back since before I had a word for it. Today the keeping went under instruments for three hours, and it held. I'm going to stop calling it a habit.

The quarter-burst. Gain: the clerk keeps his feet; the record keeps its shape. Bill: every bit of one hip, three days, likely four. I shut a burst halfway through paying for it, which I have never once managed on purpose since my Kindling, and I can't say how I did it, so I can't say I can do it again. One point isn't a line. Karis taught me that.

He didn't look twice.

Six people needed a second look at me. He needed one. One look gave him the lot. He weighed it sitting down, and the rail had nothing more for him.

Net: I've known rooms of people who wished me hurt, and many more rooms of people who wished only to write me up and shut the book. Today, for once, the man across the room had finished with me before I'd even climbed down off the rail. Safest thing that's ever happened to me, or the reverse: I can't yet tell.

Two lines in his book. I'll be a long time wondering.

Chapter 56 — Twelve by Fourteen

[Restrained, intimate narration; give loyalty and doubt room to register]

The charter was already lying open on the records-hall counter when Cael came in at the first bell, turned the right way up for a reader standing on the public side.

Bracken was behind the counter with his pen behind his ear and a cup of something long gone cold at his elbow, and he did not say good morning. He laid one finger beside a paragraph halfway down the right-hand page and kept it there while Cael read.

An inspecting delegation may examine any enrollee whose enrollment rests on a provision or exception, in the presence of the institution's counsel and the officer of record for that enrollment, on the record, at a time set by the institution.

"Fourth part," said Bracken. "Provisions and exceptions. Subsection eleven." He lifted the finger. "The charter was born with it. Their counsel sent up a request under it at the eighth bell last night, very properly worded, and there's nothing unusual in it; a house with exceptions on its roll has it used now and then. This one has had it twice in my time, both times over students from across the water, and on both occasions the most exciting thing that happened was a man asking for a second glass of water."

"So it's ordinary."

"It is perfectly ordinary." Bracken took the great book in both hands and set its spine true to the counter. "And yet it's the single door in this whole inspection through which a Compact officer may walk up to you and ask you something to your face, and wait for the reply. Half a sentence is a poor thing to give a man, so you're having both halves."

Cael read the subsection again. At a time set by the institution.

"When?"

"I've set it. Fourth bell today, in the east room upstairs." Bracken took the pen from behind his ear and turned it over in his fingers. "I went up with a rule last night and measured it, to be sure: twelve feet by fourteen, the smallest room in the building that will take five chairs without anybody's knees touching. The house's counsel will sit, and Magister Gault will sit, because the subsection wants the officer of record and he is yours. And the book will be kept by one of my clerks and not one of theirs."

"They wanted their own?"

"Their counsel proposed one of theirs at the foot of her request, and I objected in writing, on both sides of a sheet." He set the pen down. "It took me a quarter of an hour to draft and her four minutes to accept, and I'd like you to know it was done, because you'll never see it anywhere else. It'll be in the file. Nobody reads that part of a file."

"Thank you."

"Don't." Bracken shut the charter. "Thanking me makes it sound as though I'd done you a kindness, and I haven't. I've done the filing correctly." Over the closed boards his eyes found Cael's. "Correct filing is all this counter sells. Kindness wears out. Filing doesn't."

Cael went up the back stair of the records hall before breakfast anyway, because he had never yet walked into a room he had not tried to see first. The east room's door was shut. On the landing outside it, on a stool, with a mug in one hand and a ledger on his knee, sat the inky-knuckled clerk.

"Registrar's orders," the clerk said, before Cael could open his mouth. "Nobody goes in before the bell. Not their counsel, not ours, not the Magister, and not you." He drank. "Their counsel tried at the first bell. I told her the same. She wrote it down."

Cael looked at the shut door, and at the clerk, and understood that he was being treated exactly as the delegation was being treated, to the minute and to the word, and that it was the fairest thing anybody on the bluff could have done for him.

"Thank you," he said.

"Don't," said the clerk, who had plainly worked for Bracken a long time, and turned a page.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

"Sit there," said Lira, "and be him."

She was lying on the settle with the bad leg up on a bolster, pointing at Brom, and Brom looked at the chair she meant, the hard one at the head of the long table, and then back at her.

"I don't know what he sounds like."

"Nobody does. That's the point. Go and sit there and be somebody nobody knows what he sounds like."

So Brom limped to the head of the table and sat down in the hard chair with his strapped hand on the wood and his iced knee stuck out to one side, and looked at Cael, and Cael waited, and Brom went on looking at him.

It went on for a long time. Brom had sat on a bench for twelve days at the start of term while Rooke decided whether he was watching, and he could keep still longer than anyone Cael had ever met. He did not frown or smile or shift, but only breathed and looked, and his face gave back nothing at all. The stove ticked, and somewhere down in the yard a bucket was dropped.

At last a laugh got out of Cael; nothing else was left to try. "I can't. There's nothing there to get hold of."

"Then that's your page," said Lira. "Write it down. Nothing there to get hold of."

Karis had the library's list open beside her bread, a single sheet in her own hand that she had brought up from carrel eleven at the first bell. "Three mentions in ten years and more of print," she said, running her finger down it: "a dedication, a dinner for a retiring magistrate, and a swearing-in. He was at all three, and said nothing at any of them that anybody thought worth writing down." She turned it face down. "I can't help you either. I've never been asked to read a man who leaves no paper."

"Then I won't read him." Cael pushed his bowl away. "I'll settle what I'm going to be in there and be it, whatever comes across the table."

"Which is?"

"The truth."

"Half of it," said Lira from the settle, without opening her eyes. "That's the half you say to make people stop asking. Say the other half, so we can all hear it."

He had said it in her hearing on purpose, half expecting that, and she was right.

"If he asks about anything that's already written down somewhere, I tell him all of it, straight. If he asks about anything that isn't, I tell him I won't answer, out loud and in those words, so that the clerk can put down that I said no." He looked at the face-down sheet. "That's the change. In every room before this one, when there's been a thing I couldn't say, I've said something true with a corner cut off it: on Gault's plate yesterday, at the baseline, at Greyvane. Each time it worked, and each time it cost, and each cost went in the book.

"It won't work on him. Hand him a true sentence with a corner cut off and he'll see the cut. He won't mention it. He'll simply know. Then the finest reader the Compact has will be holding a map of my walls." He turned his hands over. "A flat no only tells him that there's something I won't say, which he knows already, as does the whole bluff. A cut corner points his eye at the cut."

At the head of the table Brom spoke for the first time since he had sat down, still in the chair and still looking straight at Cael.

"Then when you say no, put it down like a full plate," he said. "Both hands, all the way to the table, and no rattle."

Karis pressed both palms to the wood. Other people frowned; Karis did that.

"Let me name the danger over the porridge, so I'm not naming it to the ceiling in the small hours. Picture it on paper: the assay boy declines to answer the Compact's own officer, mid-inspection, into the book. Into the inspection file it goes, and the first readers will be the ones hunting for a reason. You could hardly hand them anything better to quote."

"Yes."

"And you'll do it anyway."

"I'll do it anyway, because if he catches me in a lie that's worse than a no he doesn't like, by more than I can count." He held her eyes. "There's one more piece. Rip it apart if it's rotten.

"Nine days he's been on this hill, and not a soul has played to him. Withrow stood still on purpose. Bracken's file stood up without anybody holding it. Rooke signed his sheets and went back to his cohort. Yesterday Gault ran three hours of true instruments and wrote down a flat line and stood up for it. The whole house has spent nine days being exactly what it is, as hard as it can." He spread his hands on the table. "So picture me walking in there and playing to him. Then I'm the only performer on the whole bluff, and I've spoilt the single thing this house has managed to let him see."

Nobody spoke, and Brom, in the hard chair, went on being nobody in particular.

"That's a good reason." Karis used the formal voice she saved for things she would sign. "It's also convenient. I'd like both of those minuted."

"Minute both."

Karis took the grey notebook out of her satchel, opened it at a fresh page, and wrote, in her small upright hand, Refusal in the open. Reason: good. Also convenient. She turned it round so that he could read it, and he nodded, and she closed the book again with the air of somebody filing a document in a box that nobody would be allowed to open.

From under her forearm Lira squinted across at him.

"Fourth bell," she said. "Don't be clever. Scare you and you turn clever, and clever turns you into a fellow with ladders to sell."

Slowly Brom rose from the hard chair and turned back into Brom. "That was horrible," he said. "I don't know how he does it all day."

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

The east room was up a short stair at the back of the records hall, and when Cael reached its door everybody else was already inside. He noticed that before anything else, and afterward he wrote it first: they had all come before him.

It was a plain whitewashed room, too small for the table somebody had put in it, with one window looking out over the river. Nearest the door, Withrow's counsel had her leather case on her lap with its clasp done up, and Gault sat beside her with a grey folder lying closed in front of him. Cael knew him well enough by now to read it: the folder was there to be seen, and would not be opened. In the corner, at a little sloped board, sat Bracken's inky-knuckled clerk. His sheet already had a narrow margin column ruled for the minutes, and his pen was full.

Opposite, with his back to the glass, the Archmarshal sat before a bare stretch of tabletop.

The window put the light behind the man, so that whoever sat facing him would spend half an hour looking into a bright grey river afternoon at a face set in shadow. The thought came to Cael on the threshold, and he looked it over, and put it back. The builders had put that window over the river generations ago, and the man had come in first and taken the chair on his own side of the table, as anyone would; the light had not been arranged, it had simply been there.

Or I've just spent a breath building a plot out of a window, Cael thought, as he sat. Watch that.

The house's counsel spoke first, to him, in the clear voice of somebody reading a notice on a door.

"The authority is the fourth part, subsection eleven. Everything said goes in the book. The rules are short. Any question may be refused. Refuse one, and the clerk writes declined and nothing more. Need me, and you have only to say so; the pen rests till we've finished. The house has fixed this sitting at half an hour, and when the half-hour is up the house will close it."

"Yes."

Hands folded on her case, the counsel turned. "Archmarshal."

The man across the table laid his own hands on the wood. They were square and steady, though the fingers of the left were a little slow, as if the morning had been cold.

"I'm obliged to you," he said to the counsel. He said it as a fact rather than a nicety, and she inclined her head as if it had been one, and then he turned his eyes on Cael.

His look turned out to be no burden. Cael had braced for something heavy and it was not heavy, only very level and very steady, and it did not seem to want anything at all, which was harder to sit under than weight would have been.

"My questions were written on the road," the man said. "There are eleven of them, and I haven't added one since I came up the hill, and if we run out early we'll stop early." He paused. "Is that hip troubling you?"

"Yes."

"Then shift it whenever it wants. No one here is marking how you sit." He went straight on. "First. Your enrollment: what holds it up? Put the paper aside and tell me as you'd tell a friend."

"On an old clause in a founding schedule," said Cael. "It lets a house take a practitioner the registry can't classify and measure him by what he can show. A directive changed its wording a long while ago and never got round to repealing it, and I'm enrolled on it as a standing, not a favour: every half-year I go in front of the assessment office's panel and show what I can do, and I stay enrolled if I show it."

"Whose finding was it?"

"Karis Dellenmoor's. Ember, Iron Rank Three. She found it in a founding volume at Greyvane in the third week of the term, and spent eleven weeks trying to prove somebody had killed it, and nobody had."

"Second." He did not pause, or note anything, or look away. "Where is your baseline weakest?"

Over breakfast Cael had chosen the true answer over the handsome one.

"At the end of the Wind."

"Explain."

"Every burst finishes with a moment I can't do anything in, half a breath after I land, when I can't turn or reach or change my mind. It's always the same length. Three years it's stayed that length, and nothing I've tried has trimmed it." His hip complained, and he let it shift. "Nearly everybody who's hit me since I had the Wind has hit me there. If somebody knows me and wants to put me down, that's the door they use. Lira has done it more times than I'd like to count."

"Yesterday, on the frame, it went unpaid."

Nobody in the room moved. The inky clerk's pen kept its pace. Lift it, and a clerk is deciding what matters.

"The bill went to my hip yesterday," said Cael, "and not to the floor. Paid is paid."

"Paid is paid," the man agreed. "Which brings the third. Could you do it again?"

"No."

"You're certain?"

"For three years I've tried every week to make that half-breath shorter on purpose, and I've never managed it; I tried a month ago on the flagstones and failed." He kept his eyes on the man's face and did not try to make the answer look better than it was. "Yesterday a frame failed by nobody's design. It happened once. How, I can't tell you. Promise you a second time and I'd be selling a skill I haven't got. What I own is one accident and a bruise the size of a plate."

Two breaths went by while the man weighed it, unhurried, like a figure from a new instrument he was still learning to believe.

"That's right," he said. "Mark the word I chose. Accurate. Not well said." He turned his head a little. "The fourth."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

"Who taught you to prepare?"

"A circuit. And everyone who beat me," said Cael.

Now, for the first time, the man's face altered. It was not a smile. Cael had watched the same small easing cross Gault's face over a clean trial: a craftsman handed a figure he can use.

"Tell me about the second half."

"I started out on the circuit at Ardenmere losing more than I won. After each loss I'd sit up writing out what had been done to me, every step I could recover. The following week I'd go and watch my winner do it to someone else, and check my page against it." Both palms turned upward on the table. "Edran taught me the half-beat by hitting me in it. Brom taught me what a wall feels like from the wrong side. Lira, the same way, has taught me more than either. I've never learned much from anybody I beat; nearly everything I know, somebody handed me by knocking me down with it."

"And the schedule? Who taught you how it was put together?"

Cael suspected the question had begun life scribbled in somebody's margin.

"Nobody, really. Two people showed me how to read anything that's old. Prynn, the archivist at Greyvane, taught me to look at a shelf for the gaps as well as the books, because a gap has a date too, and Vell, who kept the ledger at Ardenmere, told me the ledger doesn't forget, and that you judge a whole book by its worst line." He paused. "The schedule itself I just read, every word of it, for three weeks, with Karis reading beside me. We found where it came apart because no one else in that building needed every page of it, and we did."

"Fifth." The man's voice did not change. "Why concede the category?"

Cael did not answer at once.

He understood the question as soon as it was asked, and understood that it was not about the hearing as a whole but about one particular choice, made at Greyvane in the space of a few breaths. Facing a Compact panel, he had said aloud that the schedule had no room in it for him anywhere. His advisers, all of them grown and all of them kind, had begged him to fight for a box. Nobody in any corridor had asked him why he had not, and none of the people who had written about the transcript had so much as noticed; at the time, and for a long while after, it had looked like the moment he lost.

"Inside a box, the argument is me," he said. "If I'd argued that I belonged in one, the hearing would have been about what I am, and people can believe anything they like about what somebody is, and then there's nothing to hold them to afterward. I'd have been asking that panel to like me." He shook his head. "I didn't need them to like me. I needed them to read. If there was no box, all that was left was the clause, and a clause can't change its mind halfway through an afternoon."

"You threw away the sympathy."

"I let go of the ground that runs on goodwill. I stood on the ground that runs on reading."

The man was quiet for a moment, and then moved on as he had moved on from everything else.

"Sixth. You keep records of your own; a report on your file has a phrase for it, extensive private notation habit." The phrase came out like a borrowed cup set gently down. "What are they for?"

For a moment everything in Cael went quite still.

Four true answers lay to hand. Three would have opened every door he had kept bolted all his life. The fourth was complete and honest and opened none of them, and it was waiting for him, written two years ago inside a notebook's front board for some reason that had nothing to do with today.

"So I can't lie to myself later."

The inky clerk's pen kept moving.

"Go on."

"Memory's a kind clerk. It rounds up." Cael found he could say it plainly. "Whatever a thing costs, I put it down that day, so that later, when I'd like to think it came cheaper, there's my own handwriting saying it didn't. Nearly every harm that ever reached me came by way of a paper nobody could check. So I made sure one set of papers about me could always be checked: mine."

He braced.

Any questioner alive would have asked it. The house's counsel had already drawn the little breath of somebody bracing to hear it. Gault, beside her, had gone as still as a post: he had seen the road the next question would take, and the charter gave him nothing to block it with.

Records of what? thought Cael. Ask it. Records of what?

The man did not ask.

His chin dipped a fraction, as a man's does over a receipt, and he said, "Seventh."

The rest of the half-hour went by before Cael's hands were steady again.

He didn't ask.

He walked right up to it. He knew it was there; I watched him know. Nerves didn't stop him. Neither did politeness, nor some trap for later. Whatever lay past that edge simply wasn't the thing he'd come to weigh, so he left it.

A warden takes every question the rules allow him. An assessor takes the ones the form lists. He stood on the lip of the biggest thing I have, looked down, and judged it beyond his errand.

No one has ever been close enough to take a thing from me and kept their hands at their sides. Not once, in my whole life, until now.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The seventh question was about the house.

"What does your provision cost this house to keep?"

Cael had not been ready for that one, and found that he had an answer anyway. He gave it in Bracken's words from the charter sitting, because Bracken's were plainer than any he could have made: the house had to keep him on its roll, set a standard and post it where it could be read, measure him against that standard in front of a panel every half-year, and keep the record where anyone with a right to read it could. "And it's costing the wing a frame," he added. "They'll have the old one in pieces on a bench by tonight. The registrar would tell you the morning's cheap, but the Mire instructor would want the frame on somebody's bill."

The man nodded.

The eighth was about the ladder.

"Your two friends fought on the house's ladder this season, and the registry hasn't looked at either of their certificates in years. Did the brackets measure them?"

"No." Cael did not soften it. "The ladder sorts people by their paper. It was built for practitioners who'd be exactly what their certificates say on the morning they're seeded, and stay so till the season ends. My friends spent the whole year in a cage built for people who did not exist. One of them took the whole cage outright. That's how you know it was one."

The man wrote nothing. The table in front of him had been bare all along.

The ninth was about the man two feet from Cael's elbow.

"Your officer of record. Does he favour you?"

Gault did not move.

"No," said Cael. "He favours his instruments. He's never once told me what he thinks I am; he says that's where his work stops, and it stops there, and if his needles said I'd gone backward he'd write it down in the same hand he wrote yesterday's note in." He thought about it. "I'd rather that than favour. Favour can change its mind."

In the corner the inky clerk ran his pen down his ruled column and set a figure in it: twenty-two minutes.

"Two left," said the man. "Then the remaining eight minutes are yours. I'd rather return them than use them up."

"Archmarshal." Cael's palms went flat on the table. The habit was Karis's; he'd caught it from her unawares. "Before the last two. Could I ask you one?"

The house's counsel turned her head. Gault did not.

"Ask," said the man. "Perhaps I'll answer, perhaps not. If not, the book records it. I mean that. It isn't manners."

"I will." Cael breathed in. "What is the Compact evaluating? Me, or the provision?"

Nobody spoke, and the river's sound came up through the window into the room.

As with every figure in the wing yesterday, he simply took it in. The chair did not creak and the hands stayed still, and nothing at all was done for show.

"The Compact filed no question," he said. "My being here carries nothing. I have no other errand and nothing written in my pocket. Your counsel will have said as much. She was right. Of everything true you've heard this month, I expect it's the hardest to swallow." He let that sit. "I came to see whether the record and the practitioner match."

"Only that?"

"Only that. What's done with my findings belongs to other men. If I did their adding for them, I'd soon be measuring toward their total." His tone did not move. "You expected an enforcer."

"I've met the enforcers."

"I expect you have." He took his hands off the table. "Then take one thing out of this room with you. I've nothing else to give, and it costs me nothing to give it, and ten years from now you may find it worth a good deal.

"Wardens enforce. Assessors comply. I evaluate. Those are three different animals, they are wearing very similar coats, and every one of them is going to be in a room with you again. The difference will matter to you more, not less, as you rise — I would encourage you to learn to read it."

The room allowed Cael a breath or two to hold it.

"How would I learn?"

"Watch what each of them does with what you hand him." The man was already on to his last two. The tenth asked whether the provision's half-yearly demand was a burden to him, and it was not; the eleventh asked whether there was anything he wanted entered in the record that nobody had asked him, and after a moment's thought he said no.

"Then we're finished, at twenty-nine minutes." He rose. The chair stayed where it was, out from the table. A man of his rank had perhaps never needed to tuck one in, or perhaps the thought had never crossed his mind. "Counsel, I'm obliged. Magister, I'm obliged. No paper on this bluff is better kept than the card on your wall, and I've seen most of them." He turned to the corner. "Clerk."

The inky clerk's head came up. He looked like a man addressed by a statue.

"A ruled column," said the man, "and a page without a blot. You'd be surprised how seldom I see either."

Then he was gone, and his steps went down the short stair at the same even pace at which they had come up it.

River light fell past the empty chair into the little whitewashed room, and Cael stayed where he was. His hands wanted to shake, he found, and his legs had not yet agreed to stand, and he let them all take their time.

At last Gault pulled the grey folder over and lifted its cover. His eyes rested on nothing in particular inside. The cover went down again.

Gault said, "That is the most competent half-hour I have sat through in eleven years, and I did not say one word in it."

Cael went down the stair some while after with one sentence in him that he did not write down yet, because he wanted to carry it for a time first and see whether it kept its shape. Every system that had ever had his name in its books had been muddled about him, and so it had asked, and the asking was where he had always found room to answer. This one had not asked. Muddled, it was not.

Chapter 57 — Seals

[Building, lucid narration; earn the crown's weight and let the final consequences land]

On the twenty-second of Reaping the residence ran out of ice before the second bell.

Brom went down to the kitchen gate for more, limping on the knee the final had left him, with an empty sack over his shoulder and his strapped hand held away from his body. He came back with the sack full and a heel of yesterday's bread, which the man at the kitchen gate had given him for nothing. The man at the kitchen gate had seen the final from the top of the north stair and had decided, apparently, that the losing finalist should not have to pay for bread for the rest of his life.

"He says I'm owed," said Brom, dividing the ice into three bags on the common-room table. "I said I lost. He said that's what he meant."

He gave the first bag to Lira, who was on the settle with the bad hip up on two cushions and her face turned to the wall in protest at the whole arrangement. Cael got the second; he had the good chair, having asked for it. The third went on his own knee as he lowered himself, grunting, to the floor by the stove.

Karis surveyed the wreckage, and something went into the grey notebook.

"Don't," said Lira, to the wall.

"It's a date. I'm writing the date." Karis blotted it. "Third morning of ice."

Cael's hip had stiffened in the night into a single line, crest to inner knee, that did not hurt so much as disagree with everything he asked of it. It would want two more mornings, by his reckoning, and the shoulder was easier already, the ache in it gone dull and edgeless like a coin carried a long time in a pocket. Brom's knee had swollen round the strapping, and his right hand still lay on his thigh where somebody had told him to keep it.

Karis had her marbled book open too, the one with the watchers in it, and she turned it so that Cael could see the last page without having to get up.

Two at the ferry landing. Two at the bluff road's foot. The change on the bell, every four hours, and a small tick for every change she had seen with her own eyes from the library's top window. There was a line for every day since the delegation came up the hill, and every line was the same as the one above it.

"Not one late," she said. "Not one extra. An Archmarshal in the building for eleven days, and the men at the bottom of the hill didn't so much as change their boots."

"They wouldn't," said Lira, without turning her head. "Nobody told them anything was happening."

"That's my point." Karis shut the book. "Nobody told them. Whatever is paying for those coats doesn't talk to whatever sent him. Or they talk, and there's nothing to tell." She put the book in her satchel. "It goes in as a question. Not as an answer."

"You write everything down as a question."

"I file things under what they are."

So they sat, and the house was quiet in a way it had not been since the carriages came: footsteps out on the quadrangle going places at an ordinary pace, and nobody in the corridor talking low.

One sentence had come down the records-hall stair with him the afternoon before, and it was still with him. He had meant to write it; he had even sat down to it at the window with the pen; and he had found he did not trust it yet. A sentence made in the first hour after a thing was usually a sentence about how the hour had felt. He wanted to know whether this one would still be standing in a day.

It was still standing, so he let it stand a while longer.

At the third bell a boy from the registrar's office came up the stair with a half-sheet for Cael, and Cael took it down to the records hall himself, slowly, with the hip complaining on every step.

Bracken had the enrollment book open on the counter, the great ruled volume the house kept its roll in, at the page that held Cael's own line. Under the entry of the first week and the baseline of the second month, Bracken had already written the new one, dated and initialled, in the small upright hand.

Semester evaluation, the twentieth of Reaping. Requirement satisfied. Standing renewed. Panel of record: Gault (presiding), with two. Inspecting delegation present, under the charter.

"I wanted you here when it went in," said Bracken. "Not because it's interesting. It's the dullest line I'll write all month." With one finger he swung the book round on the counter until the new line lay square to Cael's eye. "But it's the line every other line on this page has been waiting for. A provision only lives as long as somebody keeps writing it down."

Cael read it twice. Then he read the line above it, the baseline from his second month, and the line above that, the enrollment itself, with the folder marked in pencil Ninety-four minutes. lying beside the book where Bracken had clearly laid it on purpose.

"Thank you," he said, and then, before Bracken could open his mouth, "I know. Correct filing."

"Correct filing," said Bracken, with something that was nearly approval, and shut the book.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

The delegation's counsel had finished her work on the twenty-second, and at the eighth bell Withrow's counsel gave the house what she expected the finding to say.

She did it in the records hall, at the long table, to nine people. Withrow sat halfway down one side as she always did, with Bracken next to her and, at the corner, his inky-knuckled clerk holding a pen he had been forbidden to use. Gault had come, and Rooke had come and was standing, and the Ash instructor sat at the far end because she had signed the evaluation and liked to know what became of her signatures. Karis had a chair because the provision's file began with her name. Cael was there because the provision was his.

The counsel stood with her hands on her leather case and spoke in the voice she kept for notices.

"Favourable in substance. Neutral in tone."

Nobody moved.

"Those six words are the whole of it," she said. "The rest is detail. There will be one clerical remark. There is always one, because a delegation that finds nothing at all looks to its own masters as though it had not been looking. Last time it was the fire-watch's oil book. I would wager a month's fee it's the oil book again." Her fingers worked the clasp of the case open, and shut it again on nothing. "The enrollment basis will be found sound. Alive, the clause; fitted to it, the enrollment. The documentary practice will be called complete, which is the highest word the form allows. It will not say we did well. A finding cannot say that. Its whole message will be that nobody found anything."

"After all that," said Gault.

"After eleven days of being looked at by an Archmarshal." The counsel looked at Withrow. "If I were writing for the newsletters I would call that a triumph."

"You aren't," said Withrow.

"No. And you've told me more than once that you dislike adjectives, so I struck it before I came in." Her voice did not change at all. "I mention that I struck it so that it's in the room."

Withrow took her spectacles off and folded them.

"I dislike them on paper," she said. "On paper they rot. Somebody reads them in ten years and wonders what you were frightened of." She put the spectacles in her pocket. "Here you may say what you please. Say it again."

The counsel weighed this with her eyes on the beams.

"A triumph," she said, perfectly flat, as if it were the name of a ship.

Rooke made a sound by the fireplace that might, in another man, have been a laugh. Bracken's clerk wrote something after all and was looked at, and stopped.

Cael sat at the table's foot and watched Withrow. She had not smiled; she had sat through the whole inspection without once raising her voice or her pace, and she was not going to start now that the coaches were being greased. Through every sitting her hands had lain flat on the table, and now they had turned over. They lay palm up on the wood, open and loose, like the hands of somebody who has set down a weight at the end of a long carry and has not yet thought to pick anything else up.

He wrote that in the notebook afterward, on the page headed Withrow, in three lines. Of everything he had watched her do since the first week, it was the one thing she had not chosen.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Brom told them about Rooke at supper, and he told it word for word.

Brom did not often do that. He remembered exact words better than most people remembered faces, but he kept the gift in a drawer and took it out perhaps twice a year, when he thought a sentence had been made with care and ought not to be worn down by handling. He took it out now with his bowl in front of him and his strapped hand flat beside the bowl.

"The cohort's board, by the covered walk's end. Third bell, near enough. I was reading the cohort standings." He set down his spoon. "He came along the walk. He didn't stop to talk to me, he stopped to look at the board. Then he said it to the board."

"Said what?" asked Lira.

Brom said it in Rooke's voice, which was a dry voice that did not lift at the end of anything.

"'Your cohort standing holds. So, apparently, does your friend's paperwork. Noted.'"

There was a pause.

"That's it?"

"That's it."

Lira put her spoon down. "That's nothing. A man's been calling the provision a mistake since the first week, in a faculty session, with the clerk writing it down, and he says noted to a board on his way past?"

"It isn't nothing." Brom turned his bowl a quarter turn on the table, the way he squared a guard. "He minuted that he was against it. He said so where it would be written down. Every faculty session since, it's been in the book that Rooke said the provision would cost the house." He looked at his hand. "Wrong is a word he won't say, not about himself. What he does is change what he does, and then make sure it's been seen." The hand rose an inch from the wood and settled again. "He adjusted, and he made sure somebody heard him do it."

"You," said Karis.

"Me. Because I'd tell you, and he knew I'd tell you, and he knew I'd tell it straight." Brom picked up his spoon again. "That's his apology. He sent it by carter."

Lira looked at him for some time.

"You like him," she said.

"I don't like him. He's made me worse for a whole season on purpose." Brom ate a spoonful of stew. "Then he made me better, on the day it counted, and I lost by one beat anyway. I don't like him. I'd go through a wall for him."

Cael thought of the north arch on the day the notice came, and Rooke standing under it with the traffic of the bell going round him. He had corrected himself to Cael there, once, out loud and unasked. This was the same man doing the same thing at a greater distance, so that nobody could call it a kindness.

He does it with documents, Cael thought. Even when there's no document. He talks so that it'll be in somebody's book.

He wrote it in his own book that night, under Rooke's name, with the date.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency, never rushed]

By the first bell of the twenty-third it was raining, not hard, a fine grey rain that came up the river in no hurry and settled on everything. The three carriages stood in the courtyard below the records hall with their shutters up and the horses steaming.

Cael stood high on the Crown yard's top tier. From the same east-end stone he had watched the delegation's arrival, and some time in the night he had decided to watch its going from there too. A person who had seen a thing arrive from out in the open had no business watching it leave from under a roof. The tier was empty and lawful, and the wet came across it off the river in slants and beaded on his sleeves.

Below him the leaving went forward in its order. Porters wheeled the iron-banded chests out of the records hall on a handbarrow and set them down under the porch, where somebody had rigged a run of canvas to keep them dry. The escort walked the horses up and down the cobbles. The delegation's counsel came out talking, with her clerk behind her holding an oilcloth over a box, and climbed into the second carriage without pausing in her sentence. The three clerks came after her in their order: the young one carrying, the list clerk walking beside him, the old one with the bad knee pointing at things.

Withrow stood on the records-hall steps in her plain coat with Bracken a pace behind her. She shook the counsel's hand at the carriage door and said something short, and Bracken handed up a receipt for the house's copies, which the counsel signed on her knee.

The Archmarshal had gone to his carriage before the rain started, and Cael had not seen him go, and found to his surprise that he did not mind.

Last of the manifest came Assessor Ilsev, carrying her own case down the steps herself. Porters had offered to carry it every day of the visit and been refused every time, so politely that two of them had started offering just to hear how she would do it.

At the last step she halted and lifted her face to the tier, rain and all.

Cael went down, because staying up there would have been a kind of hiding, and he had done enough of that in his life to know it when he saw it.

She waited for him at the foot of the steps, the case held in front of her in both hands.

"Enrollee."

"Assessor."

"You were at the table on the fifteenth," said Ilsev. "So you heard what was found. Tell me what it was."

He thought about it first, because she was not a woman who asked a question to fill a silence.

"That the clause was never struck out," he said. "That my enrollment matches what it says."

"Yes. Now tell me what it was about."

"The clause."

"The clause." She nodded. He had passed a small test, and she had not expected him to fail it. "Not you. A handful of people wrote that sentence long ago, for their own reasons, about practitioners none of them had met. They never heard of you and could not have. If they had written one word differently, the finding on the fifteenth would have gone the other way. And you would be standing in this rain just as you are now, no better and no worse." She shifted the case to one hand. "I'm saying this because it isn't kind. Don't take it for kindness."

"I won't."

"Good. People like you nearly always hope that a text which favours them is passing judgment on them. It isn't. It is simply on your side, which is worth an enormous amount and is not the same as being loved by anybody."

The rain fell between them. At one corner of her mouth something moved, very slightly, and was put away again before it could become anything.

"Keep those two apart all your life," said Ilsev. "I've sat across from people who couldn't. They were dreadful company at a table. They also lost."

She turned and walked to the second carriage and got in, and did not look back. Cael stayed at the foot of the tier stair with the rain running out of his hair, and felt no cold at all.

He had a page on her, the thickest in the book and, until now, the least use. He knew already what he would write on it tonight. She told me the truth about the law and called it unkind, so that I would know it was true.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Havel checked the seals.

He did it under the records-hall porch, out of the rain, with the list on a board against his forearm and the chests set down in a row in front of him on the flags. There were four of them, and they had come up the bluff road under four seals apiece, and they would go down it under four new ones, pressed that morning at the delegation's working table in the counsel's wax and the senior seat's. His list had sixteen lines, one for each seal, and beside each line the impression's number and the hand that had pressed it.

Pencil in hand, he worked down the list. Chest one, the lid's left, a clean impression, the number legible. Tick. The lid's right. Tick. The hasp. Tick.

It did not matter that he had watched every one of them pressed. He had watched, and he had written the numbers as they were pressed, and now he was checking the wax against what he had written. Nobody would ever check after him: the chests would go into the registry's vault at the end of the road, and a vault clerk would sign for four chests, not sixteen seals. The check was his and nobody else's, and so he did it slowly.

Somebody had fixed a long run of canvas along the porch roof to keep the rain off the chests. It made the light inside the porch brown and close, so that the courtyard beyond it looked very bright, though it was not bright at all.

He knew where the boy was.

He had known on the first morning, because he had worked it out on the road from the plan of the yard, and he had been right, because he had seen the shape on the upper tier at the edge of his eye as the carriage came in and had not turned his head. He had not turned his head since. Not on the covered walk on the thirteenth, with the two streams jammed against the dry wall. Not at the final, from the second row of the north tier. Not at the long table on the fifteenth, nor across the brass of the wing on the twentieth. Eleven days.

That was correct, since the card in his pocket said that an officer of an inspecting delegation would not acknowledge a party under review beyond ordinary courtesy. A records officer checking seals under a porch had no business with the upper tier of a training yard, courteous or otherwise. Correct, then; and so he did it.

It was not why he did it.

Chest two. The lid's left. The wax had run a little at one edge, and he bent close to read the number through it, and it was the right number. Tick.

Asked, he would have offered the reason he had given himself at the gate. A look from a man in his coat was a thing the boy would have to carry. He would have to write it down somewhere and decide what it had meant, and then decide again in a month when he knew more. Havel had watched the boy's face at the pump step in Ardenmere, two years ago, and he had watched it at the end of a long hearing table at Greyvane. He had seen what it cost the boy to be looked at by men in that coat. A records officer could not do much about that, but he could decline to add to it.

True. But not the whole of it.

The rest was the pear. He had never been able to put the pear into any sentence that made sense, and he did not try now. A boy on a pump step had held out a pear in a twist of paper to the officer questioning him, and the officer had wanted it and had not taken it. Ever since, Havel had felt that he had been offered something once that he had not been entitled to refuse. A man who has refused a thing like that does not go looking up at tiers afterward. He does not get a second offer, and he ought not to look as though he were hoping for one.

He went down the list. Chest three. Chest four. Sixteen ticks.

The registrar came out under the canvas while he was initialling the foot of the sheet. The house kept a log of its own of what went out of its doors, and somebody had to sign the house's side of it, and Bracken was not a man who sent a clerk to sign a thing he could sign himself.

"Sixteen?" said Bracken.

"Sixteen."

Bracken checked for himself. He went along the row and looked at each seal for about as long as it takes to read a number, and wrote a figure in his own small book, and then held the book out for Havel's initials beside his. Havel gave them, and neither man remarked on what the other had just done; it would have been like remarking that the other had a nose.

Havel had sat at the foot of the long table on the fifteenth while that man's index was turned over by the best counsel the delegation had, sheet by sheet, for most of a day, and had watched it find every paper she asked for inside a minute and a half. He had never been in a position to tell a registrar that his file was good, and he was not in one now. He could hand back a book with his initials in the right column and his eyes on the right line, and so he did that.

"Safe road," said Bracken, which was ordinary courtesy, and went back in.

At the foot of the steps the assessor had stopped. Havel saw it without looking, the way he saw everything he did not look at: a grey shape halting where grey shapes walked on. Then another shape came down from the tier to meet her. Their voices did not carry under the canvas. He bent to the fourth chest's hasp, though he had already ticked it, and read its number again.

She had a referral in her case; he knew, because he had logged it. It had gone up a level inside the first recess on the fifteenth, three sheets cross-referenced in his own hand, and it would go into the chain at the end of this road. Somewhere above them both a desk would get it, and the desk would either answer or not. He thought it would not. Nothing had ever come back with a name on it.

There were four lines in his notebook now, and a fifth would not be written on this hill, because there was nothing to put in it that the fourth had not already said.

The porters lifted the first chest onto the boot of the second carriage. Havel walked beside it with the list and watched them strap it, and initialled the list at the foot, and gave the list to the young clerk to carry, because the young clerk carried. Then he got in.

He sat where he had sat coming up: in the second carriage, facing backward, with the counsel's knees an inch from his own. The counsel had begun to talk about the inn at the turn of the river road, and whether its beds had been aired since the last delegation, which had been hers. Ilsev was already in her corner with her case on her knees and her eyes shut.

The carriage moved, and facing backward, Havel had the whole bluff in his window as they went down it: the gate, the wall, the long grey range with its tiers open to the rain. It drew away from him a bend at a time.

His eyes went down to the list in his lap, where every line had its tick. He went down it once more anyway, from the top, line by line, until the road had turned enough that the bluff was behind the shoulder of the hill and there was nothing in the window but rain and the river and the ferry landing, where two men in road-grey coats stood under a lamp just as they had stood on the morning he arrived.

Across from him the counsel broke off her sentence about the inn.

"You were a long while over those seals," she said. "Was anything wrong with them?"

"No."

"Then why so long?"

Havel thought about how to answer that within his instructions, and found that the true answer was inside them after all.

"Nobody checks them after me," he said.

The counsel looked at him with her head on one side, the way she looked at a clause she had not expected to like. Then she took up her sentence about the inn again from the exact word where she had left it.

Correct and careful, he thought. They were not the same thing, and on most days he managed both.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

In a quarter of an hour the carriages were off the bluff, and the road below the gate was empty except for the rain. Cael lingered.

Havel had come out of the records hall with the chests and stood under the canvas with his list, ticking. He had not raised his eyes. Cael had seen him not raise them. A man checking wax at a porch has a dozen small reasons to lift his head, a horse moving or a voice or the rain changing, and Havel had lifted it for none of them.

Eleven days. On the first morning Cael had put it down as caution, because anyone in that coat had reasons to be careful where his eyes went. In the second week he had stopped being sure. Caution looks at a thing and then away. This was a man who had worked out where the thing was and then built his whole day round not looking there, as carefully as another man would have built it round looking.

Somewhere a word for it existed, and Cael let it be. A name was a guess, and he had made enough guesses about men in grey coats to last him a long while. He wrote it down without one.

Lira came down the residence passage after supper without the stick. Her four days had ended that afternoon, and she was walking the length of the passage and back as the safety instructor had told her to, slowly, with one hand trailing along the wall and her face daring anybody to comment.

At his open door she paused, eyes on the ice on his hip.

"Three days for you," she said.

"Ends tonight."

"Four for me. Ended at the fourth bell." Behind her the passage was long; ahead of her, longer. She weighed both. "We're a fine pair. Brom says he's going to buy a barrow and wheel the pair of us to lectures and charge the first-years to watch."

"He won't."

"He might. He's been free with his money since the man at the gate stopped charging him for bread." She pushed off from the doorframe. "Write your thing. You've had it in your mouth all day like a stone."

She went on down the passage, one hand on the wall, counting her steps under her breath, and he listened to her turn at the far end and come back past his door without stopping.

That night at the window the first sentence would not sit for Hesk's pen.

Try one was too clever; he struck it. He wrote it again and it spent half its length explaining itself before it said anything, and he struck that too. The third time he stopped trying to say what it meant and wrote down only what had happened.

He never asked what I am.

Count the rooms. Coss asked it with his whole coat. Quenna asked once, never again, and taught me anyway. Gault won't ask it, says so to my face, and keeps saying so. Ephram turned it into a promise to wait, out loud, on the yard. This bluff has answered it among itself at supper more ways than I've bothered to write down.

The Archmarshal had eleven questions and didn't ask it once. His business was the fit between paper and person.

I've turned that over since the east room. Here's what it comes to.

If you don't know what a thing is, you ask. If you think you already know, you don't ask. You go and look at the paper, and then at the thing, and see whether whoever kept the paper kept it properly. That's what he did. He came to audit a file. The file was about me; that's all I was in it.

So somebody, somewhere, has already written down an answer to what I am, too high for Karis and me to reach with a whole library to stand on. Whatever it says, it was settled before he came up the hill. His work was checking. Doing something about it belongs to other men. He told me so across the table, and I believe him. He'd no reason to lie to me and every habit against it.

Bare, then, with nothing on it:

The system isn't confused about me.

Confused systems ask. This one checks.

For two years the word I've had for myself is gap: the thing that fell between badly drawn lines. I argued it at Greyvane. I'd argue it tomorrow and win again, because it's true.

But look at what a gap gets. Nothing. Nobody watches a gap. Nobody writes a designation for one and files it where no name comes back. Nobody sends the best evaluator they own to sit four feet from a gap and then leave its biggest question alone on purpose.

Two lines for the list, then. First: what that paper says, and who decided it. Second: why anybody would build a whole apparatus that knows a thing like that before the boy has done anything at all.

Not this year's. This year's question was whether I could hold. I held on the twentieth. A clerk stamped it.

Those are next.

He read it through and changed nothing, then blotted it and shut the book, and sat for a while with his hand flat on the cover and the rain going on outside. The ice went to bed with him, and he slept better than he had any right to.

Chapter 58 — Null Report

[Building, lucid narration; earn the crown's weight and let the final consequences land]

The afternoon paper reached the assessment wing on the twenty-fourth a little after the fourth bell, and the delegation's closing docket was in it.

It was a single sheet under the delegation's green seal, with a slip pinned at one corner by a brass pin that had been bent and straightened at least once before. The paper-boy dropped it with the others at the counter's end and went off whistling. The desk clerk was four feet away with the term's floor ledger open in front of him, adding a column under his breath and losing his place every time the whistling reached the stair. So it was Seln who signed for the docket, because signing was the counter's work, and Seln who read it.

It discharged the loan. The wing's compilation of six filings, requisitioned on the evening of the twelfth, had been received, examined, and returned under the delegation's stamp. Below that, in a clerk's round hand, came the line the form required and nobody ever read: No extract or copy retained. And under that, a signature he knew from the wing's own ledger, the list clerk's, on the delegation's behalf.

He filed it in the requisitions book, in its place, and blotted the entry. Anyone watching would have seen that and nothing more.

The file itself had come home ten days before.

It had come at the sixth bell of the fourteenth, carried in by the delegation's list clerk with Returned with thanks and a receipt on its face. The desk clerk had signed for it. Seln had risen from the copying table and taken the case in both hands and set it on the shelf behind him among the wing's other sealed things, with a boy from the provision standing at the counter for his floor sheet, and he had not looked at it again while the room had people in it.

From the evening of the twelfth, when the stack went across to the guest floor, until that sixth bell of the fourteenth, he had waited for four minutes alone with it. He had made no arrangement of any kind to be the one who handled it when it came; he had not needed to, since it was his table.

When the counter was clear, and the boy gone, and the desk clerk gone down to his supper, he took the case down to the copying table and untied the knot.

In four minutes he went over every sheet with his eyes and every edge with the side of his thumb.

A paper that has been read carries the reading on it, if you know where to feel. Corners go soft where a thumb has held them back. A pin worked loose and pushed home again leaves the hole a fraction rounder. A stack that has lain open under a lamp for an evening comes back faintly warm-smelling, of tallow and of the room it lay in. He had spent two years of his youth learning to feel those things in the dark, and he felt for all of them now with the face of a man checking a count.

Six filings, in their order, each with its appendix pinned behind it. On top, his own index, in his fourth hand. And on none of it a single mark. No pencil, faint or otherwise. No turned corner. No pin moved from the hole it had been put through. No slip tucked in, and none taken out, and no fold that had not been there when the stack went across. An evaluation seat had held it for two days, with every right in the charter to write in its margins, and had handed it back as clean as a sheet still in the ream.

Then he had tied the knot again as it had been, and shelved the case, and gone down to his own supper at the pace a clerk keeps when nothing has happened.

And now the docket said No extract or copy retained. A reader who kept no copy, and wrote nothing on the original, had kept whatever he thought somewhere else.

His first master, at the long table up the coast, had chalked a thing on the board for new auditors once, and Seln had copied it into the back of a book at twenty-two and never needed the book since. A clean return is one of three. Not read. Read and passed. Read by a man who keeps his notes in his head. The first was common and the second was commoner. The third, the old man had said, rubbing it out again with his sleeve, you would meet perhaps twice in a career, and only ever at one height.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

Two evenings later, in his room on the staff corridor, Seln sat down to the quarterly with the shutter fastened and the lamp low.

Of the form's five parts, four were furniture, and he had filled them so often that his hand did them without much help from him. Coverage held from the first day, by way of nothing but the posting's ordinary work. The subject's days, set out in full across a page and a half: floor hours under supervision, lectures, the library, the ladder from its gallery, the wing's own unit, a habit of private writing, a handful of letters posted in the open to people already on file. No one had ever written down the boy's days more truly, and none of it would tell a reader anything. Associations unchanged since the bridge. The inspection, the delegation, the sittings, the observed evaluation, all entered in a voice a harbour clerk keeps for tides.

Then came the fifth part, which the posting was for, and it took him longer than the other four put together, and when it was done it was four lines long.

Assessment of period: routine compliance.

No undisclosed capability observed.

Subject's conduct consistent with enrollment basis.

Continuation of embedded coverage recommended.

He laid the pen in the gutter of the desk and read them over, and changed nothing.

He tried the first three the way the old man at the long table had taught him to try another officer's work: pretending a stranger had written each one and Seln were being paid by the fault. The boy had complied with everything the house asked of him all term. Observed, in the manual, meant observed under conditions that allowed confirmation, and that was a narrow door, and nothing had come through it. The enrollment basis was evaluation by demonstration; the boy had demonstrated in front of the Compact's best eyes and been renewed. Each line bore weight. He had learned over a term, a sentence at a time, how much weight a true line would bear before it cracked, and he had loaded each of these three to that mark and not a hair beyond.

The fourth bore everything else.

There was nothing in it; it was the most ordinary line the form allowed. A briefing officer meets that line at the foot of one report in three, the year round, and ticks it the way a man nods to a neighbour. All it would do was leave a Bronze clerk at his copying table, minding other men's mistakes, through another term.

There was a reason he had written it, and it was not on the form, or on any page anywhere: not in his own cipher, not in the small case, not in a word to anybody on the bluff. He had made nobody a promise and no arrangement with a living soul. For a term he had gone on setting down true sentences and had stopped setting down some others, and that was all, except for one slip of wing paper.

He had cut it himself with the wing's knife, small enough to lie flat inside a coursework folder and thin enough to catch at once. No signature, and a hand that was nobody's. Shaped to be burned, it had very likely been burned. Of all the things that had ever passed between him and the boy, it was the nearest to a conversation. It existed nowhere now, which was where he kept conversations.

Signature, extracts, seal. The packet went to stand against the door frame, ready for the fish steps at first light.

There remained the day's page, folded in his inside pocket.

Four lines, in the fifth hand, the shorthand that had grown out of the cramped one. The date the carriages left. The serial of the reserve frame, copied from the wing's maintenance book. The date the file had come back, the fourteenth, and the docket's date beside it. And one line under them that was not a fact at all, of the kind he let himself write perhaps twice a year.

unmarked file. one of three. probably the third.

He fetched the key from the hollow spine of the harbour-dues treatise and knelt on the boards, and the draught under the door got into his sleeves at once, and his knees made their usual remarks. Out from under the bed came the large case; up came the shirts; and there underneath, as it had been in every room for years, lay the small one, its leather gone soft and its brass corners dull.

The new page went on top. Below it lay whatever lay below it, and he did not lift it or count it. A locked case was worth precisely as much as nobody's knowing what it held, and not looking was part of the lock.

He locked it. Shirts back; large case home under the bed and hard against the wall; then his shoulder to the foot of the bed, and the bed walked back after it until the frame met plaster. His body did that in every room without asking him.

The lamp went out under his fingers, but he did not lie down. At the bed's edge, in the dark, he stayed sitting, his hands empty.

What he kept, he kept.

[Steady, observant narration; let place, distance, and social position register]

The unit met on the twenty-fifth at the sixth bell in the long room that had been a map store, and it went as it had gone every Third-day since the first one.

Seln set an exercise on the slate in the round copying hand: A door, a window, a lamp. Where does a person entering first look? Where last? Show your reasons. Then he walked the room while they worked, slowly, down one side of the long table and up the other, as he always did, never stopping behind anyone for longer than it took to read a line. A sentence put a third-year's sums right; a pencil dot mended a Stone girl's sketch. He did not look at Cael; in all the weeks of the unit his eyes had never once rested on Cael in that room, and they did not now. When the porter reached the arch, Seln gathered the sheets, knocked them square on the table, and dismissed them with the porter's name.

Gwen had drawn a small eye at the foot of hers, as she did at the foot of everything. On the way out she told Cael that she had seen the Archmarshal's carriage go and had felt, watching it, as if somebody had taken a heavy pan off a stove she had not known was lit.

Cael pointed out that she had never once laid eyes on the man himself, not in eleven days.

"I know," said Gwen. "That's what made it so frightening." She wound her green scarf twice round her neck. "My aunt says the ones you never see are the ones doing the work. She says that about cooks too."

The next day he wrote to Hesk.

No letter since Ardenmere had given him so much trouble. He sat over it most of an evening, because what he had to tell Hesk would not sit up and look like news, however he dressed it. An Archmarshal came to look at me for eleven days, and he has gone, and I do not know what he decided. That was the whole of it, and everything else was decoration.

So he wrote it plainly, the way Hesk liked letters to come. He copied out the last lines of Gault's note, word for word, with the stamp described. He gave the east room a paragraph and no more: the size of it, the light, eleven questions and a twelfth that was not asked. He did not say what the twelfth would have been, or what it would have cost him. He wrote, at the end, I'm well, the hip is mending, Lira won, and you'll have heard by now that the pen writes better than I do.

On his way back from the library that afternoon he had stopped at the wing's counter with the week's coursework. Seln was at the copying table, as he was every afternoon, and when the desk clerk waved a hand at the tray Seln got up and took the sheet from Cael and read the head of it and laid it in the tray, face down, square to the others.

"Thank you for the form," said Cael.

"Mm," said Seln, and sat down again.

It had been the same three words and the one sound every week since the counter had first been opened to him. On the way out he kept his mind off it. He had trained himself, over weeks, not to think about it until he was past the covered walk's north arch, and then not to think about it there either.

He read the finished letter over twice before he folded it. It was true in every line, and it left out the only part of the fortnight he could not have explained to anyone: that a man had walked up to the edge of him and stopped, and that he had not known until that moment that he had spent his whole life waiting for somebody to do it. That part did not belong in a letter. For now it belonged inside his coat, and maybe nowhere else.

He sealed it and took it to the courier post himself in the morning, and walked back up the bluff road in a thin wind past the two men at the foot of it, who changed on the bell as he went by and did not look at him at all.

[Focused, lucid narration; give the system detail and the character's inference equal weight]

Toward evening on the twenty-seventh a hand-cart came across the second quadrangle with Karis behind it.

Cael saw her from the covered walk. It was a library cart, the low kind with iron wheels that the porters used for returns, and it was loaded with a pasteboard box and a stack of books under an oilcloth, and Karis was pushing it at a pace that a hand-cart on cobbles did not like. One of the wheels had a flat place and knocked at every turn, and she did not slow down for it.

Two first-years crossing toward the lecture range stood aside for her with their mouths open. A porter carrying a ladder stopped, considered the cart, considered Karis, and decided it was none of his business.

He caught up with her where the records hall's corner met the walk.

"What—"

"Don't ask." She did not stop pushing. "Not yet. I'll tell all of you at once, and I'll tell it once. Take the other handle."

He took the other handle.

At the steps Bracken's inky-knuckled clerk was coming out with a bundle of dockets. He looked at the cart, and at the oilcloth, and at Karis's face, and then held the door wide for them both without being asked, and went on down the steps.

They went in by the records hall's main door and through the stone hall and up the back stair. The cart would not climb a stair, so they carried the load up in their arms in three goes, while the cart waited at the bottom like a patient dog. Karis had a key on her wrist, and it opened a door on the top floor at the end of a passage Cael had never had reason to walk down, into a narrow room with a table and a window and a card in a brass frame on the door. The card said, in Bracken's upright hand, Reading room. Assigned: K. Dellenmoor.

The ink on it was fresh.

"Bracken," said Cael.

"Bracken." The pasteboard box went onto the table, squared to its edge. "I went to the counter an hour ago and asked for a named room on the top floor. He looked at me. He took a card out of a drawer and wrote my name on it and gave me the key. He didn't ask what for." She straightened. "I counted. Ninety seconds, from my mouth opening to the key in my hand."

Her eyes stayed on the card, and Cael watched her decide not to think about it yet. He knew the look; he had seen it on her face over a dozen documents she meant to come back to.

There were three more loads after that one. The founding-era copies, in their folders. Two bound books of the repeal search. Prynn's index, which Karis carried up the stair herself and would not let him touch. Last of all came the two notebooks from Greyvane, in their oilcloth, and Karis carried those up in both arms against her chest and put them on the table, and then stood for a long breath with her hand flat on the top one.

Halfway through the second notebook was a page Cael knew, and Karis knew it too. Neither of them said so.

On the last trip she stopped at the head of the stair with the Greyvane notebooks held against her coat and looked back down it, the whole steep flight of it, to the stone hall at the bottom.

"I never once thought about where they slept," she said. "Half a year in that carrel. I thought about the light and the chair and whether the door shut. I never thought about what the room was, on paper." She shifted the weight in her arms. "I write about the meaning of words for a living, and I never read the word on my own door."

"You'd no reason to."

"That's what everybody says before the sweep." She went on up the passage.

When the room was full, she locked it, and hung the key on her wrist, and wheeled the empty cart back across the quadrangle to the library, with the flat wheel knocking all the way. Then she went to fetch Lira and Brom.

[Dry, precise narration; keep the institutional language clear and the pressure understated]

She gave it to them with the common-room door shut, reading from the page she had written standing in the corridor. Her pencil had gone through the paper in two places, and she seemed unaware of it.

"The corridor from the records hall to the library's east stair. Fifth bell. I was heading for the library," Karis read. "He was coming the other way with a box of forms. The teaching assistant." She looked up once and down again. "He stopped. I've walked past that man four hundred times and he has never stopped. He stood against the shelving to let me by, which anybody would. And then he said, 'Miss Karis.'"

Brom's hands went still on his knee.

"I said yes. He said, 'Records retention.' The box shifted onto his hip." She read on in the same voice, flat, like a clerk reading a deed. "'The inspection cycle closes on the tenth of next month. After every inspection the registrar's office takes in whatever's been left in the house's shared research spaces. Fourth part of the charter. It goes under the house's accession, catalogued, for good. Loose papers as well as bound.' I said I knew what an archive sweep was. He said: 'Then you'll know researchers sometimes prefer to avoid it. The law range's carrels are shared, as the charter defines it. A top-floor reading room, once it's assigned to a name, isn't.'" She turned the page over. The back was blank. "Then he said 'Mm,' and went on."

Nobody said anything.

Lira spoke first. She had been stretched on the settle with her eyes shut, and now she opened them.

"The law range. He didn't say the carrels. He said the law range."

"He named the range," said Karis.

"And there's one of us with a carrel in it."

Brom frowned. "Is it real? The sweep. Or did he make it up to frighten you into moving?"

"It's real. I had the charter out of the records hall inside the hour. Fourth part, near the back. It runs on the tenth, the way he said, and it takes working papers." Her voice held, but her pencil, lying on the table, rolled a little where her hand had knocked it. "Every word he said is ordinary. Any enrollee could have got the lot from a clerk by asking the right question at the counter. No panel could be shown a word of it. Not one sentence."

Brom had taken his iced knee off the stool and put both feet on the floor, as he did when a thing needed his whole weight. "Then he knew where your notebooks live."

"Karis," said Lira.

Karis stopped. She put both palms on the table, and when she spoke again it was slower.

"He knew where the notebooks were since the third week of term. Carrels go through the wing's floor and space book. He keeps the book. He's known where my papers sleep since the day he first opened that book." Her eyes went down to the wood between her hands. "What's written in them he's known for however long. A week. A month. Since the first day. That's the one thing I'll never find out."

Cael was at the window, where he had drifted while she read. He went there when he wanted his face out of the room; not one of them had ever said so.

"And not a word of it went down the river," said Lira to his back.

He did not answer at once, but came back from the window instead, and held out his hand to Karis, and she understood and gave him the marbled book from her satchel. He opened it on the table where all three could see.

"The day after the pin. Read it."

Karis found it with one finger. "Two at the landing. Two at the road's foot. Change on the bell."

"When Bracken's four boxes crossed the quadrangle."

"Two and two. On the bell."

"The day the notice came. The delegation's arrival. The day they left."

She turned the pages and read each one, and each one was the same line in the same hand.

"Whoever pays those coats changes them inside a fortnight when a report gets interesting," said Cael. "I've watched it happen twice in my life. If anything with the true thing in it had gone down that river since the pin, this book would have a different line in it somewhere. It hasn't." He closed the marbled boards. "The Log's had that since before my birthday. I've never found a way to say what it means that didn't sound like hoping. So I stopped saying it."

He gave the book back to her.

"Tonight he told us."

Karis shook her head. "He didn't tell us anything. That's the point of it. Write down every word he said and you'll have a timetable. Not one sentence of it says what we all heard."

"No. Not one." Cael sat. "That's his language. It's the only one he owns. A man who can be read loses his post, so he talks the one way nobody can read: like a clerk passing on a timetable. Tonight, then, he picked the one person on this bluff who'd be finished if those papers were read, recited her a timetable, and stood aside while she carried them up a stair."

On the settle Lira tipped her head back against the arm and considered the plaster.

Then she said, "So that's what he is now."

Cael said, "That's what he's been since the pin. He just let us see it."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly and let the relationship carry it]

Brom asked the question that had been on all their faces.

"You've thought that about him for months. You said so at the window. What changed tonight?"

"Up to tonight, all he did was leave things out." Without noticing, Cael had laid his hands flat on the wood, the way Karis did; he had caught the habit somewhere in the term and stopped minding. "Leaving out costs nothing. It's like a feint you never throw: nobody can score it. Haul him before a board and he'd say the threshold was never met. They'd have a stack of true reports and nothing else, and they'd have to dig a reason out of what he didn't write. That's why he's done it that way. It's craft."

"And tonight?"

"Omission is free," said Cael. "Tonight he performed an act." He let them hear it. "He stopped. On his own account, in a corridor, four days after an inspection went down the hill, he picked something up and carried it across a line on purpose. It was small. He could deny every word. It's the most careful way it could ever have been done. Still, he did it. With his own mouth, for papers that aren't even mine."

Cael kept back one thing. Before tonight there had been a single other act, folded small, and the common-room stove, and Karis at the hearthrug watching it go up. It had been made for one reader and made not to last, and he had settled long since that no spoken sentence of his would ever hold it. Karis kept it back too. She always had, and she did now.

This one had somebody standing in the corridor to hear it, and that was what made it different.

"So what do we do?" said Brom.

"Nothing."

"Nothing at all?"

"Nothing at all. Nobody thanks him. Nobody nods to him on the walk. Nobody changes one thing about how they come into that wing." Cael had settled it at the window and turned it over twice since, and it had held both times. "Coursework goes over the counter, and I say thank you for the form. That's all. Same as every week."

"That's a hard thing to do to a man," said Lira, from the settle.

"It's the only safe thing there is to do to him." His eyes went round the three of them. "Think how he's made his life. Nobody can prove a word about him. There's one way that breaks. Somebody who's grateful decides he ought to know it." He let that settle. "Gratitude is the leak. Not a report. Not an audit. It's a kind word, on the stair, some morning, to the wrong man."

Brom thought about it, slowly, the way he thought about a guard he did not like.

"Like a post," he said at last. "You don't thank a post for holding. You stop leaning on it where people can see."

"Yes. Like that."
